1e26brwaxft: All matter is made of atoms: a tiny nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons. Nuclear energy comes from the forces that hold that nucleus together.
29mjfcwl4gb: Everything around us, from air to steel, is made of **atoms**. An atom is the smallest portion of a chemical element that retains its properties: an iron atom is still iron, but if we split it, we no longer have iron. The word comes from the Greek *átomos*, “indivisible”, because the philosophers Leucippus and Democritus imagined in the 5th century BC that matter must be made of pieces that could not be divided any further. Today we know that the atom does have parts, and that the way they are held together conceals the energy of nuclear weapons, of reactors and of the Sun itself.
o2ubyqe2x: Diagram of an atom: a nucleus with protons (positive charge) and neutrons (no charge), and electrons around it. The true proportions are impossible to draw: at this scale the nucleus would be invisible.
xglo8ahl0w: **Protons**: particles with a positive electric charge that live in the nucleus. Their number, called the *atomic number* (Z), defines the element: every atom with 1 proton is hydrogen, with 6 it is carbon, with 92 it is [[uranio|uranium]] and with 94 it is [[plutonio|plutonium]].
16gyk0i3yrs: **Neutrons**: particles of almost the same mass as the proton but with no electric charge. They are also found in the nucleus. Because they have no charge, a free neutron can approach another nucleus without being repelled, which is why it is the “bullet” that triggers [[fision|fission]].
3p6gsq8zxt: **Electrons**: negatively charged particles about 1,836 times lighter than a proton, which occupy the region surrounding the nucleus. They are responsible for all of chemistry: bonds, reactions and, therefore, the energy of [[explosivos-convencionales|conventional explosives]].
3vtaw8c0ks: The sum of protons and neutrons is the *mass number* (A). Thus uranium-235 has 92 protons and 143 neutrons, which add up to 235. Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons are [[isotopos|isotopes]].
sadbxtmq6m: An atom measures about one ten-billionth of a metre (0.1 nanometres). Its nucleus is between ten thousand and a hundred thousand times smaller. If the atom were a football stadium, the nucleus would be a chickpea in the centre of the pitch and the electrons would be specks of dust drifting around the stands. And yet that chickpea holds more than 99.9% of the mass. Ordinary matter is, in reality, almost entirely empty space.
mmoykrduw8: The nucleus poses a puzzle: protons all carry a positive charge and, at such short distances, they repel one another with an enormous force. Why does it not fly apart? Because there is another interaction, the **strong nuclear force**, which attracts protons and neutrons to one another with an intensity far greater than the electric repulsion, but only at distances the size of a nucleus. Beyond that, it all but vanishes. The Japanese physicist Hideki Yukawa proposed the first theory of this force in 1935, which earned him the Nobel Prize in 1949.
11da88bs1az: This competition between two forces explains almost everything that follows. In light nuclei the strong force dominates comfortably. In very heavy ones, such as uranium, there are so many protons that the electric repulsion, which acts over a longer range, begins to gain ground: the nucleus is like a water drop that is too large, trembling and on the verge of splitting. That is why the heaviest elements are [[radiactividad|radioactive]] and some of them can undergo fission.
bn3sojytgu: If we precisely weigh a helium nucleus and compare it with the sum of the two protons and two neutrons that make it up, we discover something surprising: the nucleus weighs *less* than its pieces taken separately. This difference is called the **mass defect**. The “missing” mass was released as energy when the pieces came together, and it is the same energy that would have to be supplied to separate them: the **binding energy**.
eag0dgmreu: The relationship between mass and energy was established by Albert Einstein in 1905 with his famous equation **E = mc²**: energy equals mass multiplied by the speed of light squared. Because that speed is enormous, a minuscule mass is equivalent to a colossal amount of energy. A single gram of matter converted entirely into energy would be equivalent to about 21 [[energia-y-tnt|kilotons]], more than the Hiroshima bomb, in which less than a gram of mass was actually transformed into energy. A common misconception deserves clarifying: Einstein did not invent the bomb or take part in its design; his equation merely explains where the energy comes from.
3s0j8zpv9y: If the binding energy per particle of each nucleus is plotted, the result is a curve that rises very quickly among the light elements, peaks around iron and nickel, and then falls slowly towards the heavy ones. That curve is the map of nuclear energy: any reaction that moves nuclei towards the peak releases energy. There are two routes: **splitting** a heavy nucleus into two medium-sized ones ([[fision|fission]]) or **joining** light nuclei into a heavier one ([[fusion|fusion]]).
1n023shbai8: Very loosely bound: fusing it releases a lot of energy
kp71et10s9: Extraordinarily stable; a typical product of fusion
1tsyvufkitg: Close to the peak: neither fission nor fusion can extract energy from it
12nlohqnt8f: Releases energy when it splits into two medium-sized nuclei
1oz9vgx2klf: The MeV (megaelectronvolt) is a very small unit of energy on a human scale, but enormous on the scale of a molecule: a typical chemical reaction releases a few electronvolts, a million times less than a nuclear reaction. That factor of a million is the key to everything: see [[energia-y-tnt|Energy and TNT equivalence]].
m3e36g0z78: Leucippus and Democritus propose that matter is made of indivisible particles.
5xtu9dd0rc: John Dalton formulates the modern atomic theory: each element has atoms of a characteristic mass.
13lvv3yy2b2: J. J. Thomson discovers the electron while studying cathode rays. He pictures the atom as a positive “plum pudding” with electrons embedded in it.
27rlonkgxjp: Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fire alpha particles at a gold foil; some bounce back. Ernest Rutherford concludes that the positive charge is concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
23guqzvv5r6: Niels Bohr proposes that electrons occupy orbits of fixed energy, which explains the light emitted by atoms.
29z7xkpxnjf: Rutherford identifies the proton as a component of all nuclei.
1px6zvx9l82: James Chadwick discovers the neutron in Cambridge. That same year Werner Heisenberg and Dmitri Ivanenko describe the nucleus as a collection of protons and neutrons.
2a3eroc1ka0: Hideki Yukawa proposes the first theory of the strong nuclear force.
1xnn0o1pjfm: The discovery of the neutron in 1932 was the starting point of the nuclear age. For the first time there was a projectile capable of penetrating any nucleus, and Enrico Fermi immediately began bombarding every element he could find with neutrons. Seven years later, that path would lead to the [[descubrimiento-de-la-fision|discovery of fission]].
1md50pp3z9f: Isotopes are variants of the same element that have the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons. Chemically they are almost identical, but their nuclear behaviour can be radically different.
vtkbjw7wxv: All atoms of an element have the same number of protons, but not necessarily the same number of neutrons. Each variant is called an **isotope**. The name was coined by the British chemist Frederick Soddy in 1913, at the suggestion of the physician and writer Margaret Todd: it comes from the Greek *isos topos*, “same place”, because all the isotopes of an element occupy the same box in the periodic table.
1guofzp42do: Uranium-235, uranium-238 and plutonium-239: the first two have 92 protons; they differ only by three neutrons, but that difference decides whether or not a nucleus undergoes fission easily.
esmt9mr9q8: An isotope is identified by the name of the element and its mass number (protons plus neutrons): carbon-12, uranium-235, plutonium-239. In scientific notation the number is written at the top left of the chemical symbol (¹²C, ²³⁵U). In this encyclopedia we use the hyphenated form, which is easier to read: U-235, Pu-239.
9sdv571fay: The chemistry of an atom depends on its electrons, and the number of electrons depends on the number of protons. That is why two isotopes of the same element react in practically the same way: water made with heavy hydrogen closely resembles ordinary water, and uranium-235 forms the same compounds as uranium-238. This similarity has an enormous historical consequence: there is no chemical reaction that separates two isotopes easily. To do so, one has to exploit the tiny difference in mass between them, which demands gigantic industrial facilities. That is the problem of *enrichment* described in [[uranio|Uranium]].
xpn0qjiogi: The nucleus, by contrast, does distinguish between isotopes. Some are stable for ever; others are [[radiactividad|radioactive]] and change over time. Some absorb neutrons avidly and others barely notice them. And, above all, a few heavy isotopes are **fissile**: they split on receiving a neutron of any energy, even a very slow one. The three fissile isotopes of practical interest are uranium-233, uranium-235 and plutonium-239.

ekiqb1rfpq: Fissile; made in reactors from uranium-238
5o2yw01xr8: Undergoes spontaneous fission; it shaped the design of the first bombs
1wu8s2otq8q: If all the known nuclei are plotted on a graph with protons on one axis and neutrons on the other, the stable ones form a narrow band called the *valley of stability*. In light elements, the ideal ratio is one neutron per proton; in heavy ones, considerably more neutrons than protons are needed to “dilute” the electric repulsion. Nuclei that fall outside the band are unstable and tend to return to it by emitting radiation: if they have too many neutrons, they usually undergo beta decay; if they are very heavy, alpha decay.
xhpnp4trmo: This rule explains why [[fision|fission products]] are so radioactive. When a uranium nucleus splits, the two fragments inherit its high proportion of neutrons, which is excessive for medium-sized nuclei. They end up far from the valley and decay in successive chains over seconds, days or decades. This is the origin of the radioactivity of [[lluvia-radiactiva|fallout]] and of reactor waste.
1irr0yqe55m: J. J. Thomson observes that neon has two variants of different mass. Soddy coins the word “isotope”.
1w49nmdtk8v: Francis Aston builds the mass spectrograph and finds isotopes in dozens of elements (Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1922).
6a1opuheb: Harold Urey discovers deuterium, heavy hydrogen (Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1934).
1pi5q24xdkj: Mark Oliphant, Paul Harteck and Ernest Rutherford obtain tritium in the laboratory by fusing deuterium nuclei.
1jxsayy0ib5: Arthur Dempster identifies uranium-235 in natural uranium.
46ftzv181i: Niels Bohr and John Wheeler deduce that it is the rare uranium-235, and not the abundant uranium-238, that is responsible for fission with slow neutrons.
7agwpuwq6f: Glenn Seaborg and his team show that plutonium-239 is fissile.
2xk8nw4qpp: Radioactivity is the spontaneous transformation of unstable nuclei, which emit alpha, beta or gamma radiation or neutrons. Each isotope does so at its own rate, measured by its half-life.
2d8b8dvvfol: An unstable nucleus does not stay that way for ever. Sooner or later it transforms into a more stable one and, in doing so, expels particles or energy. This spontaneous process is **radioactivity**, and what is thrown off is **ionising radiation**: radiation with enough energy to knock electrons out of the atoms it passes through, break molecules apart and damage the DNA of cells. It should not be confused with non-ionising radiation, such as visible light, radio waves or microwaves, which lacks that ability.
mixhaql20j: In 1896 the French physicist Henri Becquerel stored some uranium salts next to photographic plates wrapped in black paper and found that the plates became fogged without any need for light. The uranium was emitting something by itself. Soon afterwards, Marie Skłodowska-Curie, who named the phenomenon *radioactivity*, and her husband Pierre Curie discovered in 1898 two elements far more active than uranium: polonium and radium. The three shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903; Marie Curie would also win the one in Chemistry in 1911, and would die in 1934 of an anaemia attributed to decades of exposure.
40lekgu7kl: In 1899 Ernest Rutherford distinguished two types of radiation according to their penetrating power, which he called alpha and beta; in 1900 Paul Villard found a third, even more penetrating, which was named gamma. In 1902 Rutherford and Soddy demonstrated something that seemed like alchemy: when it decays, one element turns into a different one.
1hwwzaxbn9p: Alpha decay (a helium nucleus is emitted), beta decay (a neutron turns into a proton and an electron is emitted) and gamma decay (the nucleus releases energy in the form of very energetic light). Below, the half-life: in each equal interval, half remains.
29geixj4gcu: **Alpha (α)**: the nucleus expels a packet of two protons and two neutrons, that is, a helium nucleus. It is a heavy, charged particle that collides at once with everything it meets: it travels a few centimetres in air and is stopped by a sheet of paper or the dead layer of the skin. Outside the body it is almost harmless; inside, if inhaled or swallowed, it deposits all its energy in a very small space and is very damaging. It is the typical radiation of uranium, plutonium, radium or polonium.
z6r88w3qzc: **Beta (β)**: a neutron in the nucleus turns into a proton and emits a very fast electron (and an antineutrino). It penetrates further than alpha: it travels metres in air and a few millimetres in the body. It is slowed by a sheet of plastic or aluminium a few millimetres thick. It can cause skin burns, such as the “beta burns” suffered by the people of Rongelap after [[castle-bravo|Castle Bravo]].
e92r7cnivq: **Gamma (γ)**: after a decay, the nucleus is usually left in an excited state and rids itself of the surplus energy by emitting a photon, light of extremely high energy. It has neither mass nor charge, so it is highly penetrating: it passes through the body, and attenuating it requires considerable thicknesses of dense materials such as lead, concrete, steel or earth. It is never stopped completely: with every given thickness it is reduced by half.
ryauq7zt94: **Neutrons (n)**: they do not come from ordinary radioactivity but, above all, from [[fision|fission]] and [[fusion|fusion]]. Having no charge, they pass easily through lead and steel. They are slowed best by hydrogen-rich materials, such as water, polyethylene or damp concrete, because in colliding with light nuclei they lose a great deal of energy in each collision, just like a billiard ball striking another of the same size. They can also make the materials that absorb them radioactive (*activation*).
1kjsdmifnrb: It is impossible to know when a particular nucleus will decay, but with a great many nuclei the behaviour is perfectly predictable. Each isotope has a **half-life**: the time it takes for half of a sample to decay. After one half-life, half remains; after two, a quarter; after ten, roughly one thousandth. The half-life does not depend on temperature, pressure or chemical combination: it is a property of the nucleus.
149736rnrmw: There is an inverse relationship worth understanding: the shorter the half-life, the more intense the radiation from a given quantity of material, but the less it lasts. An isotope with a very long half-life, such as uranium-238, is only weakly active; one with a short half-life, such as iodine-131, is very active but disappears within weeks. That is why [[lluvia-radiactiva|fallout]] is extremely intense in the first hours and decays quickly, while long-lasting contamination is left by isotopes such as caesium-137.
f04leqij6f: Intermediate step in the production of [[plutonio|plutonium]]
1ybccyqmfmi: Natural gas from the subsoil; main source of natural dose
1bmeaio6w2y: Fission product; becomes fixed in the bones
a2rr834ych: Fission product; contaminates soils for centuries
1g4kye4bvke: Almost the age of the Earth
nfeiq2acl7: Often the nucleus that results from a decay is also unstable and decays again, and so on. Uranium-238, for example, goes through a chain of fourteen steps (passing through radium and radon) until it becomes lead-206, which is stable. That is why uranium mines contain radium and give off radon, and why uranium miners suffered extremely high rates of lung cancer for decades.
16oupmi4hip: Radioactivity is not a human invention. We live surrounded by it: the radon that seeps from the ground, the potassium-40 in our own bones and muscles, the carbon-14 in food, the uranium and thorium in rocks and the cosmic rays that reach us from space. This *background radiation* exposes each person, on average, to about 2.4 millisieverts a year (see [[unidades-de-radiacion|Radiation units]]). The heat that keeps the Earth’s interior molten comes, in large part, from the decay of those elements.
krbgo9suxu: The radioactivity of an object is different from the radiation it receives. An object exposed to gamma rays or X-rays does not become radioactive; one exposed to neutrons can become radioactive, and one contaminated with radioactive dust is radioactive for as long as the dust remains. This distinction is essential for understanding the [[radiacion-inicial|initial radiation]] and the [[lluvia-radiactiva|fallout]] of an explosion.
uhz1cvbo7i: Fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two medium-sized fragments after it absorbs a neutron. Each fission releases about 200 MeV, tens of millions of times more than a chemical reaction, and new neutrons that can cause further fissions.
2g2ptnfh3mp: **Nuclear fission** is the division of a heavy atomic nucleus into two lighter nuclei. In practice it is almost always induced by firing a neutron at a nucleus of uranium or plutonium. The nucleus absorbs the neutron, becomes deformed, stretches like an oscillating water drop and finally splits into two fragments that fly off in opposite directions at enormous speed, accompanied by two or three new neutrons and by gamma radiation. It is the process that powers nuclear reactors and [[arma-de-fision|fission weapons]], and the first stage of all [[bomba-de-hidrogeno|thermonuclear weapons]].
1mchjam2cov: A neutron strikes a uranium-235 nucleus; the nucleus becomes deformed and splits into two fragments (for example, barium and krypton), releasing two or three neutrons and a great deal of energy.
m8a8oo918l: As explained in [[atomo|The atom]], two forces compete inside a nucleus: the strong nuclear force, which binds all the particles together but only over a very short distance, and the electric repulsion between protons, which is weaker but has a longer range. In a nucleus as large as that of uranium, with 92 protons, the balance is precarious. Niels Bohr and John Wheeler described it in 1939 with the **liquid-drop model**: the nucleus behaves like an electrically charged drop. If it receives a small input of energy, for example that brought by a neutron when it is captured, it begins to vibrate. If it stretches far enough and forms a “waist”, the strong force can no longer hold the two ends together, the electric repulsion pushes them apart and the nucleus divides.
1844cxjab3j: Not all heavy nuclei behave in the same way. In uranium-235 and plutonium-239, the mere fact of capturing a neutron supplies enough energy for fission, even if the neutron arrives almost at rest. These isotopes are called **fissile**. In uranium-238, by contrast, capture is not enough: it undergoes fission only if the neutron arrives already very fast, with a lot of energy of its own. It is said to be **fissionable** but not fissile. Moreover, when uranium-238 captures a slow neutron without undergoing fission, it transforms over time into plutonium-239: that is why it is called **fertile** (see [[plutonio|Plutonium]]).
1ca0a29jnm7: This distinction explains two historical facts. On the one hand, natural uranium, which is almost entirely uranium-238, cannot sustain an explosion on its own, and for a weapon the proportion of the rare uranium-235 has to be increased by means of the extremely costly enrichment process described in [[uranio|Uranium]]. On the other, uranium-238 does undergo fission with the very fast neutrons of [[fusion|fusion]], which is exploited in fission-fusion-fission weapons (see [[bomba-de-hidrogeno|The hydrogen bomb]]).
1cdmmy5lbze: The neutrons born in a fission fly off at about 20,000 kilometres per second: these are **fast neutrons**. If they pass through a material containing light nuclei, such as water or graphite, they collide with them again and again and gradually lose speed until they reach the temperature of their surroundings, moving at barely a few kilometres per second. These are the **slow** or **thermal neutrons**, and the material that slows them is called a **moderator**. Enrico Fermi discovered in Rome in 1934, almost by chance, that neutrons slowed down by passing through paraffin were far more effective at inducing nuclear reactions.
dq2u74kde4: Physicists measure the probability that a neutron will cause a reaction with a quantity called the **cross-section**. The intuitive idea is that of a target: imagine that each nucleus is a bullseye and that its size is not the geometric one, but the “apparent size” it presents to the neutron. The bigger the target, the easier it is to hit. That apparent size changes enormously with the neutron’s speed: for uranium-235, a slow neutron “sees” a target hundreds of times larger than a fast one does. It is as if, passing slowly by the nucleus, it had more time to be caught.
23viak31zxz: The cross-section is measured in a unit with a curious name, the **barn**, equivalent to an area of 10⁻²⁴ square centimetres. Its origin is a joke by two physicists at Purdue University in 1942: for a nucleus, that area was as big “as a barn door”. The name also served as a code word during the war.
10dtt0f9i3q: This gives rise to a fundamental difference between reactors and weapons. A **reactor** uses a moderator to slow the neutrons and take advantage of the large cross-section of slow neutrons, which allows it to run on slightly enriched or even natural uranium. A **weapon**, on the other hand, cannot wait for the neutrons to slow down: the reaction has to be completed before the heat itself disperses the material, so it works with fast neutrons and needs highly concentrated fissile material. A reactor cannot explode like a bomb, although it can suffer serious accidents for other reasons, as at [[chernobil|Chernobyl]].
czplaefik3: What comes out of a fission
1wu01b1zpnt: **Two fission fragments**: almost never equal. Most often one has a mass of around 95 and the other around 140, such as a krypton and a barium, or a strontium and a xenon. Hundreds of possible combinations are known.
13od52rtilv: **Two or three new neutrons** (about 2.4 on average in uranium-235). They are what make the [[reaccion-en-cadena|chain reaction]] possible. A small fraction is not emitted immediately but seconds later, from the fragments: these are the *delayed neutrons*, thanks to which a reactor can be controlled.
25jggg5rir4: **Prompt gamma radiation**, which forms part of the [[radiacion-inicial|initial radiation]] of an explosion.
94qhd3vhgw: **Neutrinos**, which escape without interacting and carry away part of the energy.
145gm83f4k4: The fragments have too many neutrons for their size and are intensely radioactive: they are the **fission products**. They decay in chains of beta and gamma emissions that can last anywhere from fractions of a second to decades. Among them are iodine-131, caesium-137 and strontium-90. In a nuclear explosion, these products mix with the dust and debris of the fireball and form [[lluvia-radiactiva|fallout]]; in a reactor, they remain trapped in the spent fuel.
3e3u04twih: Each fission of a uranium-235 nucleus releases about **200 MeV**. The sum of the masses of everything that comes out is slightly less than the mass of the original nucleus and neutron, and that difference is converted into energy according to E = mc². Most of it appears as the kinetic energy of the two fragments, which repel each other electrically and fly apart; as they slow down against neighbouring atoms, that energy is transformed into heat.
11rzu2niu0d: Fate of the energy of a fission
1mx9j12vjg5: Motion of the fragments (converted into heat)
1q5vuabe58a: Subsequent decay of the fission products (beta and gamma)
bt2txqvcjy: To get an idea of what this means: when a molecule of methane burns or a molecule of TNT explodes, a few electronvolts are released. A fission releases two hundred million electronvolts. Per unit of mass, the complete fission of a fissile material yields on the order of **twenty million times** more energy than the same mass of TNT. That difference, not any technical detail, is what separates a conventional bomb from a nuclear one (see [[energia-y-tnt|Energy and TNT equivalence]]).
1nc4zezz14w: Some heavy nuclei undergo fission from time to time without needing to receive a neutron: this is **spontaneous fission**, discovered in 1940 by the Soviets Georgy Flyorov and Konstantin Petrzhak. In uranium it is extremely rare, but in certain isotopes, such as plutonium-240, it is much more frequent. Each of these spontaneous fissions emits neutrons that appear at unpredictable moments, and that small detail forced the abandonment in 1944 of the gun design for plutonium and the development of [[implosion|implosion]] (see also [[tipo-canon|Gun-type weapon]]).
20a2stu5fkp: The full story is told in [[descubrimiento-de-la-fision|The discovery of fission]]. In short: from 1934 several laboratories bombarded uranium with neutrons, believing they were producing heavier elements. The German chemist Ida Noddack suggested that same year that perhaps the nucleus was breaking apart, but nobody took her seriously. In December 1938, in Berlin, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found barium, an element with half the mass of uranium, among the products. Hahn wrote, bewildered, to his former collaborator Lise Meitner, who had fled Germany because of her Jewish origins. Over Christmas, walking in the snow in Sweden with her nephew Otto Frisch, Meitner realised that the nucleus had split in two and calculated, using Einstein’s formula, that about 200 MeV was being released. Frisch borrowed the word *fission* from biology, the division of a cell.
148a8t124l7: Enrico Fermi bombards uranium with neutrons in Rome. Ida Noddack proposes that the nucleus could split apart.
r64b02c1qk: Hahn and Strassmann detect barium in uranium irradiated with neutrons.
hx92tdats: Meitner and Frisch interpret the result as a fission; Frisch confirms it experimentally. Bohr takes the news to the United States.
1ni0156musg: Frédéric Joliot-Curie, Hans von Halban and Lew Kowarski, in Paris, show that each fission releases several neutrons: the [[reaccion-en-cadena|chain reaction]] is possible.
2ffrjawwi1p: Bohr and Wheeler publish the theory of fission based on the liquid-drop model.

26b2in52rvt: Hahn alone receives the Nobel Prize in Chemistry; the exclusion of Meitner is now regarded as one of the great injustices of the prize. Element 109 bears her name: meitnerium.
1sxhzgma9cw: If the neutrons from each fission cause new fissions, the process multiplies generation after generation. Controlled, it is a reactor; uncontrolled within a fraction of a microsecond, it is a nuclear explosion.
1j9yl3enfi: Each [[fision|fission]] of uranium-235 releases two or three neutrons. If at least one of them reaches another fissile nucleus and splits it, new neutrons will be produced that can repeat the process. This succession of fissions that trigger one another is the **chain reaction**. It is the central idea of all nuclear technology: without it, fission would be a laboratory curiosity releasing energy atom by atom; with it, a piece of material can release in a fraction of a second the energy of thousands of tonnes of explosive.
161xgicvp8z: Generation by generation: one neutron causes a fission, which releases several neutrons, which cause several more fissions. If each generation is larger than the previous one, the number of fissions grows exponentially.
7ft7mjfa6f: The first to imagine it was the Hungarian physicist Leó Szilard. According to his own account, one morning in September 1933, while waiting for a traffic light to change at Southampton Row in London, he thought that if an element could be found that emitted two neutrons when struck by one, a reaction could be produced that would grow without limit. He had just read Rutherford dismissing any idea of extracting energy from atoms as “moonshine”. Szilard patented the concept in 1934 and assigned the patent to the British Admiralty to keep it secret. He did not yet know which element might serve: fission would not be discovered until five years later.
15ng399bn2c: In March 1939, weeks after the discovery of fission, Frédéric Joliot-Curie’s team in Paris and, separately, Szilard and Fermi in New York confirmed that each fission did indeed release more than one neutron. The chain reaction was possible. Alarmed at the possibility that Nazi Germany might build a weapon, Szilard drafted that summer the letter signed by Albert Einstein that reached President Roosevelt (see [[carta-de-einstein|Einstein’s letter]]).
1elz9ldonh7: Not every neutron released causes a new fission. Some escape through the surface of the material, others are absorbed by nuclei that do not undergo fission (impurities, uranium-238 or any other material) and others simply do not find a target. What matters is the average number of neutrons in each generation that manage to cause a fission in the next. Physicists call this the **multiplication factor** and represent it with the letter *k*.
125o6byaokf: **k less than 1 (subcritical)**: each generation is smaller than the last. Any reaction that begins dies out on its own. This is the state, for example, of new fuel stored safely.
1cv8ljwq3hd: **k equal to 1 (critical)**: each generation is equal to the last. The reaction remains steady, at a constant power. This is how a running nuclear reactor operates.
1aehv2ec1d0: **k greater than 1 (supercritical)**: each generation is larger than the last and the reaction grows exponentially. In a reactor this is used for brief moments to raise power, in a very controlled way. In a weapon, the aim is for *k* to be as high as possible.
19imy90norc: Whether a body of material is subcritical or supercritical depends on its composition, shape, density and surroundings. This is the concept of [[masa-critica|critical mass]], which is explained in its own article.
1n6hcnli22t: Exponential growth defies intuition. Remember the legend of the inventor of chess who asked as his reward for one grain of wheat on the first square, two on the second, four on the third, and so on: by the time he reached square 64 there was not enough wheat in the whole world. With a reaction that doubled the number of fissions in each generation, after 10 generations there would be about a thousand simultaneous fissions; after 20, a million; after 40, a trillion, and a few dozen more generations are enough to reach the trillions of trillions of fissions needed to release the energy of a nuclear explosion.
uomrpk2n7z: What turns this into an explosion is speed. A fast neutron takes only a few billionths of a second to cross the material and cause the next fission, so the whole sequence of generations is completed in less than a microsecond. In that time, the energy released heats the material to tens of millions of degrees, vaporises it and makes it expand. As it expands, the density falls, more neutrons escape, *k* drops below 1 and the reaction stops. The whole history of fission weapons is, at bottom, the struggle to keep the material together long enough for an appreciable fraction of it to fission before it disperses (see [[arma-de-fision|Fission weapon]]).
1kg4ype0y1y: If the chain reaction is so fast, how is it possible to control a reactor? The answer lies in the **delayed neutrons**. A small fraction of the neutrons, less than one per cent, is not emitted at the instant of fission but seconds or minutes later, when certain fission products decay. A reactor is designed to be critical only when those straggling neutrons are counted; this way, power changes over scales of seconds or minutes and the operators or automatic systems have time to react by moving the control rods. A weapon, by contrast, works only with prompt neutrons: it waits for no one.

It was directed by Enrico Fermi, with a team that included Leó Szilard, Walter Zinn, Herbert Anderson and Leona Woods, the only woman present. As a precaution, a few young men waited on top of the pile with buckets of cadmium solution to shut it down if anything went wrong.

Arthur Compton telephoned James Conant with a coded phrase that became famous: “The Italian navigator has landed in the New World.” It was the practical starting point of the [[proyecto-manhattan|Manhattan Project]] and of the great [[plutonio|plutonium]] production reactors at [[oak-ridge-y-hanford|Hanford]].

21q6ia2n1pt: When a chain reaction occurs unintentionally outside a reactor, it is called a *criticality accident*. 1tt37sb30i5: Critical mass is the minimum quantity of fissile material capable of sustaining a chain reaction. It is not a fixed number: it depends on the shape, density, purity and surroundings of the material.
14o5icrduqz: A [[reaccion-en-cadena|chain reaction]] is only sustained if, on average, each fission causes at least one more. In a small piece of fissile material, most neutrons escape through the surface before finding a nucleus to split, and the reaction dies out. If the piece is larger, each neutron has to travel through more material before leaving, and the probability that it will cause a fission increases. There is a point at which losses and gains balance exactly: the quantity of material needed to reach it is called the **critical mass**.
1r2hy5j89dy: On the left, a subcritical assembly: too many neutrons escape through the surface and the reaction dies out. On the right, a supercritical one: the neutrons find nuclei before escaping and the reaction grows. Qualitative diagram.
10ru4m37cit: A number that is not a number
1by9z5tu32a: It is common to hear critical mass spoken of as if it were a fixed figure for each material. It is not. It is the result of a neutron balance, and anything that alters that balance changes it. This encyclopedia gives no figures, but it does explain the factors involved, which are the same ones studied by nuclear safety in any facility that handles fissile material.
pelzvk7p0c: **The material**: each isotope has its own probability of undergoing fission and its own number of neutrons per fission. z4wyohwc9k: **The purity**: any impurity that absorbs neutrons without undergoing fission is a loss. The more diluted the fissile material, the harder it is to achieve criticality.
20uw8gja54w: **The geometry**: neutrons escape through the surface, so the shape that minimises leakage is the one with the least surface for a given volume, the sphere. A long, thin cylinder or a thin sheet of the same mass loses many more neutrons. That is why the nuclear industry stores solutions of fissile material in narrow or flat tanks, with shapes that can never become critical.
1cxn6szidb2: **The density**: if the same material is compressed, the nuclei are closer together, the distance a neutron travels before finding one is shorter and fewer escape. A mass that is subcritical at normal density can become supercritical if it is compressed. This principle is the basis of [[implosion|implosion]].
163jwdzeknd: **The surroundings**: a material that sends back inwards some of the neutrons trying to escape, called a **reflector**, reduces leakage and, with it, the mass required. Even water or a person’s body can act as a reflector, which has been behind several accidents.
14w9uewsiam: **The moderators**: in solutions or mixtures with water, neutrons are slowed and their probability of causing fissions changes. This mainly affects fuel facilities and laboratories, not weapons.
1cfqolx2jrz: A **subcritical** assembly cannot sustain the reaction. A **critical** one keeps it steady. A **supercritical** one makes it grow. Every [[arma-de-fision|fission weapon]] is based on keeping the material in a subcritical configuration until the desired moment and then passing, very quickly, to a highly supercritical one. There are two historical ways of doing this: bringing separate pieces together ([[tipo-canon|gun-type]]) or compressing a single piece ([[implosion|implosion]]). The speed of that transition is essential: if it is slow, the reaction can start too early and the material disperses with a power far below that intended.

1lru9p2lygw: For safety reasons, this encyclopedia offers no figures for critical masses or any other design parameter. The concepts explained here are those taught in any nuclear physics course and in criticality safety training.
2macn298h8: Fusion joins light nuclei, such as those of hydrogen, into heavier ones and releases enormous amounts of energy. It is what makes the Sun shine and the source of most of the power of thermonuclear weapons.
1bz0jrv7atn: **Nuclear fusion** is the reverse process of [[fision|fission]]: instead of splitting a heavy nucleus, two light nuclei are joined to form a heavier one. Because the product, typically helium, is much more tightly bound than the starting nuclei, the difference in mass is released as energy. It is the reaction that powers the Sun and all the stars, the one that experimental fusion reactors seek to tame and the one that provides a good part of the power of [[bomba-de-hidrogeno|hydrogen bombs]].
3mer214igb: A deuterium nucleus and a tritium nucleus fuse to form a helium-4 nucleus and a very fast neutron. The reaction releases 17.6 MeV.
26y6ik6rkfd: All nuclei carry a positive charge and repel one another. For two of them to approach closely enough for the strong nuclear force to capture them, they have to collide at enormous speeds and overcome that repulsion, known as the **Coulomb barrier**. The way to achieve this on a large scale is to heat the fuel to temperatures of tens or hundreds of millions of degrees: at such temperatures atoms lose their electrons, matter becomes a **plasma** and the nuclei move so fast that some collide with enough energy. That is why we speak of **thermonuclear** reactions: nuclear, but triggered by heat.
29tluif47ez: According to classical physics, not even those temperatures would be enough. Fusion is possible thanks to a quantum phenomenon, **tunnelling**, explained by George Gamow in 1928: a nucleus has a certain probability of “passing through” the barrier even though it lacks the energy to climb over it. At the centre of the Sun, at about 15 million degrees, each proton takes on average thousands of millions of years to fuse, but there are so many of them that the Sun converts about four million tonnes of mass into energy every second.

200sdwxa3u8: In a weapon there is no practical way to heat the fuel to those temperatures except with a fission explosion. This is exploited in two ways: in [[fision-potenciada|boosted fission]], a small quantity of fusion fuel makes a fission weapon more efficient; in the [[bomba-de-hidrogeno|hydrogen bomb]], fusion is the main source of energy and allows yields of megatons.
1e0tt2t6za: Since the 1950s, attempts have been made to produce electrical energy with controlled fusion. The challenge is to maintain a plasma at hundreds of millions of degrees for long enough and at sufficient density for it to produce more energy than is spent heating it; the British physicist John Lawson formulated the necessary condition in 1955, known as the *Lawson criterion*. There are two main strategies:
1ct5v3uv925: **Magnetic confinement**: the plasma is held suspended inside a doughnut-shaped chamber by extremely intense magnetic fields. The most widespread design is the **tokamak**, devised by Igor Tamm and Andrei Sakharov in the USSR in the early 1950s. The British JET set in 2023 the record for energy produced in a single pulse (69 megajoules), and the great international project **ITER**, under construction at Cadarache (France), with European and Spanish participation, aims to demonstrate an energy gain from the 2030s onwards.
bi5zg6ftn9: **Inertial confinement**: a small capsule of fuel is compressed and heated in a fraction of a nanosecond with very powerful lasers. On 5 December 2022, the National Ignition Facility (NIF) at Livermore, California, achieved **ignition** for the first time: the reaction released more energy (3.15 MJ) than the lasers deposited in the capsule (2.05 MJ), although far less than the whole facility consumed.
1i57ofcum3d: Controlled fusion has attractive advantages: abundant fuel (deuterium is extracted from water), no risk of an uncontrolled chain reaction and waste with a much shorter life than that of fission. 1wgkwgfn8ah: The yield of nuclear weapons is expressed in tonnes of TNT equivalent: a kiloton is a thousand tonnes and a megaton, a million. It is a convention that allows very different explosions to be compared on a single scale.
qnimshr72t: When it is said that the Hiroshima bomb had a yield of 15 kilotons, it means that it released the same energy as the explosion of 15,000 tonnes of **TNT** (trinitrotoluene). This way of expressing the energy of an explosion, called **yield** or **power**, was born during the [[proyecto-manhattan|Manhattan Project]], when scientists needed to explain to military officers and politicians a quantity for which no reference existed. Comparing it with the best-known military explosive was the most intuitive way of conveying it.

The result is that, kilo for kilo, nuclear material yields tens of millions of times more than the best chemical explosive. we4j2t54yd: The most counterintuitive effect of the nuclear scale is that the radius of destruction grows much more slowly than the yield. The area destroyed grows with the yield raised to the power of two thirds.

1vs1f37cjv1: Uranium is the heaviest naturally occurring element that is abundant on Earth. Its scarce isotope 235 is fissile: it fuels nuclear reactors and was the material of the Hiroshima bomb.
ozdiwaezq: **Uranium** is a silvery metal, very dense (almost twice as dense as lead) and slightly radioactive. With atomic number 92, it is the heaviest element found in appreciable quantities in nature. It is present in almost all rocks, in the soil and in seawater in minuscule concentrations, and in certain deposits it is concentrated enough to be extracted. For a century and a half it was a curiosity used to colour glass and ceramics; since 1939, it has been the raw material of the whole nuclear industry.
17xwgxmj8v4: The German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth identified uranium in 1789 in a mineral called pitchblende, from the silver mines of Joachimsthal (today Jáchymov, in the Czech Republic). He named it in honour of the planet Uranus, discovered eight years earlier. In 1896, Henri Becquerel discovered [[radiactividad|radioactivity]] precisely with uranium salts, and the Curies extracted radium and polonium from tonnes of pitchblende from those same mines. For decades, uranium was a by-product of radium mining, used to give glass a characteristic yellowish-green tint that glows under ultraviolet light.
zd428n9yvk: Everything changed with the [[descubrimiento-de-la-fision|discovery of fission]] in 1938. In 1939 Bohr and Wheeler realised that it was uranium-235, which makes up less than 1% of natural uranium, that was responsible for fission with slow neutrons. During the war, most of the uranium for the [[proyecto-manhattan|Manhattan Project]] came from the Shinkolobwe mine in the Belgian Congo, of exceptional richness, supplemented with mines in Canada and on the Colorado Plateau.
ftbbixpmkv: Today the largest uranium producers are Kazakhstan, which mines around 40% of the world total, Canada, Namibia and Australia, which has the largest known reserves. A growing share is obtained without excavation, by dissolving the uranium in the deposit itself and pumping the solution to the surface (*in situ leaching*). The ore is processed to obtain a yellowish concentrate of uranium oxide, the so-called **yellowcake**. In Spain there were uranium mines and processing plants in several provinces, above all in Salamanca, until 2000, and the Juzbado factory (Salamanca) produces fuel assemblies for nuclear power stations.
25vy0lja86a: As explained in [[isotopos|Isotopes]], uranium-235 and uranium-238 are chemically identical. To increase the proportion of the fissile isotope, a process called **enrichment**, one can only exploit the tiny difference in mass between them, little more than 1%. The separation has to be repeated over and over in huge, energy-hungry facilities, and for that reason enrichment was for decades the main obstacle to making weapons and remains the focus of international non-proliferation monitoring. Commercial reactors use **low-enriched** uranium, in which uranium-235 is still a small minority; weapons need **highly enriched** uranium. The body responsible for verifying that civilian uranium is not diverted is the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).
1w2epsy1a0q: Over the course of history several methods have been used, which are only named here:
18llj947zwo: **Electromagnetic separation**: Ernest Lawrence’s *calutrons*, at the Y-12 plant in Oak Ridge, deflected uranium ions with giant magnets. It was the method that produced the material for Little Boy. Because of a shortage of copper during the war, their coils were made with silver lent by the US Treasury.
17unn6vhdzl: **Gaseous diffusion**: it passed a gaseous uranium compound through porous barriers. The K-25 plant at Oak Ridge was in its day the largest building in the world. It dominated production until the 1980s.
1i3rw5du8cz: **Thermal diffusion**: used briefly at the S-50 plant at Oak Ridge in 1944 and 1945.

It was developed in the USSR in the 1950s with the participation of the German Gernot Zippe. Because of its small size and low consumption it is also the most worrying from the point of view of proliferation.
1pdudsuj1j4: **Laser methods**: they exploit the fact that each isotope absorbs light slightly differently. They are still under development.
2e9qwtrxir4: See [[oak-ridge-y-hanford|Oak Ridge and Hanford]] for the history of the first plants.
1q278kohuiw: **Electricity**: nuclear power stations produce around 9% of the world’s electricity and about a fifth of Spain’s. The fuel is made in the form of ceramic pellets of uranium oxide.
1ptez9m8ufm: **Naval propulsion**: nuclear submarines and aircraft carriers use compact reactors that allow them to sail for years without refuelling.
1s6kw4bp30l: **Weapons**: highly enriched uranium was the material of [[tipo-canon|Little Boy]] and forms part of many modern weapons.
1arq9otshl1: **Depleted uranium**: the residue of enrichment, with less uranium-235 than natural uranium. 184h3qy9u76: **From weapon to wall socket**: between 1993 and 2013, the US–Russian programme known as *Megatons to Megawatts* down-blended the highly enriched uranium from thousands of dismantled Soviet warheads to turn it into power station fuel; during those years it generated around a tenth of the electricity in the United States.
47mp8tnenw: Natural and depleted uranium are weakly radioactive, because their half-lives are extremely long. Their main danger is **chemical**: like lead or mercury, it is a toxic heavy metal which, if ingested or inhaled in soluble form, damages the kidneys above all. As an alpha emitter, its radiation is dangerous chiefly if the particles are inhaled and remain in the lungs. The most serious radiological risk in mining is not uranium itself but **radon**, the radioactive gas it produces as it decays: uranium miners in central Europe and the United States, many of them Navajo workers, suffered very high lung cancer rates for decades before mine ventilation became widespread. Enriched uranium is more radioactive, but its main risk in industry is that of a [[accidentes-de-criticidad|criticality accident]].
1zkp6otfs9f: Plutonium is an element that barely exists in nature and is made in nuclear reactors from uranium-238. Its isotope 239 is fissile and was the material of the Trinity test and the Nagasaki bomb.
2d0hqkvqr9q: **Plutonium** is a silvery metal that tarnishes in air, extraordinarily dense and with a physical behaviour so strange that metallurgists regard it as the most complicated element in the periodic table. It has atomic number 94. Unlike [[uranio|uranium]], it practically does not exist in nature: all the plutonium handled today has been made by humans in nuclear reactors since 1942. It is one of the two fissile materials from which nuclear weapons are built.

u99hn0nv3w: In 1940, Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson obtained at Berkeley the first element heavier than uranium, neptunium (93). Months later, the young chemist Glenn Seaborg and his collaborators bombarded uranium in the Berkeley cyclotron and isolated element 94. In March 1941 they showed that its isotope 239 underwent fission with slow neutrons even more readily than uranium-235. The discovery was kept secret until after the war. In August 1942, Burris Cunningham and Louis Werner obtained in Chicago the first sample of a plutonium compound visible to the naked eye, barely a speck. Two years later it was being produced on an industrial scale. Seaborg and McMillan received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1951, and element 106 is called seaborgium in his honour.
o8ocflv36: Plutonium is made in a nuclear reactor. When a nucleus of uranium-238, the abundant, non-fissile isotope, captures a neutron, it becomes uranium-239, which within a few minutes undergoes beta decay and turns into neptunium-239; this, within a couple of days, undergoes another and becomes plutonium-239. Every uranium reactor produces plutonium as an unavoidable by-product. The great advantage that the scientists of the [[proyecto-manhattan|Manhattan Project]] saw is that, being a different element from uranium, plutonium can be separated by **chemical** means, something much simpler than isotope enrichment. This process of separation from irradiated fuel is called **reprocessing**.
e6fqummbxd: To produce plutonium for military purposes, dedicated **production reactors** were built: the X-10 graphite reactor at Oak Ridge (1943), a prototype, and Reactor B at Hanford, in Washington State, which reached criticality in September 1944 and produced the plutonium for the [[prueba-trinity|Trinity]] test and the [[nagasaki|Nagasaki]] bomb. The USSR built its first production reactor at the Mayak complex, in the Urals, in 1948; the United Kingdom, the Windscale piles; France, the Marcoule reactors. Several of these sites suffered serious accidents and contamination (see [[kyshtym|Kyshtym]] and [[windscale|Windscale]]).
