That is why a distinction is made between *weapons-grade* plutonium, produced with short irradiations to minimise plutonium-240, and *reactor-grade* plutonium, from the fuel of power stations.
y99u68ot1a: **Plutonium-241 and 242**: heavier isotopes present in reactor-grade plutonium. 241 decays into americium-241, the material in many smoke detectors.
1qqdsi175u6: The discovery of the spontaneous fission of plutonium-240 in reactor plutonium, in 1944, was a crisis at [[los-alamos|Los Alamos]]: it forced the abandonment of the gun design planned for plutonium and the development, in record time, of [[implosion|implosion]].
3ql0pxg4gq: **Weapons**: the great majority of modern nuclear weapons use plutonium in their core or in their primary.
2ezqdfbol8t: **Fuel**: plutonium recovered from spent fuel can be mixed with uranium to make **MOX** (mixed oxide) fuel for power stations. It is also the intended fuel of fast breeder reactors, which produce more plutonium than they consume.
22gfl0j2ty7: **Energy in space**: the plutonium-238 in radioisotope generators.
21uffwjdcam: Plutonium has a reputation as “the most toxic substance known”, which is an exaggeration: its chemical toxicity is not extraordinary. Its danger is radiological. As an alpha emitter, outside the body it poses hardly any risk, because the skin blocks it; but if fine particles are **inhaled**, they can stay in the lungs or pass into the blood and settle in the bones and liver, where they irradiate the tissues continuously for decades and increase the risk of cancer. That is why it is handled in sealed glove boxes. Between 1945 and 1947, eighteen people were injected with plutonium without their informed consent in medical experiments by the US Government, which were not fully revealed until the 1990s.
xobx7sh290: Plutonium production left an enormous environmental legacy. The Hanford complex, with millions of litres of high-level liquid waste stored in underground tanks, is the largest and most expensive environmental clean-up project in the United States. In the USSR, the contamination of Mayak and the River Techa affected tens of thousands of people. After the Cold War, the United States and Russia declared tens of tonnes of military plutonium surplus, whose final fate remains not entirely resolved.
1vjto00d3xi: Deuterium, tritium and lithium are the fuels of fusion, both in experimental reactors and in thermonuclear weapons. Lithium deuteride made it possible to build solid, transportable hydrogen bombs.
h9pq2urm5p: [[fusion|Fusion]] needs light nuclei that join with relative ease and release a lot of energy when they do. The natural candidates are the heavy isotopes of hydrogen, **deuterium** and **tritium**, and a light metal, **lithium**, which makes it possible to produce tritium. Their history is tied both to energy research and to the development of the [[bomba-de-hidrogeno|hydrogen bomb]].
66w8b559vm: Deuterium is hydrogen with a neutron in the nucleus. It is stable and abundant: roughly one in every 6,400 hydrogen atoms in seawater is deuterium, so the oceans hold a practically inexhaustible reserve. It was discovered by Harold Urey in 1931. Water made with deuterium, **heavy water**, is an excellent neutron moderator, and for that reason it played a strategic role in the Second World War: the Norwegian plant at Vemork, which produced it for the German nuclear programme, was the target in 1943 of a famous act of sabotage by Norwegian commandos trained by the British. Today it is used in CANDU-type reactors and as a tracer in chemistry and medicine.
b63cpvxshp: Tritium is hydrogen with two neutrons. It is radioactive, emits very weak beta radiation and has a half-life of about 12.3 years, so in nature it exists only in traces formed by cosmic rays. It is made in reactors, mainly by irradiating lithium with neutrons. Its civil uses are illuminated exit signs that work without electricity, the dials of some watches and night sights. Because its radiation barely passes through the skin, it is not very dangerous externally, though it is if ingested in the form of tritiated water.
16ov9ywn6qe: The deuterium-tritium reaction is the easiest to ignite and the most energetic per unit of mass, hence its importance. But tritium poses two problems: it is expensive to produce and, because it decays, roughly 5% is lost every year. Weapons that use it must have it replenished periodically, and that is why the United States maintains tritium production in Tennessee Valley Authority reactors and at the Savannah River plant.
hpjoccqgv2: Lithium has two stable isotopes: lithium-6 and the much more abundant lithium-7. When lithium-6 absorbs a neutron it splits into a helium nucleus and a tritium nucleus. In other words, lithium-6 is a tritium “factory”. This allowed an elegant solution for weapons: combining lithium and deuterium in a solid compound, **lithium deuteride**, a stable white salt. Inside a weapon, the neutrons from the explosion convert the lithium into tritium at the very moment it is needed, and this fuses with the deuterium present.
1k92btkl208: The first hydrogen bomb, [[ivy-mike|Ivy Mike]] (1952), used liquid deuterium at more than 250 degrees below zero, which required enormous cryogenic equipment: the device weighed about 80 tonnes and filled a building. The Soviets, at the suggestion of the physicist Vitaly Ginzburg, opted for lithium deuteride from the outset. Weapons that use it are called **dry**, as opposed to cryogenic ones, and are the only ones that can be carried on an aircraft or a missile. The first American test of a dry weapon, [[castle-bravo|Castle Bravo]] (1954), also revealed that lithium-7, which had been assumed to be inert, also took part in the reactions, with a result far greater than predicted (see [[armas-de-tres-etapas|Three-stage weapons]]).
dmx3q8br8w: The separation of lithium isotopes on an industrial scale at the Y-12 plant at Oak Ridge, in the 1950s, used enormous quantities of mercury, a good part of which ended up in the environment. It is another example of the environmental cost of the nuclear race.
16g8gp42tja: The easiest reaction; the one ITER and the first reactors will use
2dlw78g2s4e: Tritium has to be made from lithium; many neutrons that activate materials
nz0tmugxui: Helium-3 is extremely rare on Earth; extracting it from the Moon has been proposed
miqlpfz6lq: Even more extreme temperatures; very far from being viable
6kzwuat1wr: In a deuterium-tritium fusion reactor, the tritium would be made in the machine itself by surrounding the chamber with a lithium-bearing “blanket” that would capture the neutrons from the reaction. No reactor has yet demonstrated that self-sufficiency.
16y7kfx60zv: From Ivy Mike to ignition in the laboratory
8cd03q88ny: Since 1952 we have known how to release enormous amounts of fusion energy in an explosion. Doing so in a controlled way has proved far harder. There are two main paths. **Magnetic confinement** holds a plasma of deuterium and tritium, at more than a hundred million degrees, suspended inside a doughnut-shaped chamber by powerful magnetic fields: this is the principle of the **tokamak**, invented in the USSR in the 1950s. **Inertial confinement** uses lasers to compress a tiny fuel capsule in a few billionths of a second, so that fusion takes place before it has time to disperse.
1usxsyzca8w: Success is measured by the **gain factor**, *Q*: the fusion energy produced divided by the energy supplied to heat the fuel. With *Q* = 1 the “break-even point” is reached. On 5 December 2022, the National Ignition Facility (NIF) at Lawrence Livermore Laboratory in California exceeded it for the first time: it obtained 3.15 megajoules of fusion from 2.05 megajoules of laser light. It was the first **ignition** in a laboratory. But the lasers had consumed a hundred times more energy from the electricity grid, so net electricity production is still a very long way off. The NIF also has a military purpose: its experiments help maintain arsenals without [[pruebas-nucleares|nuclear tests]].
22s4ig97xkw: [[ivy-mike|Ivy Mike]], the first large-scale release of fusion energy.
gq3sq6dto3: The British ZETA reactor announces fusion neutrons. Months later it is admitted that they did not come from thermonuclear reactions.
r5ovru5za2: The Soviet T-3 tokamak reaches some 10 million degrees; a British team confirms it in Moscow with laser measurements, and the tokamak prevails worldwide.
28c5qttc3l0: The European JET, at Culham (England), produces significant fusion power for the first time with deuterium and tritium.
qzfilk71ds: JET power record: 16 megawatts, with a gain factor of around 0.67.
21fvrq6wwip: JET produces 59 megajoules in five seconds.
lrefhyffer: JET’s final record, 69 megajoules, shortly before closing after forty years of operation.
10pgy7zn0ko: The NIF exceeds 8 megajoules, with a gain of more than 4.
4ikff567sf: According to the schedule revised in 2024, ITER, at Cadarache (France), will begin research with plasma around 2034 and with deuterium and tritium around 2039. Its goal is *Q* = 10.
12ctyf8dga4: The first fusion power stations will need tritium to start up, and the world has very little. The main civil source is **CANDU** heavy-water reactors: in their moderator, deuterium captures neutrons and gradually turns into tritium, which Canada extracts at the Darlington station (Ontario) for sale. A good part of ITER’s fuel will come from there. As many of those reactors approach the end of their lives, several studies warn that the available tritium could run short just when it is most needed. That is why it is so important that future reactors prove they can make their own with lithium blankets.
16f4jykx8i3: Tritium also has a highly coveted “daughter”: when it decays it becomes **helium-3**, a gas that barely exists on Earth and is used to detect neutrons and to cool experiments close to absolute zero. Almost all of the helium-3 in the United States came from the tritium in its weapons programme, which is gradually decaying in the stockpiles. After 11 September 2001, the massive deployment of radiation detectors at ports and borders sent demand soaring and, around 2008, caused a serious shortage. It is a curious example of how nuclear arsenals, basic science and border security depend on the same stocks of one isotope.
nr9hdpyazh: Radiation is measured with several quantities: the activity of a source (becquerel, curie), the dose absorbed by matter (gray, rad) and the equivalent dose, which estimates biological damage (sievert, rem).
17ucl66tc7q: Few things cause as much confusion as radiation units. There are several because they measure different things: how much a source decays, how much energy the radiation deposits in a material and how much biological damage that energy causes. In addition, old units, still widely used in the United States and in the literature on nuclear weapons, coexist with those of the International System. This article puts them in order.
2bl0lpgtwmi: **Activity** measures how many nuclei in a sample decay per second. Its international unit is the **becquerel** (Bq), equal to one decay per second, in honour of Henri Becquerel. It is a tiny unit: the human body contains about 4,000 Bq of natural potassium-40. The old unit is the **curie** (Ci), originally defined as the activity of one gram of radium and equivalent to 37,000 million becquerels. Activity says nothing about danger by itself: that depends on the type of radiation, its energy and whether the source is outside or inside the body.
12q4ibycxzj: The **roentgen** (R), named after Wilhelm Röntgen, the discoverer of X-rays, measures the ionisation that gamma or X-radiation produces in air. It was adopted in 1928 and widely used during the Cold War: the civil defence dosimeters and fallout maps of the period speak of roentgens per hour. Today it has fallen out of use, but it appears in many historical texts.
1wy3x85xain: The **absorbed dose** measures how much energy radiation deposits in each kilogram of matter. Its international unit is the **gray** (Gy), equal to one joule per kilogram, in honour of the British physicist Louis Harold Gray. The old unit is the **rad**, which equals one hundredth of a gray. One gray is a ridiculous amount of energy in thermal terms (it would raise the temperature of the body by less than a thousandth of a degree), but deposited in the form of ionising radiation it is enough to cause acute radiation syndrome.
ztdcso4hmd: Equivalent and effective dose: the sievert
1psswf1nuub: Not all radiation does the same damage with the same energy. An alpha particle concentrates its energy along a very short track and breaks DNA far more severely than a gamma ray. To take this into account, the absorbed dose is multiplied by a **weighting factor** according to the type of radiation, and the result is the **equivalent dose**, measured in **sieverts** (Sv), in honour of the Swedish physicist Rolf Sievert. The old unit is the **rem**, one hundredth of a sievert.
2fsd50b23i5: One step further is the **effective dose**, also in sieverts, which additionally weights the sensitivity of each organ to estimate the overall long-term cancer risk. It is the quantity used in radiological protection, in legal limits and in comparisons of medical doses.
hsjyyqnsom: Rule of thumb: for gamma rays, which are the dominant radiation in [[lluvia-radiactiva|fallout]], a roentgen, a rad and a rem are approximately equivalent, and 100 of any of them is roughly equal to 1 Gy or 1 Sv. For acute effects (those that appear within hours or days) specialists prefer to speak in grays; the sievert is reserved for long-term risk.
29sa2556e2e: Annual limit for the public (artificial exposures)
13kik8hr15i: World average natural radiation in a year
1gkxzjnya1s: Computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen
r07yn227g8: Areas of high natural radiation, such as Ramsar (Iran)
be5m1mefyy: Up to more than 100 mSv a year
2ecsnx3jz3x: Lethal dose for half of those exposed without treatment
mtipog4le0: Two ideas help in interpreting these figures. The first is that **time** matters a great deal: receiving 4 Gy in a few minutes can be fatal, whereas the same dose spread over a lifetime has a much smaller effect because cells repair part of the damage. The second is that, below about 100 mSv, the increase in cancer risk is so small that it is very difficult to measure; radiological protection assumes, out of prudence, that any increase in dose carries some risk, on the order of an additional 5% probability of fatal cancer per sievert. The effects of radiation on the body are covered in [[efectos-en-la-salud|Health effects]].
275qba6hx28: A brief history of the units
1tajgqykz3g: The curie is defined, in honour of Pierre and Marie Curie.
2888gf3g1qq: The roentgen is adopted as the unit of exposure to X-rays and gamma rays.
1kqukqaw7n1: The rad is introduced as the unit of absorbed dose; shortly afterwards, the rem.
q7lui8c47h: The General Conference on Weights and Measures adopts the gray and the becquerel.
228tm9l5pze: The sievert is adopted as the unit of equivalent dose.
1511jxpz9o7: The atomic bomb, or A-bomb, gets its energy from a fission chain reaction in uranium or plutonium. There are two ways of triggering it: the gun method and the implosion method.
2fosu9j4loa: A **fission weapon**, popularly called an *atomic bomb* or *A-bomb*, is a device that releases in a fraction of a microsecond the energy of a fission [[reaccion-en-cadena|chain reaction]] ([[fision|fission]]) in highly enriched uranium or in plutonium. It is the type of weapon that destroyed [[hiroshima|Hiroshima]] and [[nagasaki|Nagasaki]] in 1945, the first that every nuclear power developed and the basis on which thermonuclear weapons are built, whose *primary* is a fission weapon.
1vswwocwf1h: The whole problem of a fission weapon can be summed up in one sentence: the fissile material has to be kept in a subcritical state, so that it is safe, and at the chosen moment brought very quickly to a highly supercritical state, so that the reaction grows and releases a great deal of energy before the material itself disperses. As explained in [[masa-critica|Critical mass]], whether an assembly is subcritical or supercritical depends on its quantity, shape, density and surroundings. The two historical solutions act on those factors:
rqek4iosju: **Gun method**: two subcritical pieces of uranium are fired at each other and, when joined, form a supercritical assembly. It is simple but slow, and works only with uranium. See [[tipo-canon|Gun-type weapon]].
17zte2idyc0: **Implosion method**: a subcritical sphere is compressed symmetrically with conventional explosives; as its density increases, it becomes supercritical. It is much faster and more efficient, and is indispensable with plutonium. See [[implosion|Implosion weapon]].
2ewk5zl3fhc: As soon as the chain reaction begins to release energy, the material heats to tens of millions of degrees and tends to expand violently. As it expands it becomes less dense, more neutrons escape and the reaction stops. In the first weapons, only a small fraction of the material managed to undergo fission: the rest was dispersed unreacted, turned to vapour. That is why designers speak of **efficiency**: the proportion of the material that actually fissions. Little Boy was a very inefficient weapon; Fat Man, although it used a different material, made use of a considerably larger fraction.
wvnlx2lk6d: To gain time, the fissile core was surrounded by a heavy casing, called a **tamper**, whose inertia delayed the expansion by a few billionths of a second. Later, [[fision-potenciada|boosted fission]] multiplied the efficiency and allowed much smaller and lighter weapons.
d0k9mtc8gy: As shown in museums and in popular works, the components of a first-generation fission weapon can be described by the function they serve:
rahnvb3wvc: **Fissile material**: highly enriched uranium or plutonium, the “fuel” of the reaction.
2v0h983npa: **Assembly system**: the gun and its propellant charges, or the sphere of conventional explosive in the case of implosion.
20r45hho6fz: **Tamper and reflector**: layers that surround the core to delay its expansion and send neutrons back inwards.
16c6ryvjkhh: **Neutron initiator**: a source that supplies neutrons at exactly the right moment to start the chain reaction.
1j7povr7m9f: **Fuzes and arming system**: radar altimeters, barometers and timers that decide the height of the burst, together with the safety devices that prevent an accidental detonation.
xxp1y4s212: **Casing**: the aerodynamic shell with its tail, which allows the whole assembly to be dropped from an aircraft or launched by a missile.
10wbszoesnx: Fission weapons cover an enormous range. At one end are the smallest ever deployed, such as the W54 warhead of the [[artilleria-nuclear|Davy Crockett]], of between 10 and 20 tonnes of TNT. At the other, the largest American pure-fission test, Ivy King (1952), with 500 kilotons, and the British Orange Herald (1957), with 720 kilotons. Above a few hundred kilotons, the method becomes impracticable: too much material would have to be accumulated in a single device, with the resulting problems of safety and cost. For yields of megatons, recourse had to be made to the [[bomba-de-hidrogeno|hydrogen bomb]].
16ju33j5qsc: When a fission weapon yields far less than expected because the reaction starts too soon or the assembly is faulty, it is called a *fizzle* in the jargon. North Korea’s first test, in 2006, with a yield of less than a kiloton, is considered a partial case of this kind.
ldf5jbu0ww: The first fission weapons of each country
1aqs7ypd5ee: USSR: RDS-1, very similar to Fat Man thanks to espionage (see [[programa-sovietico|Soviet programme]]).
qgcaa9m5o2: United Kingdom: Hurricane, in the Montebello Islands (Australia).
106wqj3eyqf: France: Gerboise Bleue, in the Algerian Sahara.
3apte5pfl1: China: Test 596, at Lop Nur; uranium implosion.
uj82izafu1: India: Smiling Buddha, presented as a “peaceful nuclear explosion”.
11hrab2c7z9: South Africa builds six gun-type weapons, later dismantled.
1jvb8k8e7tm: Pakistan: Chagai-I, two weeks after the Indian tests.
16mgwr8v6yp: Israel has never confirmed or denied possessing nuclear weapons, although an arsenal has been attributed to it since the late 1960s. See [[potencias-nucleares|Nuclear powers]] and [[pruebas-nucleares|Nuclear tests]].
1v4gpvfge4c: The simplest design of fission weapon: inside a tube, one piece of uranium is fired at another to form a supercritical assembly. It was the method of Little Boy, the Hiroshima bomb, and of the South African weapons.
a79f1jlyso: The **gun-type weapon** is the simplest way to build a [[arma-de-fision|fission weapon]], and the only one that has been used in war without having been tested beforehand. The idea is that of an artillery gun placed inside a bomb: at one end of the tube there is a piece of highly enriched uranium, the *target*; at the other, another piece, the *projectile*. Neither is capable on its own of sustaining a [[reaccion-en-cadena|chain reaction]]. When a conventional propellant charge, like that of a gun, is fired, the projectile travels along the tube and fits into the target. The two pieces together form a supercritical assembly and the chain reaction is set off.
wp30g9wehk: Gun principle: two subcritical pieces, separated along a tube, are joined when the projectile is fired at the target and form a supercritical assembly. Conceptual diagram.
1ceyqdckb33: Why it works only with uranium
15g2t2gbnby: The method has a fundamental flaw: it is **slow**. On a human scale, the projectile travels extremely fast, but on a nuclear scale the time it takes to cover the final stretch is an eternity. During that interval, the assembly is already slightly supercritical but not yet complete. If a stray neutron appears at that moment, the reaction begins too early, with the material still poorly assembled, and the energy generated pushes the pieces apart before an appreciable fraction can undergo fission. The result would be an explosion with a yield far below that planned: a **predetonation**.
24x9hti87hj: With uranium-235 the risk is acceptable, because uranium undergoes hardly any spontaneous fission and very few “stray” neutrons appear within it. With reactor-produced plutonium it is unacceptable: it inevitably contains plutonium-240, which undergoes spontaneous fission and emits neutrons continuously. In the spring of 1944, Emilio Segrè’s group at [[los-alamos|Los Alamos]] measured plutonium from the first reactors and found that its spontaneous fission rate was far higher than that of the laboratory samples used until then. In July 1944 the **Thin Man**, a plutonium gun bomb more than five metres long that was already under development, was cancelled, and the whole effort of the laboratory was turned to [[implosion|implosion]]. The gun design was reserved for uranium, and was simplified into a shorter bomb: Little Boy.
d2gvhl7tlj: Little Boy, uranium gun-type bomb dropped on Hiroshima. Length 3 m, diameter 71 cm, about 4.4 tonnes.
8nu37s6tp: 6 August 1945, 08:15, from the B-29 Enola Gay
5zotgkmijv: About 580–600 m above Shima Hospital, Hiroshima
11sebp4ypap: Little Boy was designed at Los Alamos under the direction of US Navy Captain William “Deak” Parsons, with the geophysicist Francis Birch in charge of the final design. Its elongated shape is due to the gun tube, which runs through much of the bomb. The scientists were so confident in the method that they did not test it before use: the Trinity test was of an implosion device. Moreover, in the summer of 1945 there was enriched uranium for only one bomb of this type, and spending it on a test would have delayed its use by months.
119ek8xo4vs: The weapon was assembled on the island of Tinian, in the Marianas. As several B-29s had crashed on take-off in the preceding days, Parsons decided to complete the arming during the flight so that an accident on the runway would not cause a nuclear explosion. He did so, with the help of Lieutenant Morris Jeppson, aboard the Enola Gay, piloted by Colonel Paul Tibbets. The bomb fell for about 44 seconds and exploded at a height of about 600 metres. Its fuzes were small radar altimeters that measured the distance to the ground, with barometers and timers as backup.
1xozzlve1k9: The explosion killed tens of thousands of people instantly or in the following days and, by the end of 1945, the number of victims was estimated at between 90,000 and 140,000. The full story of the bombing is told in [[hiroshima|Hiroshima]] and that of the survivors in [[hibakusha|Hibakusha]]. Paradoxically, Little Boy was a very inefficient weapon: only a small fraction of the uranium it contained underwent fission; the rest was dispersed unreacted.
28vs8zgwzxv: Works only with highly enriched uranium, the most expensive material to produce
2c7bkp4p1id: Needs no nuclear tests to be relied on
19i92tbrfry: Makes very poor use of the material: needs much more than an implosion for the same yield
19qdklwiu1q: Very robust against impacts, useful for penetrator bombs and artillery shells
1zrnfa5eimp: Long and heavy because of the gun tube
aghz0gvsao: Dangerous in accidents: an impact, a fire or the ingress of water could favour an unwanted reaction
133ff6rjhr4: The United States built a few more Little Boy units after the war and retired them in 1950. The gun method survived in niches where its robustness was an advantage: the Mk 8 and Mk 11 penetrator bombs, designed to pass through soil or concrete before exploding, and the 280 mm (W9, that of the [[artilleria-nuclear|Grable]] test) and 203 mm (W33) artillery shells, which had to withstand the acceleration of being fired. All were retired. Modern weapons use implosion, which is far more efficient and safe.
1z4oyr2n00: South Africa: the only arsenal voluntarily dismantled
12c2n3xvm9n: Precisely because of its simplicity, the gun design was the one chosen by South Africa, the only country that has built its own nuclear weapons and dismantled them by its own decision. The programme was launched in the 1970s, in the midst of a border war in Angola and with growing international isolation because of *apartheid*. The country enriched its own uranium at the Valindaba plant, near Pretoria, with a locally developed method.
23c3d42kzzi: In 1977, a Soviet satellite detected the shafts of a nuclear test being prepared in the Kalahari Desert, and pressure from Washington and Moscow forced the site to be abandoned. Between 1982 and 1989 six gun-type weapons were completed, and a seventh was left half-finished. Their function, as their leaders later explained, was above all political: a threat of a test that would force the Western powers to intervene in the event of an invasion. In 1989, President Frederik de Klerk ordered them dismantled; in July 1991 South Africa acceded to the Non-Proliferation Treaty and in March 1993 De Klerk publicly revealed the existence of the programme. The IAEA verified the dismantlement. The so-called Vela incident, a double flash detected by an American satellite over the Indian Ocean in September 1979, remains unexplained officially; many analysts attribute it to an Israeli test, perhaps with South African collaboration.
xb79vzhrxh: Because it is the simplest design, the gun type is the one of greatest concern in nuclear terrorism scenarios. That is why the protection of highly enriched uranium and its conversion to low-enriched uranium in research reactors around the world are international security priorities.
7avpe8s3t8: In an implosion weapon, a subcritical sphere of fissile material is compressed symmetrically by conventional explosives until it becomes supercritical. It is the principle of the Trinity Gadget, of Fat Man and of all modern nuclear weapons.
1ozoql5u43p: The **implosion weapon** solves the plutonium problem with an idea as brilliant as it was hard to put into practice. Instead of joining two pieces, as in the [[tipo-canon|gun method]], one starts with a single sphere of fissile material which, at its normal density, is subcritical. That sphere is surrounded by a thick layer of conventional explosive. When this is detonated, a shock wave is generated that advances towards the centre and squeezes the sphere from all directions at once. The metal, compressed by pressures of millions of atmospheres, increases in density; the nuclei are brought closer together, fewer neutrons escape and the assembly becomes highly supercritical in a tiny fraction of the time a gun requires.
5s773rpw77: Implosion principle: the shock wave of the converging explosive compresses a subcritical sphere symmetrically; as its density increases, it becomes supercritical. Conceptual diagram.
1x59gdn208c: As explained in [[plutonio|Plutonium]] and in [[tipo-canon|Gun-type weapon]], reactor-made plutonium contains plutonium-240, an isotope that undergoes spontaneous fission and emits a continuous flux of neutrons. In a slow assembly, one of those neutrons would almost certainly start the reaction before the assembly was complete and the bomb would destroy itself with a ridiculous yield. The only way out was to assemble much faster, so fast that the stray neutrons would not have time to spoil it. Implosion achieved this. When the problem was confirmed in the summer of 1944, Los Alamos went in a few weeks from regarding implosion as a side line to staking everything on it.
11zxdbvp0wp: Implosion had another advantage as well: since compression raises the density, the same supercriticality is achieved with much less material, and a larger fraction of it undergoes fission. That is why it is the principle of all modern nuclear weapons, whether of uranium, plutonium or both, and of the *primaries* of [[bomba-de-hidrogeno|thermonuclear weapons]].
1nlba4p265b: It was proposed by the physicist Seth Neddermeyer in April 1943, at one of the first meetings at Los Alamos. His idea was to wrap a shell of fissile material in explosive and crush it inwards. Many of his colleagues considered it impractical, and Neddermeyer worked for months with a small team, blowing up metal cylinders surrounded by explosive in a nearby canyon. The results were discouraging: the cylinders came out twisted and asymmetrical.
uaziee7u0n: In September 1943, the mathematician John von Neumann visited the laboratory and pointed out that, with enough explosive, compression would not merely bring the material together but would squeeze it to densities far above normal, which drastically reduced the amount of material needed. From then on implosion was taken seriously, and in 1944 the chemist George Kistiakowsky, an explosives expert from Harvard, took over the division devoted to it. In August 1944, Oppenheimer reorganised the laboratory around that objective.
1qivt3u17qr: The problem was **symmetry**. A shock wave that starts at the surface of an explosive is not naturally spherical: each detonation point generates a wave that expands in all directions, and the waves from neighbouring points collide, forming jets and zones of irregular pressure. If the compression is uneven, even slightly, the sphere does not compress but deforms: it flattens, cracks or squirts jets of metal through the weak points, and the reaction does not reach its potential. It was like trying to crush an orange with your hands without the juice escaping between your fingers.
1iwptqx1upn: The solution was the so-called **explosive lenses**, proposed by the British physicist James Tuck and by von Neumann himself. Just as a glass lens shapes a beam of light, these pieces of explosive shaped the shock wave so that it reached the whole surface of the sphere at the same time. Making them with the necessary precision and getting them all to fire practically simultaneously was one of the greatest technical challenges of the [[proyecto-manhattan|Manhattan Project]]; the specific design of these systems remains protected information. To check progress, Bruno Rossi’s team developed diagnostic methods that made it possible to “see” the compression inside the metal at the instant of the explosion.
2aaqtgkpjvl: The outer shape of Fat Man, a large sphere with a tail, is a direct consequence of this principle: the bomb was, in essence, an enormous sphere of explosive with the core at its centre, surrounded by the fuzes, the detonation wiring and an ellipsoidal casing.
l9ei7c7lyt: The Gadget, the first nuclear device in history, on its 30-metre tower at Alamogordo (New Mexico). It was a plutonium implosion device without a bomb casing.
h0wn2sbdls: Since implosion was so novel and so uncertain, it was decided to test it before using it. The test device, known simply as *the Gadget*, was assembled at a ranch in the Jornada del Muerto desert in New Mexico and hoisted to the top of a 30-metre steel tower. On 16 July 1945, at 5:29 in the morning, it exploded with a yield that was re-estimated in 2021 at 24.8 kilotons, well above what many scientists had bet on. The desert sand fused into a greenish glass that was called **trinitite**. Oppenheimer would later recall a verse from the *Bhagavad Gita*: “Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.” See [[prueba-trinity|The Trinity test]].
1j5gluvln4i: Fat Man, plutonium implosion bomb dropped on Nagasaki. Length 3.25 m, diameter 1.52 m, about 4.7 tonnes.
2ga601l59rg: About 500 m above the Urakami valley, Nagasaki
1y5xzlf2w0w: Fat Man was, in essence, the same design as the Gadget inside a bomb casing. Its name, like those of Little Boy and Thin Man, is attributed to the physicist Robert Serber, who took it from characters in detective novels and films. On 9 August 1945 the B-29 Bockscar, piloted by Major Charles Sweeney, took off from Tinian for its primary target, Kokura. The city was covered in smoke and haze, and after several passes and with fuel running short, the aircraft headed for the secondary target, Nagasaki. Through a gap in the clouds, the bombardier Kermit Beahan released the bomb, which exploded over the industrial Urakami valley, some three kilometres from the intended aiming point. The hills surrounding the valley protected part of the city, but it is estimated that by the end of 1945 between 60,000 and 80,000 people had died. See [[nagasaki|Nagasaki]].
21ssih9x86q: The first implosion bombs were assembled almost by hand, in a process lasting days that required teams of specialists. From 1949 mass-produced versions arrived, such as the Mk 4, and during the 1950s the design was refined to make it smaller, lighter, more efficient and safer. The first Soviet bomb, the RDS-1 (1949), was a very close copy of Fat Man, thanks to the information supplied by the spy Klaus Fuchs; see [[programa-sovietico|Soviet programme]].
2fgglzr4e4q: Modern weapons incorporate safety principles that derive directly from implosion. Because the reaction occurs only if the compression is almost perfectly symmetrical, a well-designed weapon is **one-point safe**: if a fire or an impact sets off the explosive on one side only, a conventional explosion occurs that disperses the material, but not a nuclear explosion. This is what happened in the accidents at [[palomares|Palomares]] (1966) and [[thule|Thule]] (1968), where the explosive of several bombs detonated on hitting the ground and contaminated the area with plutonium, without a nuclear explosion. Insensitive explosives, far harder to detonate by accident, are now also used.
rsguqmvtxt: A small quantity of fusion fuel at the centre of a fission weapon produces, when heated, a burst of fast neutrons that multiplies the efficiency of the fission. It is the technique that made small, light weapons possible.
1r7o1revz6n: **Boosted fission** (*boosting*) is a technique that combines fission and fusion in a single stage. A small quantity of a mixture of deuterium and tritium is introduced into a [[arma-de-fision|fission weapon]]. When the chain reaction is already under way and the centre of the weapon reaches tens of millions of degrees, that mixture fuses. The energy contributed by [[fusion|fusion]] is modest, but each reaction releases a very fast neutron, and that burst of neutrons causes many additional fissions just when the fission reaction would be starting to die away through the expansion of the material.
1t666oilrbi: The result is that a much larger fraction of the material undergoes fission. It is, then, an accelerator of fission, not a thermonuclear weapon properly speaking: most of the energy still comes from fission. Its great value lies in what it allows: much smaller and lighter weapons for the same yield, **variable-yield** weapons and compact primaries for [[bomba-de-hidrogeno|hydrogen bombs]]. The vast majority of modern weapons are considered to use boosted primaries.
1sj4l1ugkjm: Edward Teller and other Los Alamos scientists put forward the idea of boosting fission with fusion.
20l2edc9w4w: Greenhouse Item test at Enewetak Atoll: first demonstration of boosted fission, with a yield of 45.5 kt, roughly double that of the same weapon unboosted.
20s34nytxfn: The USSR tests the RDS-6s, Andrei Sakharov’s layered design, or *sloika*, with 400 kt. It combined layers of fusion fuel and uranium; it was a different concept, halfway between boosting and the thermonuclear weapon, which could not be scaled up to megatons.
1j5ve38jb4q: The United Kingdom tests Orange Herald, with 720 kt, initially presented as a hydrogen bomb. It is now considered the largest fission weapon ever tested, with a small contribution from fusion.
a8t0q5plka: North Korea claims to have tested a hydrogen bomb; the observed yield led many analysts to think that it was rather a boosted weapon.
250fjl1hoez: Tritium is [[radiactividad|radioactive]], with a half-life of about 12.3 years: each year around 5% of what a weapon contains decays. That is why boosted weapons need their fusion fuel to be replenished periodically, and why tritium production is a permanent part of the military nuclear industry of any power. An arsenal without new tritium would lose a good part of its capability over the years. See [[combustibles-de-fusion|Fusion fuels]].
1nvz1z5dghj: Boosted is not the same as thermonuclear
2cquj0tmts5: From hundreds of kilotons to megatons
zjyrjelrb: The details of how the fusion fuel is introduced and used in a boosted weapon are secret. Only the general principle described here is publicly known.
1lisyl0ieji: Tritium, a clock ticking for nuclear arsenals
2wnv4umu3b: Because tritium decays, the capability of an arsenal of boosted weapons depends on an industrial chain that cannot be allowed to stop. The United States learned this in the late 1980s: the ageing Savannah River production reactors in South Carolina, beset by safety problems, were shut down in 1988, and for about fifteen years the country made no new tritium. It managed because, at the end of the Cold War, it dismantled thousands of warheads and recovered the tritium they contained, but that stockpile dwindled every year.
1nczpf9aovc: The solution was an unusual one: since 2003, special lithium-bearing rods have been irradiated in a civilian reactor operated by the Tennessee Valley Authority, the Watts Bar plant, and the tritium is then extracted at Savannah River. It is one of the few cases in which a commercial power station contributes directly to a weapons programme, and it has sparked debate about the separation between civil and military uses of nuclear energy. Because of its strategic value, tritium and the equipment for producing and handling it are subject to international export controls.
22a7epwf5l9: The five Savannah River production reactors come into operation, making plutonium and tritium for the US arsenal.

1b1gnyhge21: Tritium is recovered from warheads dismantled after the Cold War.

2b49icnzwbj: How we know a weapon is boosted
d2l4ve0kvd: Because designs are secret, independent analysts deduce the use of boosting indirectly. One clue is the relationship between size and yield: a small, light warhead with a yield of hundreds of kilotons can hardly be a pure fission weapon. Another is industry: a country that builds facilities to produce tritium probably needs it for its weapons. A third is [[pruebas-nucleares|nuclear tests]]: seismic stations make it possible to estimate the yield of an underground explosion, and the monitoring network of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty can detect the radioactive gases that escape from it, although they almost never reveal details of the design.
zrlono5tbv: This is how North Korea's January 2016 test was interpreted: Pyongyang announced it as a [[bomba-de-hidrogeno|hydrogen bomb]], but its yield, estimated at about 10 kilotons, fitted a boosted fission weapon better. The September 2017 test, with an estimated yield of the order of 100 to 250 kilotons according to various studies, already seemed to correspond to a two-stage weapon.
232rec3n7y8: Boosting also has an arms-control dimension. Mature arsenals can be maintained for decades without testing, provided they replenish their tritium; by contrast, a country that wants to miniaturise its weapons for the first time almost certainly needs to test them. That is why the ban on testing is regarded as an effective barrier against the development of compact, powerful weapons.
3wtpdauvqj: Thermonuclear weapons, or H-bombs, use a fission explosion, the primary, to compress and ignite a second, fusion component, the secondary. Their yield can reach tens of megatons.
u35fx3n9pi: The **hydrogen bomb**, **H-bomb** or **thermonuclear weapon** obtains most of its energy from the [[fusion|fusion]] of heavy isotopes of hydrogen. Because fusion occurs only at temperatures and pressures that only a [[fision|fission]] explosion can create, every thermonuclear weapon contains a fission weapon inside it that acts as a trigger. The leap in yield compared with atomic bombs was gigantic: from Hiroshima's 15 kilotons, yields rose in seven years to the 10,400 of [[ivy-mike|Ivy Mike]], and in sixteen to the 50,000 of the [[tsar-bomba|Tsar Bomba]].
1akmed882a3: The idea of using an atomic bomb to ignite heavy hydrogen arose even before the atomic bomb existed. In September 1941, during a walk in New York, Enrico Fermi remarked to Edward Teller that a fission explosion might be able to heat deuterium enough to fuse it. Teller became obsessed with the idea. In the summer of 1942, at a secret seminar convened by Oppenheimer in Berkeley, Teller presented what would soon be called **the Super**, and during the war he kept working on it at Los Alamos, often to the detriment of the tasks he was assigned. See [[la-super|The Super]].
1e9yxjha11o: The original concept, later known as the **classical Super**, consisted of using a fission bomb to ignite one end of a long cylinder of liquid deuterium, in the hope that thermonuclear burning would propagate by itself along the cylinder, like a flame along a fuse. If it worked, the yield would have no limit: it would be enough to lengthen the cylinder.
1iintg4gtxz: Why the classical Super did not work
oevgtycywd: In 1950, the Polish mathematician Stanisław Ulam and his collaborator Cornelius Everett made a hand calculation, with slide rules and mechanical calculators, of what would happen. Soon afterwards, Ulam and Fermi repeated the analysis in more detail, and the first electronic computers confirmed their conclusions: the Super would not work. The fuel, at the normal density of a liquid, lost energy as radiation far faster than fusion generated it. The “flame” died out before it could spread. Moreover, the design demanded enormous quantities of tritium, which was extremely expensive to produce. Teller, who had championed the idea for years, suffered a severe blow.
27t381o7hpn: Meanwhile, on 29 August 1949, the USSR had tested its first atomic bomb, years earlier than Washington had expected. In October, the General Advisory Committee of the Atomic Energy Commission, chaired by Oppenheimer and including Fermi and Isidor Rabi, recommended against undertaking a crash programme for the hydrogen bomb, on technical and moral grounds: in an annex, Fermi and Rabi described it as a weapon whose unlimited power made it an instrument of genocide. In January 1950 it emerged that the physicist Klaus Fuchs, who had worked at Los Alamos, had spied for the USSR. On 31 January 1950, President Truman announced that the United States would go ahead with the hydrogen bomb. Oppenheimer's opposition was one of the arguments used in 1954 to revoke his security clearance (see [[oppenheimer|Oppenheimer]]).
22ld0rhapbr: The solution came in early 1951. Ulam proposed that, instead of heating the fuel directly, the energy of a first fission explosion should be used to **compress** it before igniting it, since at higher density burning is far more efficient and loses less energy. Teller added that this compression could be achieved better with the **radiation** from the first explosion than with its shock wave. On 9 March 1951 the two signed the report describing the concept, known ever since as the **Teller-Ulam design** or *radiation implosion*. Who deserved credit for the idea became the subject of a bitter dispute between them for the rest of their lives.
ya5s16wmuh: Conceptual diagram of a two-stage weapon: the fission primary emits a burst of radiation that fills the case and compresses the secondary before the blast wave of the explosion arrives.
7g7z3kmsbf: As described in popular accounts, the concept has three main elements:
hzjxxp967z: **The primary**: a fission weapon, normally [[implosion|implosion]]-type and [[fision-potenciada|boosted]], which acts as the trigger.
15y5wu4qfyz: **The secondary**: a separate component containing the fusion fuel and fissionable material.
1d7mvad7pvu: **The radiation case**: a casing that encloses the two.
1w36q5qxc21: When the primary detonates, most of its energy escapes in the form of X-rays, which travel at the speed of light, much faster than the material debris of the explosion. This radiation fills the interior of the case and heats its surfaces; the resulting pressure compresses the secondary with enormous force and very symmetrically, in a tiny fraction of a second, before the primary's shock wave can destroy everything. The compressed, heated fusion fuel ignites. The specific details of how this is achieved are state secrets in every nuclear power.
1kccqhvubq5: Conceptual diagram of a two-stage thermonuclear weapon: primary, secondary and radiation case. It does not depict any real weapon.
1ltm7841z8l: On 9 May 1951, the **Greenhouse George** test showed that the radiation from a fission explosion could ignite a small quantity of fusion fuel. On 1 November 1952 came the definitive test: **Ivy Mike**, on Enewetak Atoll, released 10.4 megatons and wiped the islet of Elugelab off the map, leaving a crater almost two kilometres across. The device, nicknamed *Sausage*, was designed in detail by the young physicist Richard Garwin from the Teller-Ulam scheme.
bnyytgjkhm: The Sausage device of Ivy Mike: about 6 m tall, 2 m in diameter and around 80 tonnes with its cooling equipment. It was not a usable weapon but an experiment the size of a building.
4ifnncvlex: From Ivy Mike to the “dry” weapon
dq61ozxngv: Ivy Mike used liquid deuterium at more than 250 degrees below zero, which required gigantic cryogenic equipment. It was impossible to drop it from an aircraft. The next step was to replace the liquid deuterium with **lithium deuteride**, a solid that is stable at room temperature, in which neutrons convert the lithium into tritium at the very moment of the explosion (see [[combustibles-de-fusion|Fusion fuels]]). Weapons that use it are called **dry**. The first US test of this kind was [[castle-bravo|Castle Bravo]], on 1 March 1954, which gave a yield almost three times higher than predicted and caused the worst contamination episode in the history of US testing.
ihsj80c106: **Scalable yield**: a fission weapon is limited by the amount of material that can be kept subcritical until the last moment. In a thermonuclear weapon, the fusion fuel has no critical mass: it cannot start a chain reaction on its own and, in principle, as much as desired can be added. A secondary can even be used to ignite a third stage (see [[armas-de-tres-etapas|Three-stage weapons]]).
22guenoxc0n: **Higher yield per kilogram**: fusion releases more energy per unit of mass than fission. The US B41 bomb of the 1960s reached about 25 megatons with a weight of under five tonnes, some 5 kilotons per kilogram of weapon, the highest ratio known.
16xde5ww21k: **Fission-fusion-fission**: the neutrons from fusion are so fast that they can split even uranium-238 nuclei, which is of no use for a chain reaction. If the secondary is surrounded by natural or depleted uranium, it fissions and contributes an enormous share of the energy. That is why, in many thermonuclear weapons, around half the yield comes from fission, and why they generate abundant [[lluvia-radiactiva|fallout]]. Weapons in which this final fission is deliberately reduced are called “clean”.
260c3go8ex0: The USSR followed its own path. Andrei Sakharov proposed a layered design, the *sloika* (“layer cake”), in 1948, tested in August 1953 with 400 kilotons; it was an advance, but it could not be scaled up to megatons. In 1954, Sakharov, Yakov Zeldovich and others arrived independently at radiation implosion, the so-called “third idea”, and on 22 November 1955 they tested the **RDS-37**, their first two-stage bomb, with 1.6 megatons. The United Kingdom, cut off from the United States by the McMahon Act of 1946, developed its own design and, after the partial failure of the first Grapple tests, achieved it in November 1957 with Grapple X; the following year a new agreement restored nuclear cooperation with Washington. China took only 32 months to go from its first atomic bomb to its first H-bomb, tested on 17 June 1967, the fastest leap on record. France achieved it on 24 August 1968 with the Canopus test.
17o41bygeyv: Ivy Mike, 1 Nov 1952 (device); Castle Bravo, 1 Mar 1954 (dry weapon)
2etipndkjng: The secret of the Teller-Ulam design was kept for decades. In 1979, the US Government tried to obtain a court order preventing the magazine *The Progressive* from publishing an article by the journalist Howard Morland that reconstructed the concept from public sources; the case was dropped when other publications disseminated similar information. What is publicly known today is the general principle described in this article; the engineering that makes it work remains secret.
1oh3d8v3yx6: A thermonuclear weapon can use the energy of its secondary to ignite an even larger third stage. This is how the greatest yields in history were reached, such as the 50 megatons of the Tsar Bomba.
6x6njsv0wq: If a fission explosion can ignite a fusion secondary, why not use that secondary to ignite another, even larger one in turn? That is the concept of **three-stage weapons**: a fission primary, a thermonuclear secondary and a third stage that receives the secondary's energy. In theory the process could be chained indefinitely; in practice, the yield of a two-stage weapon is more than enough for any military purpose, and three-stage weapons were a Cold War rarity. Their design details have never been made public.

15phyc07q9b: 27 t; about 8 m long and 2.1 m in diameter
1ccz318rajp: The Tsar Bomba was the largest explosion ever caused by human beings. It was designed by a team at the Arzamas-16 weapons institute that included Andrei Sakharov, Viktor Adamsky, Yuri Babayev, Yuri Smirnov and Yuri Trutnev, on the personal orders of Nikita Khrushchev, who wanted a show of strength in the midst of the Berlin Crisis and on the eve of the 22nd Congress of the Communist Party. The original design called for about 100 megatons. However, a good part of that yield would have come from the fission of uranium in the final stages, with an enormous amount of fallout that would also have fallen on Soviet territory. The designers **replaced that uranium with inert material**, which halved the yield and made it, paradoxically, one of the “cleanest” weapons in history in proportion to its size: barely 3% of its energy came from fission.
1npk51sheww: The bomb, so large that it did not fit in the aircraft's bay and hung partly outside, was dropped from about 10,500 metres. A parachute weighing several tonnes slowed its fall to give the bomber time to get away some 45 kilometres; even so, the blast wave made the aircraft drop abruptly by nearly a kilometre. The fireball reached about 8 kilometres in diameter and came close to touching the ground despite the height of the burst. The cloud rose to more than 60 kilometres, seven times the height of Everest. The flash was seen from a thousand kilometres away, windows were broken in Norway and Finland, and the atmospheric pressure wave circled the Earth three times. See [[tsar-bomba|Tsar Bomba]].
1lgqp7qwijb: Militarily, the Tsar Bomba was almost useless: too heavy for practical use and deliverable only by a slow aircraft that was easy to intercept. Its value was political. Sakharov himself, who years later would become a dissident and Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1975), wrote in his memoirs about his growing unease at the arms race as a result of these tests.
2abubqnv1qe: The US **B41** bomb, in service from 1961 to 1976 with a yield of up to 25 megatons, is believed to have been a three-stage weapon too. It was the highest-yield weapon the United States ever deployed and, at under five tonnes, the one with the highest yield per kilogram in history. The USSR deployed warheads of about 20 megatons on the heavy R-36 missiles. From the 1970s onwards, improved missile accuracy and the [[energia-y-tnt|scaling law]] (several small weapons destroy more surface area than one large one) led the superpowers to abandon these giants in favour of smaller, more numerous warheads.
2c99ggtylfh: The history of multistage weapons also offers an example of how unpredictable their physics can be. **Castle Bravo**, tested on 1 March 1954 at Bikini Atoll, was the first US “dry” hydrogen bomb, with lithium deuteride as fuel. About 6 megatons were expected. It went off with 15, the largest US explosion in history. The error was due to the lithium. In addition to lithium-6, the fuel contained a large proportion of **lithium-7**, the more common isotope, which the designers considered practically inert. It was not: under bombardment by very fast neutrons, lithium-7 also broke apart, producing additional tritium and more neutrons, and the reaction was far more intense than calculated.
pdaouyt9qp: The consequences were serious. A shift in the winds carried the fallout towards the inhabited atolls of Rongelap and Utirik, whose inhabitants, evacuated late, suffered burns, radiation sickness and, years later, thyroid cancers. The Japanese fishing boat *Daigo Fukuryū Maru* (*Lucky Dragon No. 5*), which was fishing outside the exclusion zone, was covered in radioactive ash; its radio operator, Aikichi Kuboyama, died months later. The incident triggered a wave of protests in Japan, inspired the film *Godzilla* (1954) and gave international momentum to the movement for a ban on testing. Castle Bravo was a two-stage weapon, but its lesson applied to all of them: the physics of these reactions could surprise their own designers. See [[castle-bravo|Castle Bravo]].
zrw5yzv38l: The neutron bomb, or enhanced radiation weapon, is a small thermonuclear weapon designed so that a larger share of its energy escapes as neutrons. It was conceived to stop columns of tanks and generated intense controversy in the 1970s.
1dgdmc0trxn: The **neutron bomb**, whose technical name is **enhanced radiation weapon**, is a low-yield thermonuclear weapon, typically around one kiloton, designed so that a much larger proportion than usual of its energy comes out as fast neutrons from fusion. In a conventional weapon of similar yield, the blast wave and heat are the dominant effects; in a neutron bomb, the [[radiacion-inicial|initial radiation]] reaches distances comparable to or greater than those of the destructive blast wave.
wj4khgd2aj: The American physicist Samuel Cohen conceived it in 1958 at the Livermore laboratory. His aim was a very specific Cold War military problem: the numerical superiority of Warsaw Pact tanks in central Europe. A tank's armour protects well against blast and heat, but neutrons pass straight through it. A neutron bomb could incapacitate crews over a larger radius than that in which vehicles were destroyed, with less collateral blast damage to the West German cities where the fighting would take place. In addition, neutrons could disable enemy missile warheads, so they were also used in anti-ballistic missiles such as the Sprint.
1iy9iwtbryz: The popular idea that it “kills people and spares buildings” is a misleading simplification. A neutron bomb is still a nuclear weapon, with a blast wave, thermal pulse and fireball that destroy everything within a considerable radius. The difference lies in the outer margin, where radiation is still lethal but the blast wave no longer knocks buildings down. There, exposed people would receive doses capable of killing them within hours or weeks. Neutrons, moreover, make the materials they pass through radioactive.

1tggoili7u9: The controversy in Europe was so intense because it touched a raw nerve: a weapon that made tactical nuclear war more “acceptable” could also make it more likely. 22wny7b0fmb: How a larger fraction of neutrons is made to escape is an aspect of the design that has not been made public and that this encyclopaedia does not address. The effect of neutrons on people is described in [[efectos-en-la-salud|Health effects]].
25d8zezllst: Neutrons carry no electric charge, so they are not slowed by the electrons of atoms, as other radiations are. 1nlg6ino088: The Soviet response was as simple as the problem: many tanks of the 1970s and 1980s, such as the T-64, T-72 and T-80, carried hydrogen-rich liners inside, sometimes with lead or boron, to reduce the radiation reaching the crew. voj9refqnv: A dose that does not kill instantly

7h9b37iakr: Tank formations and enemy warheads in flight
102tc3syi7t: No enhanced radiation weapon is known to be deployed today. 1d8p21cqool: A dirty bomb, or radiological dispersal device, combines a conventional explosive with radioactive material to contaminate an area. It produces no nuclear explosion; its main effect is fear, contamination and the cost of clean-up.
1jlkoq41k0u: A **dirty bomb**, or radiological dispersal device, is a device that uses a conventional explosive to scatter radioactive material over an area. **It is not a nuclear weapon**: there is no fission or fusion, and the explosion is that of an ordinary bomb. What distinguishes it is the contamination it leaves behind. Because of its relative simplicity, it is one of the scenarios that most concern security services, although, fortunately, one has never been successfully detonated in an attack.
1ov03y72qdi: Expert analyses agree that most casualties of a dirty bomb would be caused by the explosion, not by radiation. As it disperses, the radioactive material is diluted and the doses the population would receive, except very close to the point of the explosion, would be low: the long-term increase in cancer risk would be small. That is why it is often described as a **weapon of mass disruption** rather than of mass destruction. Its most serious effects would lie elsewhere:
2dfuqkk8cbl: **Panic and fear**: fear of radiation can provoke chaotic evacuations and swamp hospitals with healthy people seeking to be examined.
no2n4mm9hy: **Contamination**: streets, buildings and vehicles would be contaminated and might have to be closed for months or years.
1awy3rv41o7: **Economic cost**: decontaminating a dense urban area can be extraordinarily expensive, and in some cases buildings would have to be demolished.
5mu8yqysx: The protective measure recommended by the authorities in the event of an explosion of this kind is simple: move away from the smoke and dust, go inside a building, remove outer clothing, wash and follow official instructions. See [[proteccion-civil|Civil protection]].

2cuj2h3mwtb: A delivery vehicle is the means that carries a nuclear weapon to its target: aircraft, ballistic and cruise missiles, hypersonic glide vehicles, torpedoes or artillery shells. Each has advantages and drawbacks that have shaped nuclear strategy.

26ualunvo0r: Rarely has a laboratory finding changed the course of history so quickly. Between 17 December 1938, when two chemists in Berlin identified barium in an irradiated uranium sample, and the summer of 1939, when the Second World War broke out, the scientific community went from not even suspecting that a heavy nucleus could break apart to discussing in hushed tones the possibility of a bomb of unprecedented power. This article tells how that idea came about; the physical phenomenon is explained in [[fision|Nuclear fission]] and in [[reaccion-en-cadena|Chain reaction]].
29vv87pd8q0: The background: the neutron and the Rome experiments
7ue4iv6euv: The story begins in 1932, when James Chadwick discovered the **neutron** at Cambridge, a particle with no electric charge which, for that very reason, can approach a nucleus without being repelled (see [[atomo|The atom]]). It was the ideal tool for exploring the interior of matter. In Rome, the young Enrico Fermi and his group, the so-called “Via Panisperna boys”, set about bombarding every element of the periodic table with neutrons. In 1934 they discovered that neutrons slowed down by passing through paraffin or water were far more effective at provoking reactions, a finding that would prove crucial.
1lkcst37u8g: When Fermi's group irradiated uranium, the heaviest element known, it obtained a bewildering mixture of radioactive substances. Fermi assumed, like almost everyone, that he had made new elements, heavier than uranium: the “transuranic elements”. That same year, the German chemist **Ida Noddack** published a critique suggesting that the nucleus might have broken into large fragments, but nobody took her seriously, partly because she provided no experimental evidence and partly because it contradicted what the physics of the time considered possible. Fermi received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1938 for his work with neutrons, and used the trip to Stockholm to avoid returning to Italy under its racial laws: his wife, Laura, was Jewish. In January 1939 he landed in New York.
22meb03mw7y: At the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Chemistry in Berlin-Dahlem, the chemist **Otto Hahn** and the Austrian physicist **Lise Meitner** had been working for three decades, joined by the chemist **Fritz Strassmann**. Since 1934 they had been trying to unravel Fermi's “transuranic elements”. Meitner, of Jewish origin, had kept her post thanks to her Austrian nationality, but after Germany's annexation of Austria in March 1938 she was left unprotected. In July of that year she fled, with the help of Dutch colleagues, crossing the Dutch border with only what she was wearing, and ended up in Stockholm, at Manne Siegbahn's institute, where she worked in precarious conditions.

At the end of 1938, inspired in part by a result from Irène Joliot-Curie and Pavle Savić in Paris, they used very fine chemical techniques to look for what they believed was radium. On 17 December they reached a conclusion that seemed absurd to them: the substance behaved exactly like **barium**, an element with roughly half the mass of uranium. On 19 December Hahn wrote to Meitner asking whether there was any physical explanation. Hahn and Strassmann's paper appeared in the journal *Die Naturwissenschaften* on 6 January 1939, written with a caution that reflected their perplexity: as chemists, they said, they had to speak of barium; as nuclear physicists, they did not dare take that step.

They turned to the **liquid-drop** model, proposed by George Gamow and developed by Bohr, which pictures the nucleus as an electrically charged drop: a nucleus as large and as highly charged as that of uranium is at the limit of stability, and the arrival of a neutron could make it oscillate, stretch and split in two.

Meitner also recalled that the sum of the masses of the fragments was somewhat less than that of the original nucleus, and that this difference, converted into energy by Einstein's formula E = mc², gave precisely that figure (see [[energia-y-tnt|Energy and TNT equivalence]]). Frisch borrowed the term **fission** from biology, where it was used for the division of cells, at the suggestion of the American biologist William Arnold. On 13 January 1939 he confirmed in Copenhagen, with an ionisation chamber, the large electrical pulses produced by the fragments. 1lr6k4ftz4x: **Oak Ridge (Tennessee)**, “Site X”: uranium enrichment plants using electromagnetic, gaseous diffusion and thermal diffusion methods, and a pilot reactor. It came to have some 75,000 inhabitants. See [[oak-ridge-y-hanford|Oak Ridge and Hanford]].
1qesjk0ses3: **Hanford (Washington)**, “Site W”: the world's first plutonium production reactors, beside the Columbia River, and the chemical separation plants.
24ozphm631g: **Los Alamos (New Mexico)**, “Site Y”: the laboratory where the bombs were designed and assembled. See [[los-alamos|Los Alamos]].
dtz376uxrm: Two routes to fissile material were pursued at once, because nobody knew which would work: **uranium-235**, which had to be separated from natural uranium (see [[uranio|Uranium]]), and **plutonium-239**, an artificial element produced in reactors (see [[plutonio|Plutonium]]). 109h1a309o4: Up to the end of 1945 the project cost about **1.9–2 billion dollars** of the time, equivalent to some 30 billion dollars in the 2020s, although conversions vary depending on the index. The budget was hidden from Congress in generic items; only a few legislators knew of its existence. mplkjf5z60: The Manhattan Project inaugurated the era of “big science”: large national laboratories funded by the state, multidisciplinary teams and a close relationship between university, industry and the military. From it emerged the laboratories of Los Alamos, Oak Ridge and Argonne, the civil nuclear industry, nuclear medicine and a good part of scientific computing. But it also left a legacy of contamination, displaced communities, workers and neighbours exposed to radiation, and the [[carrera-armamentistica|arms race]] that the signatories of the Franck Report feared. Since 2015, the three main sites have formed the Manhattan Project National Historical Park.
ke50rgr0th: A secret laboratory built in 1943 on an isolated mesa in New Mexico, where a team led by Oppenheimer designed and assembled the first atomic bombs. Today it is Los Alamos National Laboratory.
1fkryvfwouu: In November 1942, Leslie Groves and J. Robert Oppenheimer were looking for a site for the central laboratory of the [[proyecto-manhattan|Manhattan Project]], which had to be isolated, easy to guard, have water and be far from the coast. Oppenheimer, who spent his summers at a ranch in New Mexico, proposed a mesa on the **Pajarito Plateau**, at an altitude of about 2,200 metres and some 55 kilometres north-west of Santa Fe, occupied by a boys' boarding school, the *Los Alamos Ranch School*. 1tf9k1y41tt: A city that did not exist
20fu2upnxt6: Officially, Los Alamos did not exist. Its only address was a post office box in Santa Fe, **P.O. Box 1663**, and newcomers reported to a small office on East Palace Avenue, where Dorothy McKibbin welcomed them and gave them a pass to go up “the Hill”. Children were born there whose birth certificates gave that post office box as their place of birth. The population, which Oppenheimer had estimated at a few hundred scientists, exceeded 5,000–6,000 people in 1945. They lived in barracks and prefabricated houses; only the old school buildings, “Bathtub Row”, had bathtubs. There were water shortages, mud, power cuts and a barbed-wire fence with guards.
fkl2dnapwi: Despite everything, social life was intense: parties, outings, concerts and a school for the children. Many scientists' wives worked in the laboratory itself as computers, technicians or administrative staff. The atmosphere was unusually open for a military project: Oppenheimer managed to get the scientists to discuss freely within the compound in weekly seminars, against Groves's judgement.
2gd8qnz4b2b: In April 1943, the physicist **Robert Serber** gave the newcomers a series of five lectures summarising what was known, collected in a document known as the *Los Alamos Primer*. 1xn2kt0ac6x: The laboratory was organised into divisions: the **Theoretical** Division, headed by **Hans Bethe**, with the young **Richard Feynman** leading the calculation group; **Experimental Physics**, with Robert Bacher; **Chemistry and Metallurgy**; and **Ordnance**, under the Navy Captain **William “Deak” Parsons**, responsible for the [[tipo-canon|gun-type]] design. **Edward Teller**, who was supposed to work in the theoretical division, concentrated more and more on his idea of a fusion bomb, the [[la-super|Super]], which brought him into conflict with Bethe.
237breofcae: The crisis came in the spring of 1944, when the physicist Emilio Segrè found that plutonium produced in reactors emitted too many spontaneous neutrons for the gun method: the reaction would start prematurely. The only way out was [[implosion|implosion]], an idea that **Seth Neddermeyer** had championed almost single-handedly since 1943 and that the mathematician **John von Neumann** had helped to develop. In August 1944 Oppenheimer reorganised the entire laboratory around it, with two new divisions: G, for the device (the *Gadget*), and X, for explosives, headed by the chemist **George Kistiakowsky**. **Enrico Fermi** arrived that same year and led a division of his own. The implosion calculations were done with Marchant mechanical calculators and, from 1944, with IBM punched-card machines, a direct forerunner of scientific computing.
1140nr9yewk: **J. Robert Oppenheimer**, director from 1943 to 1945, admired for his ability to understand all the problems at once. See [[oppenheimer|Oppenheimer]].
1brs8tbms9e: **Hans Bethe**, a German émigré, head of the theoretical division; he would receive the Nobel Prize in 1967 for explaining how stars shine (see [[fusion|Nuclear fusion]]).
1jj116oy6c1: **Richard Feynman**, who became famous at the laboratory for opening safes for fun and getting around postal censorship; his wife, Arline, died of tuberculosis in Albuquerque in June 1945.
2g4r5q5lp8t: **Enrico Fermi**, the “Pope” of physics, consulted by everyone.
2g1qtxrrjpc: **Niels Bohr**, who visited the laboratory as “Nicholas Baker” and even then advocated sharing the secret with the USSR to avoid an arms race.
15rg6p0jtpi: **Klaus Fuchs**, a physicist of the British mission, who worked on implosion and passed information to the USSR.
6g5unpzfio: **Stanisław Ulam**, a Polish mathematician, who years later would play a key role in the hydrogen bomb.
76dhk13cqj: Accidents and the end of the war
2265nm3dnjn: Work with fissile material was dangerous. On 21 August 1945, the physicist Harry Daghlian received a lethal dose when he dropped a reflector block onto a plutonium core during an experiment; he died 25 days later. 1966c27m8ax: Oppenheimer resigned on 16 October 1945 and was succeeded by **Norris Bradbury**, who directed the laboratory for 25 years. 153nto799k: Pajarito Plateau, New Mexico, about 2,200 m above sea level
f8h4iyv0qt: Design and assembly of the Gadget, Little Boy and Fat Man
1nmudyqpzcm: The two secret industrial cities of the Manhattan Project: at Oak Ridge (Tennessee) the uranium for Little Boy was enriched, and at Hanford (Washington) the plutonium for Trinity and Fat Man was produced. obp0v12jzv: If [[los-alamos|Los Alamos]] was the brain of the [[proyecto-manhattan|Manhattan Project]], Oak Ridge and Hanford were its factories. The great obstacle to building a bomb was not understanding the physics, but producing fissile material: uranium-235 had to be separated from natural uranium, where it is very scarce, and plutonium had to be created in reactors, nucleus by nucleus. Both processes required colossal facilities, built in record time and without knowing whether they would work.
2bougm0rn5h: Oak Ridge: the city that was not on the maps
2a67k3so0ez: In September 1942, Groves acquired some 24,000 hectares of valleys and hills along the Clinch River in eastern Tennessee, near Knoxville. About a thousand farming families were evicted with only a few weeks' notice. The site, officially called the **Clinton Engineer Works** and known as “Site X”, had abundant electricity thanks to the dams of the Tennessee Valley Authority. The city of **Oak Ridge** grew to about 75,000 inhabitants in 1945, making it the state's fifth-largest city, although it appeared on no map. Like the rest of the American South, it was segregated: Black workers lived in precarious barracks, the so-called *hutments*, often separated from their families.
29bhbqv9fd: Since nobody knew which isotope separation method would work on an industrial scale, Groves built them all. All of them exploit the small mass difference between uranium-235 and uranium-238 (see [[isotopos|Isotopes]] and [[uranio|Uranium]]):
gcqzl8t3om: **Y-12**, **electromagnetic** separation with the *calutrons* designed by Ernest Lawrence (the name comes from *California University cyclotron*). Uranium ions trace arcs in a magnetic field, and the lighter ones follow a slightly tighter path. As copper was scarce because of the war, the magnet coils were made with about 13,000 tonnes of silver loaned by the Treasury, which was returned after the war. The calutrons were operated by thousands of young people from the region, the “calutron girls”, who watched dials without knowing what they were producing.
23v6ixgl874: **K-25**, **gaseous diffusion**: uranium, in the form of a gaseous compound, was passed through thousands of porous barriers in cascade; the lighter molecules pass through the barriers slightly faster. 1q19zn57m9r: **X-10**, a pilot **graphite reactor**, the first to operate continuously, which started up on 4 November 1943 and produced the first quantities of plutonium for the chemists to study its separation. It is the origin of today's Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

All the highly enriched uranium for **Little Boy**, the [[hiroshima|Hiroshima]] bomb, came from Oak Ridge. 2et2hamceb9: Hanford: reactors beside the Columbia River
rvolf73pj0: Producing plutonium required high-power reactors, cooled with vast amounts of water and far from population centres in case of an accident. In January 1943 a semi-desert area on the banks of the **Columbia River**, in the state of Washington, was chosen. The towns of Hanford and White Bluffs were evacuated, and the **Wanapum** people lost access to their traditional fishing places and way of life. The chemical company **DuPont** agreed to design, build and operate the facilities on the condition, imposed by itself, of taking only one dollar of profit. At the peak of construction, in 1944, some 45,000 workers lived in the Hanford camp.
2cdczmcl6ct: **B Reactor**, the world's first industrial-scale nuclear production reactor, reached criticality on 26 September 1944. A few hours later its power began to fall mysteriously until it stopped, and it recovered after a while. The physicist John Wheeler identified the cause: a fission product, xenon-135, was absorbing neutrons and “poisoning” the reactor. The problem was solved because the DuPont engineers, out of caution and against the opinion of some physicists, had left room for many more fuel tubes than planned. D and F reactors followed. The irradiated fuel was processed in enormous chemical separation plants, the “canyons”, concrete buildings more than 250 metres long operated by remote control.
qv925uqd1h: Hanford's plutonium fuelled the device for the [[prueba-trinity|Trinity test]] and the **Fat Man** bomb dropped on [[nagasaki|Nagasaki]]. During the Cold War, Hanford came to have nine production reactors and made most of the plutonium in the American arsenal.

2etevltecgd: Both sites left an enormous environmental footprint. At Hanford, radioactive substances were released into the air and the river for decades; the best-known case is the **Green Run** of 2 December 1949, a deliberate release of radioactive iodine to test monitoring techniques that could be applied to the USSR. The neighbours exposed over the years, Hanford's *downwinders*, have sought recognition and compensation for decades. Hanford is today the most contaminated nuclear site in the United States: some 200,000 cubic metres of high-level liquid waste are stored in 177 underground tanks, some of them leaking, and its clean-up, begun in 1989, will go on for decades and cost hundreds of billions of dollars. 1ng1r9y3og0: Hanford's **B Reactor**, the **X-10 graphite reactor** and other facilities are preserved as monuments and, since 2015, form part of the Manhattan Project National Historical Park.
