c0u52dx2c2: Most of the workers at Oak Ridge and Hanford did not know what they were making until President Truman announced the bombing of Hiroshima on 6 August 1945. The local newspapers headlined that day that the city had made the atomic bomb.
vp7r6wcgop: American theoretical physicist (1904–1967) who directed the Los Alamos laboratory during the Manhattan Project and is known as the “father of the atomic bomb”. After the war he opposed the hydrogen bomb programme and in 1954 lost his security clearance at a hearing that divided the scientific community.
1ovo0bqur1g: **Julius Robert Oppenheimer** is one of the most complex figures of the twentieth century: a brilliant physicist of encyclopaedic culture, able to read Sanskrit and to quote the English metaphysical poets, who directed the building of the atomic bomb, afterwards became the most influential scientist in the United States and ended up sidelined by his own Government in the midst of the anti-communist witch-hunt. His life sums up the moral and political dilemmas of science in the nuclear age.
z00nhoj91j: He was born in New York on 22 April 1904, into a well-off Jewish family of German origin; his father had made a fortune importing textiles. He studied at the Ethical Culture School in New York and at Harvard, where he graduated in chemistry in three years, in 1925. He went to Europe, the cradle of the new quantum mechanics: first to the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, where he went through a serious personal crisis, and then to Göttingen, where he took his doctorate in 1927 under **Max Born**. With him he developed the **Born–Oppenheimer approximation**, which is still the basis of quantum chemistry today.
13dpg07z8i: In 1929 he returned to the United States and divided his time between the University of California at Berkeley and the California Institute of Technology (Caltech). There he built the first great American school of theoretical physics. His work in the 1930s was remarkable; the most visionary, published with his student Hartland Snyder on the very day in 1939 that Germany invaded Poland, described the gravitational collapse of a star to form what we now call a **black hole**. With George Volkoff he also studied the mass limits of neutron stars.
1lwh4vd0wmb: Until the mid-1930s, Oppenheimer lived with his back turned to politics. The Great Depression, the persecution of the Jews in Germany, which affected part of his family, and the Spanish Civil War led him to support left-wing causes. He donated money to the Spanish Republic through organisations linked to the Communist Party, although he never joined. His girlfriend of those years, the psychiatrist Jean Tatlock, was a communist, as was his brother Frank and the woman he married in 1940, Katherine “Kitty” Puening, the widow of an International Brigades volunteer killed in Spain. Those relationships would haunt him all his life.
6jtlb9h972: In 1941 he joined the studies on the bomb and in the summer of 1942 he led a seminar at Berkeley on its design, in which Teller's idea of a fusion bomb was also discussed in depth for the first time. In October 1942, General Groves chose him to head the weapons laboratory, even though he had no administrative experience or Nobel Prize, as many of his future subordinates did, and even though the security services advised against his appointment because of his communist contacts. Groves saw in him the ambition, the quickness of mind and the ability to grasp the whole that he needed.
pobarmlakd: The gamble paid off. At [[los-alamos|Los Alamos]], Oppenheimer recruited a constellation of scientists, defended free internal discussion against military secrecy, understood every technical problem in detail and knew how to take difficult decisions, such as the 1944 reorganisation around [[implosion|implosion]]. In 1943 he made a mistake that would weigh on him: he took months to report, and then with contradictory versions, that his friend the literature professor Haakon Chevalier had told him that an acquaintance could pass technical information to the Soviets, the so-called “Chevalier incident”.
2azcaqsx80e: It was he who named the first nuclear test *Trinity*, perhaps inspired by a sonnet by John Donne. kj6rp6qs4s: After the war, Oppenheimer was a celebrity: he appeared on the cover of *Time* and became the Government's leading scientific adviser. 2crc7qj4fi6: In October 1949, after the first Soviet bomb, the committee he chaired unanimously recommended against launching a crash programme to build the hydrogen bomb, for technical and moral reasons. It was not a trial but an administrative procedure with rules that left him defenceless: the AEC's prosecutor had access to FBI wiretaps and secret documents that the defence could not see.
y2e2rfmwqf: Dozens of scientists testified in his favour, among them Bethe, Fermi, Rabi and Bush. Teller, by contrast, said that he would prefer to see the country's vital interests in hands that he understood better, a statement that earned him the contempt of a good part of his colleagues. The board concluded, by two votes to one, that Oppenheimer was loyal, but that his clearance should not be renewed because of “defects of character”, his associations and his lack of enthusiasm for the hydrogen bomb. vl8m0dbedc: On 16 July 1945, at 5.29 in the morning, the United States detonated in the New Mexico desert the first nuclear device in history, the “Gadget”, a plutonium implosion bomb. Its yield, re-estimated in 2021, was about 25 kilotonnes.

m9thv6328j: An area of the Alamogordo Bombing and Gunnery Range was chosen for the test, on a desert plain that the Spanish conquistadors had named the **Jornada del Muerto** (“Dead Man's Journey”), because of the danger of crossing it on the old Camino Real de Tierra Adentro. 7hfcdxr7w1: Japan announced its surrender on 15 August 1945, after the bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the entry of the USSR into the war. 204gxc6g6p8: In the summer of 1945, the war in the Pacific was decided but not over. But it still had millions of soldiers in the archipelago, in China and in South-East Asia, and its military leaders were preparing a defence of the islands to the last, the plan *Ketsu-Go*, in the hope of inflicting so many casualties on the invaders that the United States would accept a negotiated peace.
24dqqq7bj3s: The United States planned to invade Japan in two phases, **Operation Downfall**: *Olympic*, the landing on the southern island of Kyushu, scheduled for 1 November 1945, and *Coronet*, the assault on the Tokyo plain, in the spring of 1946. The casualty estimates used in 1945 varied greatly depending on who made them and for which phase; after the war, defenders of the decision circulated figures of a million American casualties or more, which historians have debated at length. What the Japanese messages deciphered by intelligence services do reveal is that, in July 1945, Japan was reinforcing Kyushu far more than expected.

It did not mention the bomb or say anything about the future of the emperor, which for the Japanese leadership was the essential question. Some of Truman's advisers, such as Under-Secretary of State Joseph Grew, a former ambassador in Tokyo, and Stimson himself, had proposed guaranteeing the continuity of the monarchy to facilitate surrender, but Secretary of State **James Byrnes** opposed it for domestic political reasons. 2c38g390j23: The question of why Japan surrendered is closely tied to that of whether it was necessary to use the bomb. The main interpretations are:
10qqgd3pevb: **The “orthodox” interpretation**, formulated in 1947 by Stimson himself in an influential article in *Harper's Magazine*: the bomb forced Japan to surrender and saved hundreds of thousands of lives, American and Japanese, that an invasion would have cost. Historians such as Richard B. Frank, in *Downfall* (1999), have defended a nuanced version: the Japanese military leaders were not prepared to surrender, and the bomb gave the emperor and the moderates the argument to prevail.

Its critics point out that the Japanese documentation does not show a government prepared to accept surrender before August.
11ur1t94nhg: **The interpretation that gives priority to the Soviet entry**, defended by Tsuyoshi Hasegawa in *Racing the Enemy* (2005): for the Japanese leaders, the Soviet declaration of war was a more decisive blow than the bombs, because it destroyed their last diplomatic hope, mediation by Moscow, and threatened a Soviet occupation. 2f58d6187al: Many present-day historians, such as J. Samuel Walker or Barton Bernstein, take intermediate positions: the combination of the two bombs, the Soviet entry and the emperor's intervention produced the surrender in August; without the bomb, Japan would probably have surrendered before the November invasion owing to the combined effect of the blockade, the bombing and the Soviet entry, but this is not certain, and the war would have lasted weeks or months longer, at an enormous human cost in Asia, where thousands of people were still dying every day. 73v5sa3roa: **Continuing the blockade and the conventional bombing**, which also killed tens of thousands of civilians and threatened a famine in the winter of 1945–1946.
kqpb96l3pc: Some documents also show that the decision, in a certain sense, was never “taken” as an isolated act: the project had been conceived from the outset to use the bomb in the war, and for most of those responsible the question was not whether to use it, but how and when. Its critics maintain that intentionally killing non-combatants is inadmissible whatever the ends: in 1956, the philosopher **Elizabeth Anscombe** publicly opposed the University of Oxford awarding an honorary doctorate to Truman, and in 1995 the philosopher **John Rawls** described Hiroshima as a great wrong. 2a9tfxvfnfr: The hibakusha are the people who survived the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. It refers to the survivors of [[hiroshima|Hiroshima]] and [[nagasaki|Nagasaki]], although by extension it is also applied to those who have suffered exposure from nuclear tests elsewhere in the world. For decades they were, besides victims, tireless witnesses: their account is the main reason why humanity knows what a nuclear weapon really does to a city.
2g7qk0bhnds: Japanese law on assistance to atomic bomb survivors, whose first version dates from 1957 and the current one from 1994, recognises four groups as hibakusha: those who were in the cities or in certain nearby areas at the time of the explosion; those who entered a radius of about 2 kilometres from the hypocentre in the following two weeks, for example to look for relatives or help with relief work; those who were exposed in other ways, such as when tending the injured or collecting corpses; and those who were in the womb of a mother belonging to any of those groups. Those recognised receive a health handbook that entitles them to free check-ups and medical care and, in certain cases, to allowances.
12rfb2sg47p: The number of recognised hibakusha peaked around 1980, at more than 370,000 people. Since then it has declined year after year: according to the Japanese Ministry of Health, in March 2025 it fell below 100,000 for the first time, with an average age of more than 86. Soon there will be no direct witnesses left, and the cities and associations are working to train “transmitters” to tell their stories.
11peig11v8e: Survivors first suffered burns, injuries from glass and debris, and **acute radiation syndrome**, which in the following weeks killed many of those who seemed unharmed. Burns often healed to form **keloids**, thick, raised scars that disfigured many young people. Towards the end of the 1940s cases of **leukaemia** began to increase, reaching a peak in the early 1950s; later solid cancers increased, such as those of the thyroid, breast, lung and stomach. Children exposed in the womb at certain stages of pregnancy suffered microcephaly and intellectual disability more frequently. To all this were added psychological wounds: the guilt of having survived, grief for entire families and the constant fear of falling ill. See [[efectos-en-la-salud|Health effects]] and [[unidades-de-radiacion|Radiation units]].
b5k4p862ps: The most studied population in the world
1div2ujsy6k: In 1947, the United States created in Hiroshima and Nagasaki the **Atomic Bomb Casualty Commission** (ABCC), which in 1975 became the **Radiation Effects Research Foundation** (RERF), run jointly by Japan and the United States. Its **Life Span Study** has followed some 120,000 people, survivors and controls, since 1950, and has reconstructed the dose each received according to their position and protection at the time of the explosion. It is the main scientific basis of international radiation protection standards.
mngwgfa09c: Its results are solid and, in part, surprising to the public. Cancer risk increases with dose, and leukaemia was the disease most clearly associated with radiation; but, in absolute terms, only a minority of the cancers suffered by the survivors studied are attributed to the bomb: most would have occurred anyway. Nor has a significant increase in hereditary diseases been detected so far among the survivors' children. These data do not diminish the gravity of what happened, but they are important for combating stigma. The ABCC was heavily criticised in Japan because, in its early decades, it examined survivors without treating them.
1s2lgf76ppx: For years, the hibakusha suffered discrimination: their illness was believed to be contagious or hereditary, many concealed their status in order to marry or find work, and their scars marked them in public. In the early years of the occupation, censorship prevented open discussion of the effects of the bomb, and public assistance did not arrive until 1957. In 1955, a group of 25 young women with severe scars, the so-called **Hiroshima Maidens**, travelled to New York to undergo reconstructive surgery, in an initiative by the journalist Norman Cousins and the pastor Kiyoshi Tanimoto.
25hgmxajywg: Non-Japanese hibakusha had it even harder. Tens of thousands of **Koreans**, many of them forced labourers, suffered the bombs; most of the survivors returned to Korea, where the district of Hapcheon came to be known as the “Hiroshima of Korea”, and they had to go to court for decades to receive Japanese assistance while living abroad. Another long-neglected group was that of those affected by the **black rain** outside the official zones: in July 2021, the Hiroshima High Court ruled in their favour, the Government gave up its appeal and in 2022 the recognition criteria were widened.
1d59kpe64sp: After the American thermonuclear tests of 1954 and the case of the fishing boat *Daigo Fukuryū Maru* (see [[castle-bravo|Castle Bravo]]), a broad movement against nuclear weapons arose in Japan. In 1955 the first World Conference against Atomic and Hydrogen Bombs was held in Hiroshima, and on 10 August 1956 **Nihon Hidankyo**, the Japan Confederation of A- and H-Bomb Sufferers Organizations, was founded. For almost seventy years, its members have told their story in schools, international forums and United Nations conferences. In 2017, the Hiroshima survivor **Setsuko Thurlow**, who was 13 in 1945, accepted, together with Beatrice Fihn, the Nobel Peace Prize awarded to the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons (ICAN), and in October 2024 the Nobel Committee awarded the **Nobel Peace Prize to Nihon Hidankyo** for its efforts to achieve a world free of nuclear weapons and for demonstrating through testimony that they must never be used again. See [[tratados|Arms control treaties]].
14ailr419za: The experience of the hibakusha has inspired an abundant literature: the poems of Sankichi Tōge and Tamiki Hara, the novel *Black Rain* (1965) by Masuji Ibuse, Kenzaburō Ōe's *Hiroshima Notes*, the comic *Barefoot Gen* (*Hadashi no Gen*), by Keiji Nakazawa, a Hiroshima survivor, and the animated film *In This Corner of the World* (2016). The story of **Sadako Sasaki** and her paper cranes has become a universal symbol.
w3r9xhjsjo: The term “hibakusha” is today also used, in a broad sense, for those affected by nuclear tests in the Marshall Islands, Kazakhstan, Nevada, French Polynesia, Algeria or Australia, and by accidents such as Chernobyl. See [[pruebas-nucleares|Nuclear tests]] and [[chernobil|Chernobyl]].
1fakm2w7oxm: The first post-war nuclear tests, carried out by the United States at Bikini Atoll in July 1946 to study the effects of the bomb on warships. The underwater Baker explosion contaminated the target fleet so badly that it is considered the first radiological disaster in history.
dh68w3gcgv: Less than a year after [[nagasaki|Nagasaki]], the US Navy and Army organised a major experiment: to find out what an atomic bomb would do to a fleet of warships. There was a great deal at stake. Some advocates of air power maintained that nuclear weapons had made navies obsolete; the Navy wanted to prove the opposite and, at the same time, learn how to protect its ships. The result was **Operation Crossroads**, the first series of post-war nuclear tests and the first carried out in view of the world.
1q1d8zr29s6: **Bikini** was chosen, an atoll in the **Marshall Islands**, in the central Pacific, which the United States had taken from Japan in the war. It was remote, had a large sheltered lagoon in which to anchor the ships, and lay far from shipping routes. But it was inhabited. In February 1946, the military governor, Commodore Ben Wyatt, asked the 167 inhabitants, after Sunday mass, to give up their island temporarily “for the good of mankind”. Their chief, Juda, agreed. In March they were moved to Rongerik Atoll, much smaller and poorer, where they went hungry. They have never been able to return permanently.
1px0x6a5r6s: Joint Task Force One, led by Vice-Admiral **William H. P. Blandy**, mobilised some 42,000 people, more than 200 ships and 150 aircraft. About 95 target ships were anchored in the lagoon: old American battleships such as the *Nevada*, *Arkansas*, *New York* and *Pennsylvania*; the aircraft carrier *Saratoga*; ships captured from the enemy, such as the Japanese battleship *Nagato*, from which the attack on Pearl Harbor had been directed, and the German cruiser *Prinz Eugen*; as well as submarines, destroyers and landing craft. Pigs, goats and rats were left on board to study the effects of radiation. More than a hundred journalists and international observers attended, including Soviets.
2essx48w6dj: Able: the bomb that missed its target
1hm1r14sebs: On 1 July 1946, the B-29 *Dave's Dream* dropped a Fat Man-type bomb, which exploded about 160 metres above the fleet with a yield of about 23 kilotons. The bomb strayed some 600–700 metres from the aiming point, the battleship *Nevada*, painted orange-red, and sank five ships. For the public, who had expected a spectacular catastrophe, it was a relative disappointment: many ships were still afloat. Four days later, the French designer Louis Réard presented in Paris a two-piece swimsuit that he christened the **bikini**, with the idea that it would cause an effect as explosive as the bomb.
e545rpubpe: On 25 July, at 8:35, the second bomb, of the same yield, exploded at a depth of about 27 metres, suspended beneath a landing craft. It was the first [[explosiones-aereas-y-de-superficie|underwater nuclear explosion]] in history. The bomb threw up an immense hollow column of water, about 600 metres across and almost 2 kilometres high, containing millions of tonnes of seawater, and a condensation cloud enveloped the fleet for a few seconds. As it fell, the column generated a **base surge**, a mist of water and radioactive sand that spread across the lagoon and drenched the ships. The *Saratoga* and the *Arkansas* sank, along with other ships; the *Nagato* sank days later.
294180mb6y9: The worst was not the destruction but the **contamination**. The ships that survived were saturated with fission products that the water had carried over them (see [[lluvia-radiactiva|Fallout]]). Sailors tried to clean them with hoses, brushes and bleach, without success, and often without adequate protection. In early August, Colonel **Stafford Warren**, the medical officer in charge of radiological safety, persuaded the commanders to suspend the work. The planned third test, *Charlie*, at great depth, was cancelled. The chemist Glenn Seaborg would call Baker the world's first nuclear disaster. Many of the surviving ships were later deliberately sunk or scrapped; the *Prinz Eugen*, towed to Kwajalein Atoll, capsized there and its wreck is still visible.
3gr7r6zb8o: Dropped from a B-29; detonation at a height of about 160 m
oy83rk1pia: Underwater explosion at a depth of about 27 m
28zw70jilmu: Crossroads showed that the main threat of an underwater or surface explosion was not the shock wave but persistent radioactivity, and convinced the Navy to disperse its fleets and to design deck-washdown systems. For the general public it was the first chance to see a nuclear explosion filmed from many angles; the images of Baker, with the column of water lifting a battleship, became icons. For the participating sailors, the so-called “atomic veterans”, a long struggle began for recognition of their illnesses.
184igrsyzf8: Crossroads inaugurated twelve years of tests in the Marshall Islands: between 1946 and 1958, the United States carried out 67 nuclear explosions there, 23 at Bikini and 44 at Enewetak, including [[ivy-mike|Ivy Mike]] and [[castle-bravo|Castle Bravo]]. The Bikinians returned to their atoll in the early 1970s, when it was declared safe, but had to be evacuated again in 1978, when it was found that they had accumulated radioactive caesium in their bodies from eating local food. In 2010, UNESCO declared the Bikini test site a World Heritage Site, as a symbol of the beginning of the nuclear age; the wrecks in the lagoon are now a diving destination. See [[pruebas-nucleares|Nuclear tests]].
1qvgn2aknkn: The USSR exploded its first atomic bomb, the RDS-1, on 29 August 1949 at Semipalatinsk (Kazakhstan), long before Washington had expected. It achieved this through an enormous industrial effort led by Beria and Kurchatov, the labour of hundreds of thousands of prisoners and information from espionage.
vzkao3c46f: Soviet physicists knew fission as well as their Western colleagues: in 1940, Georgy Flyorov and Konstantin Petrzhak discovered the spontaneous fission of uranium in Leningrad. But the German invasion of June 1941 paralysed almost all research. The Soviet atomic programme was born from the combination of an intuition, that of the scientists themselves, and a certainty, that supplied by the spies.
1vkkro9rfjy: In 1942, the young Flyorov, then a lieutenant in the air force, noticed that American, British and German physicists had stopped publishing on fission. He deduced that the subject had become secret and wrote to Stalin asking him to have the USSR begin work on a bomb. At the same time, the intelligence services were passing to Moscow information on the British MAUD report, obtained through John Cairncross, one of the so-called “Cambridge Five”. In 1943 a small programme was created, whose scientific direction was entrusted to the physicist **Igor Kurchatov**, who founded Laboratory No. 2 in Moscow, today's Kurchatov Institute. Kurchatov, nicknamed “the Beard”, received espionage documents directly and used them to guide the work, without revealing their origin to most of his collaborators.
247il965v6k: The USSR had access to an extraordinary amount of information about the [[proyecto-manhattan|Manhattan Project]]. **Klaus Fuchs**, a German physicist who had taken refuge in the United Kingdom and a member of the British mission at [[los-alamos|Los Alamos]], handed over detailed information on the [[implosion|implosion]] design and, later, on the first ideas for the hydrogen bomb. **Theodore Hall**, a young American physicist, did the same independently, which allowed the Soviets to confirm the data. Other agents, such as David Greenglass and George Koval, provided additional information. Thanks to this, the first Soviet bomb was, by express decision of the leadership, a very close copy of Fat Man: it was safer to reproduce a proven design than to risk a failure.
hcwumh1kn0: Fuchs was uncovered thanks to the **Venona project**, the American decryption of Soviet messages. He confessed in January 1950, was sentenced in London to 14 years in prison, served nine and afterwards settled in the German Democratic Republic. His arrest led to Harry Gold, Greenglass and the couple **Julius and Ethel Rosenberg**, executed in the United States on 19 June 1953 in a case that remains controversial, especially as regards Ethel. Hall was never tried. Historians debate how much time espionage saved the USSR: the most usual estimate is one to two years, although the industrial effort would have been just as necessary.
1rr9dk4a5qn: Hiroshima convinced Stalin that the bomb was the absolute priority of the state. On 20 August 1945 a Special Committee was created, chaired by **Lavrentiy Beria**, the feared head of the political police, with unlimited resources. A nuclear industry was organised from scratch: uranium mines in Central Asia, in Czechoslovakia (Jáchymov) and in the Soviet zone of Germany (the Wismut company, in Saxony), in which tens of thousands of people worked in terrible conditions; hundreds of thousands of **gulag** prisoners built the facilities; and German scientists captured at the end of the war worked on specific problems, such as isotope separation.
26qel34d4h5: **F-1**, the first Soviet reactor and the first in all of Europe, reached criticality in Moscow on 25 December 1946.
1xwhwd3e2ra: **Chelyabinsk-40**, today Ozyorsk, in the Urals, with the **Mayak** complex: the first plutonium production reactor started up in June 1948. Haste and lack of precautions caused serious exposures of workers and the contamination of the Techa River, and in 1957 the [[kyshtym|Kyshtym]] disaster.
dlyxxenkia: **Arzamas-16**, the former monastery village of **Sarov**, some 400 kilometres from Moscow, where the KB-11 design bureau was founded in 1946, directed by **Yuli Khariton**: the Soviet equivalent of Los Alamos.
zvpdtiuf58: **The Semipalatinsk test site**, on the steppe of north-eastern Kazakhstan, chosen for the tests.
26ok4g96uy2: On 29 August 1949, at 7:00 local time, the **RDS-1**, which the scientists called *Pervaya Molniya*, “First Lightning”, exploded on a 30-metre tower at the Semipalatinsk test site. Its yield was about 22 kilotons. It is said that Beria embraced Kurchatov and Khariton, and it was said that those responsible would have been severely punished had the test failed. The United States did not expect a Soviet bomb before the mid-1950s. A WB-29 reconnaissance aircraft flying over the North Pacific collected air samples containing fission products on 3 September, and on 23 September Truman announced that the USSR had carried out an atomic explosion. The American nuclear monopoly had lasted four years.
1v7u1h2vpbv: Plutonium implosion, very similar to Fat Man
14s8axxow23: Igor Kurchatov; weapon design: Yuli Khariton (KB-11, Arzamas-16)
149pwxyo62f: While the atomic bomb was being completed, a group led by **Igor Tamm** and made up of **Yakov Zeldovich**, the young **Andrei Sakharov** and **Vitaly Ginzburg** studied the possibility of a fusion weapon. Sakharov proposed a design of alternating layers of fusion and fission material, the *sloika* or “layer cake”, and Ginzburg suggested using lithium deuteride as fuel (see [[combustibles-de-fusion|Fusion fuels]]). The **RDS-6s**, tested on 12 August 1953, yielded about 400 kilotons: it was a fission weapon heavily boosted by fusion, not a true two-stage bomb, but, unlike [[ivy-mike|Ivy Mike]], it was transportable, and the USSR presented it as its first hydrogen bomb. The true two-stage solution, developed independently by Sakharov, Zeldovich and others in 1954, was tested on 22 November 1955 with the **RDS-37**, air-dropped, of 1.6 megatons. See [[la-super|The Super]].
1zc0yp5vo2f: Between 1949 and 1989, 456 nuclear explosions were carried out at Semipalatinsk, 116 of them atmospheric in the early decades, with serious consequences for the health of hundreds of thousands of inhabitants of the region, who were never adequately warned or evacuated. A Kazakh popular movement, *Nevada-Semipalatinsk*, led by the poet Olzhas Suleimenov, contributed to its closure, decreed by President Nursultan Nazarbayev on 29 August 1991, the anniversary of the first test. From 1955 the USSR also used the Arctic archipelago of **Novaya Zemlya**, where the largest explosions in history were carried out, among them the [[tsar-bomba|Tsar Bomba]]. Kurchatov died in 1960, a national hero. Sakharov, three times Hero of Socialist Labour, became the most famous dissident in the USSR and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1975.
wugyecg419: The Super: the hydrogen bomb debate
25u5j0g7rfp: The “Super” was the name the Los Alamos scientists gave to the fusion bomb. After the first Soviet bomb, in 1949, an intense debate opened about whether to build it; Truman decided to go ahead in January 1950, and in 1951 Ulam and Teller found the principle that made it possible.
1lq3ocpflab: The [[bomba-de-hidrogeno|hydrogen bomb]] or thermonuclear bomb obtains most of its energy from the [[fusion|fusion]] of light nuclei, the same process that powers the Sun. Its yield has, in principle, no practical limit. The history of its development in the United States is that of an idea pursued for a decade by a single man, **Edward Teller**, of a moral and political debate at the summit of the state, and of a conceptual breakthrough that came when the decision had already been taken.
1sjawdkugre: In September 1941, during a conversation in New York, Enrico Fermi asked Teller whether the heat of a fission explosion could ignite the fusion of deuterium. Teller became passionate about the idea. At the summer seminar of 1942 in Berkeley, led by Oppenheimer, the “Super”, as it came to be called, was discussed in depth, together with the unsettling possibility that a nuclear explosion might set the atmosphere on fire, which calculations by Hans Bethe and others ruled out. At [[los-alamos|Los Alamos]], Teller devoted most of his time to the Super rather than to the atomic bomb, which brought him into conflict with Bethe and forced Oppenheimer to give him a group of his own.
7m4q3cfjdk: The design studied at that time, the so-called “classical Super”, relied on the heat of an atomic bomb igniting a cylinder of fusion fuel, with the burning then propagating by itself. In April 1946 a conference on the Super was held at Los Alamos, attended by Klaus Fuchs, who passed on what he learned to the USSR. When the war ended the project lost priority: the laboratory emptied, and the calculations were too complex for the machines of the day.
17c2267eobk: The first Soviet bomb, in August 1949 (see [[programa-sovietico|Soviet nuclear programme]]), set off the crisis. Teller, the Berkeley physicists Ernest Lawrence and Luis Alvarez, AEC commissioner **Lewis Strauss** and Senator Brien McMahon called for an emergency programme to build the Super before the Soviets did. The Atomic Energy Commission's **General Advisory Committee**, chaired by Oppenheimer, met from 28 to 30 October 1949 and unanimously recommended against undertaking such a programme.
8km7ff13wg: The report had two annexes, which are foundational documents of twentieth-century scientific ethics. The majority, led by James Conant and Oppenheimer, argued that the Super had no limit on its yield, that it would serve mainly to exterminate civilian populations and that it could become a weapon of genocide; it proposed that the United States renounce it. The minority, made up of **Enrico Fermi** and **Isidor Rabi**, went further: it called the Super necessarily evil from any point of view and proposed that the President invite other nations to make a solemn commitment not to build it. The committee also gave technical reasons: nobody knew whether the classical Super would work, and developing it would divert resources from the production of fission bombs.
2cru9srdmx3: The AEC itself was divided: its chairman, David Lilienthal, and commissioners Sumner Pike and Henry Smyth were opposed; Strauss and Gordon Dean supported the programme. The Joint Chiefs of Staff and the Department of Defense backed it firmly. Truman commissioned a report from a special committee made up of Secretary of State Dean Acheson, Secretary of Defense Louis Johnson and Lilienthal, which recommended going ahead. On **31 January 1950**, after a meeting lasting barely a few minutes, Truman announced that he had ordered the AEC to continue work on all forms of atomic weapons, including the so-called hydrogen bomb or superbomb. A few days earlier, on 27 January, Klaus Fuchs had confessed in London, and the news of his arrest, on 2 February, seemed to confirm the worst fears. In April, the document **NSC-68** laid the foundations for a massive rearmament.
1pxygjysdue: A dead end and a new idea
x1nnvhihu3: In 1950, calculations by the Polish mathematician **Stanisław Ulam** and Cornelius Everett, done largely with slide rules, and then simulations by Fermi and Ulam and by John von Neumann on the first computers, showed that the classical Super would not work: the fuel cooled down before the burning could propagate. Teller was devastated, and his relationship with Ulam became very strained.
1634t9mdz1z: In early 1951, Ulam had an idea that Teller reformulated and improved within a few weeks. Explained only in conceptual terms, the key was to **separate the stages**: instead of trying to ignite the fusion fuel directly with the heat of the atomic bomb, the energy of a fission primary is used to first **compress** the fusion secondary to enormous densities, which makes its ignition possible. Teller added that the agent of this compression had to be the radiation from the first explosion, which travels much faster than the materials themselves. This principle, **radiation implosion**, was set out in a report signed by both men on 9 March 1951 and is known as the **Teller-Ulam design**; its general operation, at a popular level, is explained in [[bomba-de-hidrogeno|Hydrogen bomb]]. The specific details of the designs remain secret.
z96w7bopoo: Who deserved credit for the idea was the subject of bitter disputes: for decades Teller tended to play down Ulam's contribution, while many colleagues considered that without Ulam the design would never have been reached. Today it is accepted that the idea came from both of them. In June 1951, at a meeting in Princeton, Oppenheimer himself acknowledged that the new approach was so technically appealing that it had to be pursued. The young physicist **Richard Garwin** designed, during the summer of 1951 and on the basis of Teller's ideas, the experimental device that would be tested in [[ivy-mike|Ivy Mike]].
gweo1se2zm: Before the Ulam-Teller idea became known, a test had already been prepared to check whether it was possible to ignite fusion. On 9 May 1951, on Enewetak Atoll, the **George** test of the *Greenhouse* series detonated a large fission device of 225 kilotons, which ignited a small quantity of fusion fuel. It was the first thermonuclear reaction brought about by human beings, although its contribution to the total energy was very small. A few weeks later, on 25 May, the *Item* test demonstrated [[fision-potenciada|boosted fission]].

jm6cg6xtam: Conference on the Super at Los Alamos.
25zo0fmuhzp: The General Advisory Committee recommends against an emergency programme.
pz7p1pbn90: Truman orders work on the hydrogen bomb to continue.
kfo77sj485: Calculations by Ulam and Everett show that the classical Super would not work.
1bc35uidmh2: Teller and Ulam's report on radiation implosion.
1hedlltr64h: The Livermore laboratory (California) is founded, driven by Teller and Lawrence.
17zqkvt0p73: Ivy Mike, the first hydrogen bomb (10.4 Mt).
28x3vkfstww: The consequences for Oppenheimer and for Teller
xc7lgegcab: Oppenheimer's opposition to the Super was one of the central arguments at the security hearing of 1954, which stripped him of his security clearance (see [[oppenheimer|Oppenheimer]]). He was reproached not only for his opinion in 1949, but for having allegedly discouraged other scientists from working on the project. Teller's testimony against him marked the rest of his life: many of his former colleagues stopped speaking to him. Teller, for his part, became the great champion of nuclear weapons during the Cold War, was director of the new **Livermore** laboratory, created in 1952 as a rival to Los Alamos, and in the 1980s was one of the main promoters of Reagan's Strategic Defense Initiative.
299mtnuh71x: The decision of 1950 is still debated. For some, renouncing the Super would have been pointless, because the USSR would have developed it anyway, as in fact it did on its own. For others, the one chance to halt the [[carrera-armamentistica|arms race]] before it reached the megaton range was lost, with a proposal of mutual renunciation that was never explored.
1btexru4c68: The first hydrogen bomb in history, tested by the United States on 1 November 1952 on Enewetak Atoll. It yielded 10.4 megatons, some 700 times the yield of the Hiroshima bomb, and wiped the islet of Elugelab off the map.
1jprapqi6c0: **Ivy Mike** was the first full test of a thermonuclear device based on the Teller-Ulam principle (see [[la-super|The Super]]). It was not a weapon but an experiment the size of a house, designed to show that the idea worked. It worked beyond expectations: the explosion was the most powerful in history up to that time and opened the megaton era.
13s5dxmpjm0: The device, called the **Sausage** because of its elongated shape, was designed on the basis of Teller's ideas by the young physicist **Richard Garwin** in the summer of 1951 and built at Los Alamos. Its fusion fuel was **liquid deuterium**, which has to be kept at temperatures close to absolute zero. For this reason the Sausage needed an enormous cryogenic plant, and the whole assembly weighed some 80 tonnes. It was a large cylindrical steel vessel about 6 metres high and 2 metres in diameter, housed in a sheet-metal building on the islet of **Elugelab**, on **Enewetak** Atoll (Marshall Islands). Its internal details remain classified; its general two-stage principle, with a fission primary compressing the secondary, is explained in [[bomba-de-hidrogeno|Hydrogen bomb]].
dttb8yoqop: The Sausage device of Ivy Mike: about 6 m high, 2 m in diameter and some 80 tonnes with its cryogenic equipment. It was a fixed experiment and could not be dropped from an aircraft.
8bt7c0ux2i: Operation Ivy, run by Joint Task Force 132, mobilised thousands of people. The device was detonated by remote control from a ship about 50 kilometres away. A long tunnel of plywood and aluminium, some 3 kilometres in length, linked the building to a neighbouring islet in order to channel the radiation towards the measuring instruments. There was political debate over the date: Vannevar Bush and others asked for the test to be postponed so as not to close the door on a test-ban agreement with the USSR, and also so as not to interfere with the presidential election of 4 November, but President Truman did not do so.
oxrpmq9d7s: On **1 November 1952** at 7:15 local time, the Sausage exploded with a yield of **10.4 megatons**, some 700 times that of the [[hiroshima|Hiroshima]] bomb. Most of that energy came from the fission of the uranium that formed part of the device, induced by the fusion neutrons, a common feature of large thermonuclear weapons. The [[bola-de-fuego|fireball]] reached about 5 kilometres in diameter; the [[nube-de-hongo|mushroom cloud]] rose to 17 kilometres in 90 seconds and ended up stabilising at more than 40 kilometres in height, with a cap more than 100 kilometres wide. In Berkeley, Teller saw the signal of the explosion on a seismograph and sent Los Alamos a three-word telegram in English: “It's a boy.”
9pxelv00xz: The islet of **Elugelab** disappeared. In its place was left an underwater crater about 1.9 kilometres in diameter and some 50 metres deep, still visible in satellite images. The radioactive debris fell on the atoll and the ocean. In the filters of the aircraft that flew through the cloud and in coral debris, the Berkeley chemists led by **Albert Ghiorso** discovered two new elements, which would be named **einsteinium** (99) and **fermium** (100), in honour of Einstein and Fermi. The discovery was kept secret until 1955.

197qzjnn4oq: About 6 × 2 m; some 80 tonnes with the cryogenic equipment
21dtrmlgxx1: About 1.9 km in diameter and 50 m deep
h9esgsyc43: Ivy Mike showed that the Teller-Ulam principle worked, but its cryogenic design was useless as a weapon. The laboratories turned to versions using solid fuel, lithium deuteride (see [[combustibles-de-fusion|Fusion fuels]]), which were tested in the Castle series of 1954 with unexpected results (see [[castle-bravo|Castle Bravo]]). A few emergency cryogenic bombs derived from the Sausage were built, the EC-16, which were never used and were withdrawn almost immediately. The USSR, which in August 1953 tested its RDS-6s, transportable but of much lower yield, and in 1955 its first two-stage bomb (see [[programa-sovietico|Soviet nuclear programme]]), entered fully into the megaton race (see [[carrera-armamentistica|Arms race]]).
17f3fd0qs9q: The largest nuclear test ever carried out by the United States: on 1 March 1954, on Bikini Atoll, a thermonuclear device yielded 15 megatons, more than double what was expected, owing to an error in the physics of lithium. qyx2evkgjq: **Castle Bravo** was the first test of the *Castle* series, with which the United States wanted to turn the principle demonstrated in [[ivy-mike|Ivy Mike]] into usable weapons, with solid fusion fuel in place of liquid deuterium. After the failures of the immediate postwar period, such as the Baruch Plan (see [[carrera-armamentistica|Arms race]]), fear of the [[lluvia-radiactiva|fallout]] from tests and the scare of the [[crisis-de-los-misiles|missile crisis]] led to the first agreements. Over time a web of treaties of three kinds was built up: those that limit **tests**, those that prevent **proliferation** to new countries and those that limit or reduce the **arsenals** of the great powers.
14sjsmichfz: The **Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty** (PTBT), signed in Moscow on 5 August 1963 by the United States, the United Kingdom and the USSR, and in force from 10 October, banned tests in the atmosphere, in space and underwater. It allowed only underground tests. It was to a large extent a response to public concern about fallout, such as the strontium-90 found in children's baby teeth. France and China, which were then starting their programmes, did not sign it and continued atmospheric testing until 1974 and 1980 respectively.
1ndqi7kpg4m: The **Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty** (CTBT), opened for signature on 24 September 1996, prohibits any nuclear explosion. It has been signed by 187 states and ratified by about 178, and its organisation in Vienna maintains an **International Monitoring System** of more than 300 seismic, hydroacoustic, infrasound and radionuclide stations, which detected all the North Korean tests. But it has not entered into force, because that requires ratification by 44 specific states with nuclear technology: India, Pakistan and North Korea have not signed it; the United States, China, Egypt, Iran and Israel have signed but not ratified it; and Russia withdrew its ratification in November 2023. See [[pruebas-nucleares|Nuclear tests]].
25fbsye155r: The **Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons** (NPT), opened for signature on 1 July 1968 and in force since 5 March 1970, is the cornerstone of the system. It recognises as nuclear-weapon states the five that had carried out a test before 1 January 1967: the United States, the USSR (now Russia), the United Kingdom, France and China. It rests on a threefold commitment: non-nuclear states renounce acquiring weapons and accept inspections by the **International Atomic Energy Agency** (IAEA); all have the right to the peaceful use of nuclear energy; and the nuclear states undertake, in its Article VI, to negotiate disarmament in good faith. With 191 states parties, it is the arms control treaty with the most members. In 1995 it was extended indefinitely.
takyfnincs: The NPT has been remarkably successful: in the 1960s it was feared that there would soon be twenty or thirty nuclear powers, and today there are nine. But it has cracks. India, Pakistan and Israel never signed it; North Korea announced its withdrawal in 2003; and many non-nuclear states complain that the powers are not complying with Article VI. The review conferences of 2015 and 2022 ended without a consensus final document. It is complemented by regional nuclear-weapon-free zones, beginning with that of Latin America and the Caribbean (the **Treaty of Tlatelolco**, 1967), and others in the South Pacific, South-East Asia, Africa and Central Asia. See [[potencias-nucleares|Nuclear powers]].

1x3r7mwmpfx: **SALT I and the ABM Treaty** (26 May 1972, Nixon and Brezhnev, in Moscow): an interim agreement froze the number of intercontinental missile launchers and submarines, and the **Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty** limited each country to two defended areas, reduced to one in 1974. The ABM Treaty was regarded as the key to [[destruccion-mutua-asegurada|mutual deterrence]]. The United States withdrew from it in June 2002.
2ctg4u5plrn: **SALT II** (18 June 1979, Carter and Brezhnev, in Vienna): set equal ceilings on launchers and on missiles with [[mirv|MIRV]]. The US Senate never ratified it after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, although both countries respected its limits until 1986.

The United States withdrew in August 2019, accusing Russia of deploying a prohibited cruise missile.
1v3hpsd0gka: **START I** (31 July 1991, Bush and Gorbachev): the first treaty to genuinely reduce strategic arsenals, to 6,000 accountable warheads and 1,600 delivery vehicles per side, with a highly detailed verification system. 22ap7q595lf: Faced with the stalemate in disarmament, a movement of non-nuclear states and civil organisations, centred on the **humanitarian consequences** of nuclear weapons and with a prominent role for the [[hibakusha|hibakusha]], promoted the **Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons** (TPNW), adopted at the UN on 7 July 2017 with 122 votes in favour. It prohibits developing, testing, possessing, using or threatening to use nuclear weapons, and obliges states to assist victims and remediate the environment. It entered into force on 22 January 2021, after reaching 50 ratifications, and in 2025 had more than 70 states parties. No nuclear power and no NATO member has signed it; its critics maintain that it ignores the reality of deterrence, and its supporters that it creates a moral and legal norm that stigmatises these weapons. The International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons (ICAN), which promoted it, received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2017.

27gkd78o4nc: The effects were far more concentrated in the communities close to the test sites:

j4xj48sg6s: At the start of 2025 there were some 12,200 nuclear warheads in the world, of which about 9,600 were in military stockpiles and about 3,900 deployed on missiles or at operational bases. Russia and the United States hold almost 90%, but the fastest-growing arsenal is China's.
lrfni1gzf3: After the peak of about 70,000 warheads in 1986 (see [[carrera-armamentistica|Arms race]]), nuclear arsenals fell dramatically thanks to arms control [[tratados|treaties]] and the end of the Cold War. 17j0v6gt9yf: In a millionth of a second, the energy of a nuclear weapon turns the air into a sphere of plasma hotter than the centre of the Sun. Its evolution explains almost all the other effects.
2y3kqrpzi3: A chemical explosion releases its energy in the form of hot gases that push the air. A nuclear explosion is different from the first instant: when [[fision|fission]] or [[fusion|fusion]] ends, the energy is concentrated in a tiny mass of vaporised material at tens of millions of degrees. At that temperature matter emits not mainly visible light but **soft X-rays**, and the air surrounding the weapon absorbs them within a few metres. That air, suddenly heated, becomes a sphere of ionised, luminous gas: the **fireball**.
lfjcrzoml9: What happens inside that sphere during the first second determines the [[onda-expansiva|blast wave]], the [[radiacion-termica|heat pulse]], the height of the [[nube-de-hongo|mushroom cloud]] and the amount of [[lluvia-radiactiva|fallout]]. That is why Glasstone and Dolan devote an entire chapter to describing it before speaking of any damage.
18p9slr3pvc: In an explosion in the lower atmosphere (below about 30 km), the typical distribution of the energy of a fission weapon is approximately as follows. The proportions change with altitude, design and yield, but they serve as a general rule:
nsb2qkwxuh: Building collapse, flying debris, injuries from glass
napzdpn1hz: Gamma-ray and neutron dose in the first minute
1z6rsh9tzjv: At high altitude, where the air is thin, this distribution breaks down: there is almost no blast wave, X-rays travel hundreds of kilometres and effects of their own appear, such as the [[pulso-electromagnetico|electromagnetic pulse]]. To compare yields, remember that they are measured in tonnes of TNT equivalent: see [[energia-y-tnt|energy and TNT]].
1xu5kuo4omf: Phases of the fireball: initial flash, expansion with the shock front, rise and formation of the mushroom.
1pffpsqpk6h: **Radiative phase** (first millionths of a second). The sphere grows because radiation heats layers of air ever farther away. It is small, almost perfectly spherical, and its surface reaches temperatures of hundreds of thousands of degrees.

189zgj3lqes: **Obscuration and thermal minimum**. The compressed air of the shock front, at a few thousand degrees, is opaque: it acts like a curtain that hides the hotter interior. Seen from afar, the brightness drops sharply. This is the **thermal minimum**, which in a 20-kiloton weapon occurs within a few thousandths of a second.
1vr1i9we9x0: **Breakaway and second maximum**. When the shock front expands and cools below about 3,000 °C, it becomes transparent again and lets the hot core be seen once more. The brightness rises to a second maximum, much longer than the first. The vast majority of the thermal energy comes from this second pulse: about four-fifths.
2do6hofety0: **Rise**. The fireball, much lighter than the air around it, rises like a balloon at more than 100 metres per second, drags up dust and smoke and gives rise to the [[nube-de-hongo|mushroom cloud]].
1f3uur2u97t: This sequence produces the famous **double flash**: a very brief first flare, a drop in brightness and a second, longer pulse. No natural phenomenon produces it, so it became the signature of nuclear explosions. The American Vela satellites carried optical sensors called **bhangmeters** precisely to detect it; on 22 September 1979 they recorded a double flash over the Indian Ocean, the so-called Vela incident, whose origin is still debated.

The time taken to reach the second maximum also grows with yield: a few hundredths of a second for a few kilotons and around a second for a megaton. In weapons of several megatons the thermal pulse lasts more than ten seconds, long enough for a person to manage to take cover, although they almost never do because they do not know what is happening.
8myvhmyvau: Tens of millions of degrees in the weapon material
4lhq2vdb5g: Several times that of the Sun at tens of kilometres
w0nizgp6mp: When the fireball touches the ground

k6cdm0deiw: A few seconds after detonation, the [[bola-de-fuego|fireball]] has stopped glowing but is still a bubble of very hot gas, much less dense than the air around it. As it climbs it deforms: the cooler air at the edges slows the outer part, while the centre keeps rising, and the bubble rolls up on itself into a **vortex ring** (a toroid) that turns inward at the bottom and outward at the top. 1c5bjl1x8ab: Half the energy of a nuclear explosion is converted into a shock wave that crushes buildings and into a wind of hundreds of kilometres per hour. It is the main cause of destruction in cities.
156czzvhgmr: As the [[bola-de-fuego|fireball]] expands, it pushes the air with such violence that a **shock wave** forms: a thin layer in which the pressure, density and temperature of the air jump abruptly. 23ptc6lbwex: Glasstone and Dolan describe the wave with two distinct quantities. **Overpressure** is the excess of pressure over normal atmospheric pressure: it squeezes objects from all sides at once and is what blows out walls, windows and roofs, especially in closed structures. **Dynamic pressure** is the force of the wind: it pushes in a single direction and tears away, overturns and carries off whatever it meets, from cars and trees to people. aklri87jsd: Wooden or light houses seriously damaged

The reflected wave travels through air already compressed and heated by the first, so it moves faster and ends up catching it. When the two merge, a reinforced vertical front forms, the **Mach stem** or **Mach wave**, which sweeps over the terrain with a higher pressure than the wave alone would have. The phenomenon was described by the physicist Ernst Mach in the nineteenth century, and John von Neumann studied it in detail during the Second World War.

1sewjvht3y8: Thule was not Greenland’s only nuclear secret. Publicly it was a scientific base, and in 1966 it yielded the first ice core to pass through the whole ice sheet to the bedrock, a key piece of evidence for studying past climate. But it was also used to evaluate **Project Iceworm**, a plan to hide hundreds of nuclear missiles under the ice, to be moved around thousands of kilometres of tunnels. 9czmyp4u7u: The **Titan II** was the largest American [[misil-balistico|intercontinental ballistic missile]] of the Cold War. This made it possible to keep the missile fuelled and launch it within a minute, but it made any leak extremely dangerous. In 1965, a fire during work on a Titan II silo near Searcy, also in Arkansas, had killed 53 workers.

1rpziyuh6vj: Several times during the Cold War and since, a technical error or a misunderstanding came close to triggering a nuclear war. In many cases it was averted by the decision of a single person.
1c4ag985bna: The logic of [[destruccion-mutua-asegurada|nuclear deterrence]] requires each side to be able to respond to an attack before the enemy missiles destroy its own. An intercontinental missile takes about 30 minutes to cross the planet, and one launched from a submarine, much less. That leaves leaders a few minutes to decide whether an alert is real. In such conditions, a sensor failure or a political misunderstanding can be as dangerous as a deliberate decision.
1u4b525q48s: On 27 October 1962, the tensest day of the [[crisis-de-los-misiles|Cuban Missile Crisis]], American destroyers were harassing the Soviet submarine B-59 near Cuba and dropping practice depth charges to force it to surface. The submarine had been out of contact with Moscow for days, with foul air and extremely high temperatures, and its crew did not know whether war had begun. It also carried a nuclear-tipped torpedo. The captain, Valentin Savitsky, wanted to use it. According to later accounts, launching it required the agreement of the three principal officers: the captain, the political officer and **Vasily Arkhipov**, head of the submarine flotilla. Arkhipov refused and persuaded the others to surface. His role was not known until decades later.
1vzh6ixrg1s: On 9 November 1979, the screens of the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) showed a massive Soviet attack. The alert was given to the bombers and interceptor fighters took off. The National Security Adviser, Zbigniew Brzezinski, was woken in the small hours and was about to call President Carter when he was told it was a false alarm: a training tape simulating an attack had been loaded into the live system. In June 1980 it happened again, this time because of a defective chip in a communications computer that was writing random figures into the alert messages.
1jvit1zwawk: Shortly after midnight on **26 September 1983**, Lieutenant Colonel **Stanislav Petrov** was on duty at the Serpukhov-15 bunker, near Moscow, which received data from the new Oko early-warning satellite system. The system announced the launch of one Minuteman missile from the United States and then of four more. The protocol required him to inform his superiors, which could trigger a response. Petrov reasoned that a real attack would begin with hundreds of missiles, not five; that the system was new and unreliable; and that the ground radars confirmed nothing. He reported a malfunction. He was right: the satellites had mistaken the reflections of the Sun on high clouds for launches. Tension was at its height, because three weeks earlier the Soviet Union had shot down Korean Air Lines Flight 007 with 269 people on board. The story became known in 1998. Petrov died in 2017.
w3li9nqrlt: Between 7 and 11 November 1983, NATO held **Able Archer 83**, an exercise that simulated escalation to nuclear war with new and more realistic procedures and communications. The Soviet leadership had been convinced since 1981 that the United States was preparing a surprise attack: the KGB had launched Operation RYaN to detect its signs, and the “evil empire” speech, the Strategic Defense Initiative and the deployment of Pershing II missiles in Europe reinforced that suspicion. Some Soviet commanders interpreted the exercise as a possible cover and placed part of their forces on alert, including aircraft carrying nuclear weapons. The double agent Oleg Gordievsky informed the British of the alarm in Moscow. A 1990 American intelligence report, declassified in 2015, concluded that the exercise may have brought relations between the two powers to the brink of war without the West knowing it.

1cdb4fm1z1w: When fissile material accidentally reaches the conditions for a chain reaction, it emits a flash of deadly radiation. Harry Daghlian and Louis Slotin died in this way at Los Alamos with the same plutonium core, the so-called “demon core”.
2d78fykhmn7: A **criticality accident** occurs when a quantity of fissile material (enriched uranium or plutonium) accidentally reaches the conditions to sustain a [[reaccion-en-cadena|chain reaction]], outside a reactor designed to control it. There is no nuclear explosion: as soon as the material heats up and expands, or someone separates it, the reaction stops. But during that fraction of a second it emits an extremely intense pulse of neutrons and gamma rays that can be lethal to anyone within a few metres. Witnesses often describe a **blue flash**, caused by the ionisation of the air, and a sensation of heat. The concept of [[masa-critica|critical mass]] explains why it depends on the quantity, the shape and what surrounds the material.
1ebozvx5u60: After the war, the scientists at [[los-alamos|Los Alamos]] went on measuring the properties of the plutonium cores made for the bombs. One of them, prepared for a possible third bombing of Japan that never took place, remained in the laboratory. On 21 August 1945, the physicist **Harry Daghlian**, aged 24, was working alone at night, with a guard as his only company, surrounding that core with blocks that reflected neutrons back towards it in order to study how it approached criticality. One of the blocks slipped from his hand and fell onto the assembly. Daghlian removed it at once, but had already received a lethal dose. He died on 15 September, 25 days later: he was the first person to die in a criticality accident.
rr3a6fk3el: The Canadian physicist **Louis Slotin**, aged 35, was an expert in this type of experiment, which Richard Feynman had christened “tickling the dragon’s tail”. They consisted of bringing together by hand two pieces that enclosed the core in order to measure the rise in activity, holding them apart with a small gap. On 21 May 1946, while giving a demonstration to seven colleagues, he was holding that gap with the tip of a screwdriver. The screwdriver slipped, the pieces came together and there was a blue flash. Slotin knocked them apart with a flick of his hand, stopping the reaction and probably saving the others, who were further away. He died nine days later, on 30 May. The other seven survived, although some with significant doses.
1o3xyrgxbd9: From then on these hand-operated experiments were banned and were carried out by remote control, from a safe distance. The core, later nicknamed the *demon core*, was used in the Able test of [[operacion-crossroads|Operation Crossroads]], in July 1946.

Two of the workers, Hisashi Ouchi and Masato Shinohara, died after months of agony; the accident was rated level 4 on the INES scale.

178079pn9zg: Facilities that handle fissile material apply a discipline of their own, **criticality safety**, which watches at once several factors: how much material is brought together in one place, the shape of the vessels, what surrounds them, whether the material is mixed with water or other substances that slow neutrons, and how concentrated the solutions are. Many tanks and pipes are made long and narrow or flat, so that too many neutrons escape through their walls for the reaction to be sustained, whatever the quantity they contain. This is what is called **safety by geometry**, and many of the accidents on the list happened precisely when liquids were transferred into a vessel that lacked it, as at Tokaimura.
8kveqcq1qr: The golden rule is the **double contingency principle**: a process must be designed so that at least two independent, unlikely errors or failures are needed before an accident becomes possible. To this are added neutron-absorbing materials such as boron or cadmium, limits written up at every workstation, and alarm systems that detect the flash of radiation and order an instant evacuation: in several accidents the reaction continued or recurred for minutes or hours, and those who ran out when they heard the alarm were saved. Since the 1960s these accidents have become far rarer, and almost all those of recent decades have been due to badly designed or disobeyed procedures rather than technical faults.
18nouve5c6h: The explosion of a radioactive waste tank at the Soviet Mayak complex contaminated a 300 km strip of the Urals. It was the third-worst nuclear accident in history and stayed secret for three decades.

18v79npaj5f: Two scales summarise the danger of a possible impact: the Turin scale, from 0 to 10, designed to communicate it to the public, and the Palermo scale, logarithmic, which specialists use to compare risks.

With more observations the cloud narrows and, in almost every case, ends up leaving the Earth out: that is why it is normal for the probability first to **rise** and then suddenly fall to zero. Two scales are used to communicate this changing risk without causing alarm or downplaying it.

uq93bpwlgg: Both scales condense two different quantities, probability and energy, into a single number, and so they lose information. The Turin scale, moreover, applies only to possible impacts within the next hundred years and does not take into account objects so small that they would break up in the air. That is why the new survey programmes are so important, such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which began operating in 2025, and NASA's NEO Surveyor space telescope, due for launch around 2027; see [[lista-sentry|the Sentry list]] and [[defensa-planetaria|planetary defence]].
29prt96762g: Watching a nuclear explosion from afar
1w9jmpk9fr6: From tens of kilometres away, a nuclear explosion arrives in three stages: a flash brighter than the Sun, a strange silence while the cloud rises and, seconds or minutes later, the roar and the wave that breaks windows. That interval can save your life.

The **flash** and the **heat** arrive together and instantly; the **blast wave**, which near ground zero travels faster than sound but at a distance slows to the speed of sound, arrives much later: about three seconds for every kilometre. At 20 km almost a minute passes between the light and the blow. Everything that witnesses describe — the day that suddenly lights up, the heat on the face, the unreal silence, the growing cloud — happens in that gap.
1urac5xsbih: We know this from the scientists who witnessed the [[prueba-trinity|Trinity test]], from the soldiers and journalists who attended the Nevada tests and, unwittingly, from the inhabitants of [[cheliabinsk|Chelyabinsk]], who in 2013 experienced the explosion of an asteroid with very similar physics. This double signature is so characteristic that the American Vela satellites carried optical sensors, the *bhangmeters*, to recognise clandestine tests; on 22 September 1979 they recorded a double flash over the South Atlantic whose origin is still disputed.

More serious is the **retinal burn**: the lens concentrates the image of the fireball on a single point of the retina, so that anyone looking directly may suffer permanent injury at distances where the skin feels nothing. Close in, it ignites wood and causes third-degree burns; somewhat farther away, first- or second-degree burns on exposed skin; farther still, only a wave of warmth. 2c7dxu3l7pz: A radioactive particle does not fall in a straight line. y0vyaafvgc: There are two main families of dams. **Masonry dams**, of concrete or stonework, resist the thrust of the water with their weight (gravity dams), with their curved shape, which transmits the thrust to the valley sides like the arch of a bridge laid on its side (arch dams), or with buttresses. **Embankment dams**, of earth or rockfill with an impermeable clay core, are cheaper and adapt to almost any terrain, but do not tolerate water flowing over the top. The former tend to break all at once; the latter by opening a breach that grows over minutes or hours. Engineers distinguish four main failure mechanisms:
2e85cngxrk2: **Overtopping.** The reservoir fills faster than the spillways can discharge and water spills over the crest. In an earth dam it begins to erode the downstream slope and opens a breach that enlarges itself. It is usually due to extraordinary rainfall (Banqiao, Derna) or to gates that cannot be opened (Tous).
29jtv55hpv8: **Internal erosion or piping.** Water seeping through the body of the dam or the ground beneath carries away fine particles and opens a conduit that grows ever faster. The warning signs are seepages of cloudy water. This is how Teton fell in 1976.
2flxtcvyni: **Foundation or abutment failure.** The rock on which the dam rests gives way or slides. This was the case at Malpasset (1959), an arch dam that lost its support on the left bank. Construction defects, as in the Vega de Tera dam, belong to this family of structural failures.
1mz9y7dzjr: **Landslide wave.** A whole hillside collapses into the reservoir and throws the water over the dam, which may remain intact. Vajont (1963) is the most terrible example. To these mechanisms are added earthquakes and deliberate attacks.

When the ellipse becomes smaller than the offset separating it from the Earth, it leaves the Earth out all at once and the probability **falls** to almost zero. wlwy3f2dj5: From 1942, Edward Teller advocated building a fusion bomb, the “Super”. Calculations by Ulam and others, in the late forties, showed that it would not work: the fuel cooled before it could burn. The first Soviet bomb, in 1949, and President Truman's decision in January 1950 to accelerate the programme put Los Alamos under enormous pressure without a viable design.
jo177c7kle: In early 1951 Ulam proposed using the energy of the fission weapon to **compress** the fusion fuel before igniting it, and Teller refined the idea by proposing that the compressing agent be the **radiation** emitted by the primary, contained in a casing. The result, the Teller-Ulam configuration, divides the weapon into two stages: a fission **primary** and a fusion **secondary** inside a **radiation case**. It is, conceptually, the principle of all later thermonuclear weapons (see the diagram).

1ndld6ddwqp: The fireball reached about 5 km in diameter. The cloud rose to about 40 km and spread over more than 150 km. 1ngv8oa21f3: Ivy Mike was carried out three days before the American presidential election, although some government advisers, such as the veteran scientist Vannevar Bush, asked for it to be postponed so as to attempt an agreement with the USSR that would avoid the race for thermonuclear weapons. i6kltqggjk: Mike was much more than a fusion bomb: most of its energy came from the fission that the fusion neutrons caused in the very structure of the device. This combination of fission and fusion is characteristic of thermonuclear weapons; see [[armas-de-tres-etapas|Three-stage weapons]].
138nivecl8i: First Chinese hydrogen bomb: 3.3 megatons over Lop Nur on 17 June 1967, barely 32 months after its first atomic bomb, the fastest leap achieved by any country.
267u4klzmkc: **Test No. 6** of the Chinese nuclear programme was its first two-stage thermonuclear explosion. 22rkkibewm7: China began its nuclear programme in 1955 with Soviet help, but in 1959–1960 the rift between Mao and Khrushchev left the Chinese scientists without advisers, without blueprints and without the promised prototype bomb. n4quhuta1t: The test took place right at the start of the **Cultural Revolution**, when political turmoil was paralysing universities and factories. 26noiajqra9: In the 1960s France was also working on its first hydrogen bomb, and the news that China had got ahead of it caused General de Gaulle considerable displeasure; it is said that he reprimanded his nuclear chiefs. 23qkma19mvt: After Test No. 6, China carried out several megaton-class atmospheric tests until 1980, the last power to abandon atmospheric testing, and continued with underground tests until 1996, when it signed the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (see [[tratados|Treaties]]).

1kwv9nn20fi: For General **Charles de Gaulle**, France's independence demanded a nuclear arsenal of its own, the *force de frappe*, not dependent on the United States. 2dhbicu44wy: The road was long. For years the physicists of the CEA did not hit on the right configuration, while China achieved its thermonuclear bomb in 1967. Some testimonies add that an informal conversation with a British scientist helped confirm that they were on the right track; the United Kingdom never officially shared its designs.
1r8l30gsuu0: The explosion, at low altitude over an atoll, produced significant contamination. Fangataufa was closed to all human presence for some six years, and was not used again for atmospheric tests. France went on carrying out tests in the atmosphere until 1974 and afterwards underground, in shafts dug into the coral, until 1996. kb3ymx9l3y: The health consequences of the tests in Polynesia remain a matter of debate. 160e5fyjnxf: First British bomb that truly worked as a thermonuclear weapon: 1.8 megatons over Christmas Island (Kiritimati), in the Pacific, on 8 November 1957.

zhrc8m49hh: British scientists had worked on the [[proyecto-manhattan|Manhattan Project]], but the McMahon Act of 1946 cut off all nuclear collaboration with the United States. The United Kingdom built its atomic bomb on its own (Hurricane test, 1952) and in 1954 decided to develop the hydrogen bomb too, convinced that without it it would lose its status as a great power and its influence in Washington. There was a hurry: it was expected that within a few years a treaty would ban atmospheric tests.
2bxs4fawesk: The first three Grapple tests, in May and June 1957 over Malden Island, were disappointing from a technical point of view: Short Granite gave about 300 kilotons, very far from the megaton sought, and [[cat-orange-herald-reino-unido-1957|Orange Herald]] turned out to be, in practice, an enormous fission bomb. Meanwhile the physicists at Aldermaston thoroughly reviewed the design and in a few months prepared a new device, Round C.
1q5n5q3n12x: The test was moved to Christmas Island, larger and with an airfield. The United Kingdom had demonstrated a thermonuclear capability of its own. In 1958 the **Grapple Y** tests followed, of about 3 megatons, the largest British explosion in history, and Grapple Z.
1lijl4q4u57: The political effect was immediate. Convinced that the British no longer depended on its help, the American Congress amended the law and in 1958 the two countries signed the **Mutual Defence Agreement**, which resumed the exchange of nuclear information and remains in force. Since then, British weapons have been closely tied to American ones, like the current [[cat-holbrook-trident-reino-unido|Trident warhead]]. The servicemen who took part in the Christmas Island tests, many of them young conscripts, sought recognition for their exposure for decades; in 2022 the British Government awarded them a commemorative medal.

182a3d1ga98: The **RDS-37** was the first Soviet two-stage thermonuclear weapon, based on *radiation implosion*, the same principle that the United States had tested in [[cat-ivy-mike-ee-uu-1952|Ivy Mike]]. 11s7l08w01g: The first Soviet step towards fusion was the **RDS-6s**, nicknamed *Sloika* (“layer cake”), tested on 12 August 1953 with about 400 kilotons. It was a single-stage weapon, with alternating layers of fission and fusion materials around a core, an idea of Sakharov's. It worked and could be dropped, but its design could not be scaled up to the megaton range: it was rather a highly boosted fission weapon (see [[fision-potenciada|Boosted fission]]).
9jewo9ov4f: In the spring of 1954 the physicists of Arzamas-16 arrived at what they call in their memoirs the **“third idea”**: using the radiation of a first fission explosion, contained and channelled, to compress a separate second stage. It was a discovery of their own, although historians debate to what extent intelligence information and the analysis of radioactive debris from the American tests contributed. Sakharov, Zeldovich and Trutnev worked on the calculations, with computing still in its infancy.
uc3msms681: As a precaution, the designers halved the planned yield by replacing part of the fusion fuel with inert material. Even so, the explosion caused more damage than expected: a temperature inversion in the atmosphere reflected the shock wave towards the ground, and in villages tens of kilometres away windows were broken and roofs collapsed. A soldier and a girl died. Sakharov wrote later that on that day he felt for the first time the moral weight of his work. At the banquet afterwards, Marshal Nedelin answered with a barrack-room joke to his toast that the weapons should never be used on cities; Sakharov remembered it all his life.
12njaf8cbw4: The RDS-37 opened the way to the whole Soviet thermonuclear arsenal, including the [[cat-tsar-bomba-urss-1961|Tsar Bomba]] six years later. See also [[programa-sovietico|The Soviet nuclear programme]].
176l48n1vls: Nuclear explosion of 1.4 megatons at 400 km altitude over the Pacific, on 9 July 1962. Its electromagnetic pulse caused failures in Hawaii, about 1,400 km away, and its artificial radiation belts disabled several satellites.
1eymijr0zp1: **Starfish Prime** was the largest nuclear test carried out in space. On the night of **8 to 9 July 1962**, a **Thor** missile launched from Johnston Atoll, in the central Pacific, carried a **W49** thermonuclear warhead to a height of about **400 kilometres**, above the orbit of today's International Space Station. There it exploded with **1.4 megatons**. There was no blast wave and no mushroom, because in a vacuum there is no air to produce them, but its effects reached much farther than anyone expected: an [[pulso-electromagnetico|electromagnetic pulse]] that caused failures in Hawaii, an artificial aurora visible thousands of kilometres away and a radiation belt that damaged satellites for months.

y99x27g0f4: In the late fifties, the military on both sides wanted to know what would happen if a nuclear explosion took place outside the atmosphere: whether it could destroy enemy warheads in flight, blind radars or disrupt radio communications. In 1958 the *Argus* series had shown that the particles from an explosion were trapped in the Earth's magnetic field and formed artificial radiation belts, like the newly discovered Van Allen belts. When the USSR broke the test moratorium in 1961, the United States prepared a series of high-altitude explosions, *Operation Fishbowl*, the most ambitious of all.
cyj6859rjc: The start was eventful. In the first attempt, on 20 June 1962, the Thor's engine stopped shortly after take-off and the missile had to be destroyed with the warhead on board: there was no nuclear explosion, but the debris contaminated Johnston Atoll and the nearby sea with plutonium. The second attempt, “Starfish Prime”, went well.
1br8d1vithq: The night the sky turned red
a8fi6iidlq: In Honolulu, where hotels had announced “rainbow parties” to watch the test, the flash lit the night sky as if it were day for an instant; then a red, green and yellow aurora appeared that lasted several minutes. That artificial aurora, formed by electrons descending along the lines of the magnetic field, was seen from the Samoa islands and as far as New Zealand, more than 3,000 km away.
1k8193rm633: The electromagnetic pulse reached Hawaii, about 1,400 km away. About three hundred streetlights on Oahu went out, burglar alarms sounded, fuses blew and a telephone microwave link between the islands of Kauai and Oahu failed. The damage was modest, because the electronics of 1962 were robust, but it surprised the scientists: the pulse was far more intense than the calculations predicted. Its study, carried out mainly by the physicist **Conrad Longmire**, made it possible to understand the mechanism, which is explained in [[pulso-electromagnetico|Electromagnetic pulse]].
