17ir9y4orj1: The electrons released by the explosion were trapped in the Earth's magnetic field and formed a very intense artificial radiation belt that persisted for years. In the following months at least six or seven satellites, a significant proportion of those then in orbit, suffered damage to their solar panels and electronics. The most famous was **Telstar 1**, the first commercial telecommunications satellite, launched precisely the day after the test: it transmitted the first live television pictures between the United States and Europe, but stopped working in February 1963 because of the radiation. The USSR also carried out high-altitude explosions in 1961 and 1962 over Kazakhstan, with similar effects.
g8qtdbb88m: Starfish Prime showed that a single explosion in space could damage electrical systems more than a thousand kilometres away and render the satellites of any country useless, its own or others'. The following year the Partial Test Ban Treaty of 1963 banned tests in space, and the Outer Space Treaty of 1967 banned placing nuclear weapons in orbit (see [[tratados|Treaties]]). Today, with societies that depend on electronics and thousands of satellites, studies of the electromagnetic pulse and of radiation in orbit still take Starfish Prime as a reference.
nflry3a9wk: In the simulator, an explosion at 400 km produces hardly any effects on the ground: there is no blast wave or fireball that reaches the surface. 1x4i0acj5e4: In 1957 the British designers were not sure that their first two-stage thermonuclear design, the one tested under the name Short Granite, would work. 1li9trscer7: From the experience of Orange Herald came the **Green Grass** warhead, of about 400 kilotons, which was fitted to the interim *Violet Club* bomb and to the first version of the *Yellow Sun*, while a genuine thermonuclear design was on its way. 1d3js733ays: The **Plowshare** programme, promoted from 1957 by the Atomic Energy Commission and by physicists such as **Edward Teller**, promised nuclear “geographic engineering”: opening harbours, canals and mountain passes with a few explosions, extracting natural gas from tight rock, or creating underground reservoirs. Sedan was meant to show how much earth a single charge could move.

Sedan was one of the tests that exposed the largest part of the American population to [[lluvia-radiactiva|fallout]], because an explosion buried at shallow depth throws huge quantities of activated soil and fission products into the air (see [[explosiones-aereas-y-de-superficie|Air bursts and surface bursts]]).
6zsycey4af: That problem was, in the long run, the undoing of Plowshare. sbul43tuz1: In 1944, the scientists at Los Alamos discovered that the plutonium produced in the Hanford reactors was unsuitable for a gun-type weapon like [[cat-little-boy-hiroshima-1945|Little Boy]]: it would have begun to react too soon and the bomb would have blown itself apart with hardly any yield. The only way out was [[implosion|implosion]], compressing a sphere of plutonium with conventional explosives arranged around it in a perfectly symmetrical fashion. It was an unprecedented and enormously difficult technique, and nobody could be sure it would work without testing it. The uranium bomb, by contrast, was considered so certain that it was never tested.
1uiqmxi7cuo: The principle of implosion: a symmetrical compression that makes a sphere of fissile material supercritical.
1ercrzv9a4u: The name of the test was chosen by **Oppenheimer**, who years later attributed it to a sonnet by the English poet John Donne. vlhdgxqy0s: A storm forced the test to be delayed by an hour and a half. 22f6mr63pwi: The physicist **Enrico Fermi** dropped some small scraps of paper as the blast wave passed and, from how far they were carried, estimated on the spot a yield of about 10 kilotons. riae6s01z8: Espionage was decisive. The German-born, naturalised British physicist **Klaus Fuchs**, who had worked at Los Alamos, and other informants such as Theodore Hall and David Greenglass, handed over detailed information on the design of [[cat-fat-man-nagasaki-1945|Fat Man]]. To avoid any risk, Beria and Kurchatov ordered that the first bomb should faithfully copy the American design, even though the Soviet scientists already had ideas of their own for a better weapon. It is said that before the test Beria warned that, if it failed, those responsible would pay the consequences.
27254ik2aby: The USSR did not announce the test. Analysis of the debris confirmed that it was a plutonium weapon, and on 23 September President Truman announced it to the world. The news was a heavy blow: it hastened the decision to develop the hydrogen bomb (see [[la-super|The Super]]) and fuelled the hunt for spies and the climate of McCarthyism in the United States. 1gsymolsxz8: After the RDS-1, the Soviets tested the RDS-2 in 1951, a lighter and more efficient design of their own, and the RDS-3, the first to be dropped from an aircraft. 143zw4l6bcv: In 1957, the USSR undertook to help China develop nuclear weapons, even to hand over a prototype bomb. apeudp37yt: The mission of 9 August was plagued with problems. p2hcwrmgm3: The deviation and the relief of the city, with hills that sheltered part of the centre and the harbour, meant that the destruction was less than it might have been, even though the bomb was more powerful than the one at [[hiroshima|Hiroshima]]. rzsr4wm6vf: On 15 August, Emperor Hirohito announced Japan's surrender by radio (see [[fin-de-la-guerra|The end of the war]]). 213kw5pnjk1: The Fat Man design was the basis of the postwar American arsenal: about 120 Mark III bombs were built up to 1949, and two of them were used in the tests of [[operacion-crossroads|Operation Crossroads]] in 1946. 1t7siear16d: The principle of Little Boy is the simplest of all nuclear weapons: inside the casing there was, quite literally, a **gun barrel**. At one end was a piece of uranium, the *target*; at the other, a charge of gunpowder and a *projectile*, also of uranium. Each piece on its own was subcritical, that is, incapable of sustaining a chain reaction. When the charge was fired, the projectile travelled down the barrel and fitted into the target, forming a supercritical assembly. A neutron source started the [[reaccion-en-cadena|chain reaction]], which released the energy in a millionth of a second (see the diagram and [[tipo-canon|Gun-type weapon]]).
1im1g5yuypv: The gun principle: two subcritical pieces that come together to form a supercritical mass.
odcbarqsco: The method was reliable but very wasteful: only a small fraction of the uranium actually underwent fission; the rest was scattered unreacted. And enriched uranium was the scarcest material in the world: producing it required the gigantic plants at [[oak-ridge-y-hanford|Oak Ridge]], which consumed a considerable share of the electricity of the United States. That is why there was only one Little Boy in 1945. The name, like that of Fat Man, was given by Robert Serber: originally a much longer plutonium gun had been designed, the *Thin Man* (“the skinny one”), and when it was abandoned, the shorter uranium weapon became the “kid”.
26pondrlosw: The parts of the bomb travelled separately to the island of **Tinian**, in the Marianas. The cruiser **USS Indianapolis** carried the uranium projectile and other components; four days after delivering them, on 30 July, it was sunk by a Japanese submarine, and most of its nearly 1,200 crew died in the sinking or were attacked by sharks, in one of the worst tragedies in the history of the US Navy. Since it was common for B-29s to crash on take-off from Tinian with their maximum load, Captain **William Parsons** decided not to load the gunpowder of the gun until the aircraft was in flight: that way, an accident on the runway would not cause a nuclear explosion. The aircraft took off at 2:45 a.m. and Parsons, on his knees in the bomb bay, completed the assembly shortly afterwards.
1ewmfia43qi: Hiroshima was a city of some 300,000–350,000 inhabitants and the seat of a military headquarters, which until then had been spared conventional bombing precisely so that the effect of the bomb could be measured. The [[bola-de-fuego|fireball]] reached hundreds of metres in diameter and the ground temperature beneath the explosion reached several thousand degrees for an instant. The [[radiacion-termica|thermal radiation]] caused severe burns at kilometres' distance; the [[onda-expansiva|blast wave]] flattened almost every building within a radius of about 1.6 km; and the fires, merging into a great firestorm, consumed some 12 km² of the city. In the following weeks the symptoms of [[efectos-en-la-salud|radiation sickness]] appeared. Today, the **Atomic Bomb Dome**, the former Industrial Promotion Hall that was left standing near the hypocentre, is a World Heritage Site.
ykplif8gyl: After the war only a few Mark I bombs were built, and they were withdrawn around 1951: the gun design was too heavy and too costly in uranium compared with implosion. A Little Boy casing without nuclear material is on display at the National Museum of Nuclear Science & History in Albuquerque, and the restored Enola Gay is at the Smithsonian's Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center, near Washington.

xdj9ecd44j: At the beginning of the 1950s, the US Army wanted its own nuclear weapon, without depending on the Air Force, in order to halt with firepower a hypothetical massive advance by Soviet divisions in Europe. The solution was an enormous gun capable of firing a nuclear warhead more than 30 km. The very elongated gun-type design fitted naturally into an artillery shell, although it required the warhead to withstand accelerations thousands of times greater than gravity at the moment of firing. See [[artilleria-nuclear|Nuclear artillery]].
v8enlxokpf: The M65 was a monster: it was transported by two tractors, one in front and one behind, and needed about fifteen minutes to be set up for firing. Among the observers of the test were the Secretary of Defense, Charles Wilson, and Admiral Arthur Radford, future Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. The test was filmed from several angles, and its images, with the shell leaving the barrel and the mushroom cloud rising over the desert, became famous.
2321imoa8o8: Grable also left a scientific lesson. When it exploded at low altitude over desert ground, the heat of the explosion instantly heated the layer of air next to the ground, and in it the shock wave advanced faster than in the rest, forming an advance wave called a **precursor**. 1l28scgd3cc: For decades, Chinese nuclear doctrine was one of **minimum deterrence**: having just enough weapons to ensure that any attack on China would receive an unacceptable response, without trying to match the superpowers. The rocket programme was led by the US-trained engineer **Qian Xuesen**, and Chinese sources attribute the design of the DF-5 to a team headed by **Tu Shou'e**. The deadlines were not met: the Cultural Revolution disrupted the research centres and factories, and the missile took more than fifteen years to become operational. 1afmkqi169q: The B43 was born in the late 1950s, when advances in thermonuclear design already made it possible to build one-megaton weapons less than half a metre in diameter and weighing less than a tonne. It entered service in 1961, when the Kennedy administration and its Secretary of Defense, Robert McNamara, were beginning to replace the doctrine of “massive retaliation” with that of **flexible response**, which called for weapons of different yields in order to respond proportionately to each threat. Being able to choose the B43's yield on the ground, before each mission, fitted that idea.

2eu893d0jxj: In the late 1960s, the United States feared that the USSR would deploy anti-missile defences around Moscow and other cities. One way of saturating them was to multiply the warheads each missile carried. The Minuteman III, deployed from 1970, incorporated for this purpose a **bus**, a final stage which, after the main engines shut down, released the warheads one by one on slightly different trajectories so that they fell on targets hundreds of kilometres apart. The W62, small and light, was designed for that role.

2w9txnum4b: From 1979, some of the Minuteman IIIs received the more powerful [[cat-w78-ee-uu|W78]] warhead, and in the 2000s the W62 was gradually replaced by the [[cat-w87-ee-uu|W87]] from the retired Peacekeeper missiles. acgiul7abh: In May 1972, Richard Nixon and Leonid Brezhnev signed in Moscow the interim **SALT I** agreement and the **Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) Treaty**. The **START II** treaty (1993) aimed to ban multiple warheads on silo-based missiles, but never entered into force. Even so, the United States decided in its 2010 Nuclear Posture Review to leave all Minuteman IIIs with a single warhead, a process that was completed around 2014. In that same year, 2010, **New START** was signed in Prague and the W62 was retired.

ne6fb48626: In the late 1950s, the American Army was looking for a way to offset the numerical superiority of the Warsaw Pact's armoured forces in Europe. The doctrine of the time contemplated using nuclear weapons on the battlefield itself, and the Davy Crockett took that idea to the extreme: a nuclear weapon at battalion level, which could be carried in a jeep and set up in position in minutes to halt a column of tanks in a narrow pass, such as the famous Fulda Gap in Germany.
iuzehrlgj1: Its main lethal effect was not the relatively modest blast but the **[[radiacion-inicial|initial radiation]]**: the intense flash of neutrons and gamma rays would have killed or incapacitated tank crews within a radius of several hundred metres, a distance very close to the range of the launcher itself. The weapon was also very inaccurate, and its use would have required the soldiers to take cover in a hurry after firing.
1zvg6j1q57m: The system was tested with live ammunition in Nevada in July 1962, in the tests *Little Feller II* (static) and *Little Feller I*, the only time a Davy Crockett was fired with its nuclear warhead: the projectile travelled about 2.7 km and exploded a few metres above the ground with about 18 tonnes. Little Feller I was part of military manoeuvres, and among the observers was Attorney General Robert Kennedy. It was also the last atmospheric nuclear explosion at the Nevada test site.
2ebtthtqlse: The Davy Crockett was retired in 1971, a victim of its slight military value and of the risks of scattering nuclear weapons among small units. Its warhead, the W54, had a longer life as a portable demolition charge for special units (the *SADM*, a “nuclear backpack”), in service until 1989. See [[artilleria-nuclear|Nuclear artillery]].
mu64en1kop: A Russian strategic “torpedo”: a nuclear-powered underwater drone with a thermonuclear payload, designed to cross oceans and explode next to an enemy coast. Up to 100 megatons have been attributed to it; independent analyses estimate about 2.
29eu6xldvyb: The **Poseidon**, known at first as **Status-6** (and as *Kanyon* in NATO), is one of the most unusual weapon systems of the nuclear age: an **autonomous underwater vehicle**, the size of a small submarine, driven by its own nuclear reactor and armed with a thermonuclear warhead. Launched from a carrier submarine, it would be designed to travel thousands of kilometres at great depth and explode next to an enemy coast or naval base. Russia presented it in 2018 as a weapon unstoppable by any defence. Its yield is a matter of debate: **100 megatons** have been mentioned, but independent analyses put it at around **2 megatons**.

1u2vdw2p8pn: The system became known in a peculiar way. In November 2015, during a meeting of President Vladimir Putin with military commanders in Sochi, the cameras of two state television channels recorded, apparently by oversight, a slide describing a “multipurpose ocean system Status-6”. The document spoke of a vehicle capable of destroying coastal economic installations and of causing “zones of extensive radioactive contamination” that would prevent any military or economic activity for a long time. Most analysts considered the “leak” to have been deliberate.
g32qnobzc3: On **1 March 2018**, in his annual address to the Federal Assembly, Putin officially presented the weapon with computer animations, together with the [[cat-rs-28-sarmat-ojiva-rusia|Sarmat]] missile, the [[cat-avangard-rusia|Avangard]] glider, the Burevestnik nuclear cruise missile and other systems. The name Poseidon was chosen afterwards in a public online vote.
1cy1bd6x7nm: The declared logic is that of a **retaliatory weapon**: a means of guaranteeing a devastating response even if an adversary managed to intercept Russia's ballistic missiles. Moscow links these systems to the American withdrawal from the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty in 2002 and to the development of missile defences. Since an underwater vehicle does not cross space or the atmosphere, defences designed against missiles are of no use against it. In exchange, it is slow compared with a missile: it would take many hours or days to cross an ocean, so it would be of no use for a surprise first strike, but rather as a last-resort threat.
rggkfu8rea: The myth of the giant tsunami
20rl7pg5e7x: Some commentators on Russian state television have claimed that Poseidon could cause a “radioactive tsunami” hundreds of metres high, capable of submerging whole islands. The scientists who have studied underwater nuclear explosions, including the American tests of the 1950s such as [[operacion-crossroads|Crossroads Baker]], agree that this is impossible: a large part of the energy is dissipated near the point of the explosion, and the waves generated, though destructive on the nearby coast, would be on a much smaller scale than those of the great seismic tsunamis. The truly fearsome effect would be another: a megaton explosion beside a port or a coastal city, with the resulting [[lluvia-radiactiva|radioactive contamination]] from the water and steam thrown into the air.
p41165lzs0: Almost everything known about Poseidon comes from official Russian statements, images released by the Ministry of Defence and open-source intelligence analysis. There is no way to verify its yield, its speed or its degree of development. Nor was it included in the New START treaty, which limited the strategic weapons of the United States and Russia until its expiry in February 2026 (see [[tratados|Treaties]]). Many experts see it as a weapon that is more political than military, intended to show that Russia can get around any defence.

22a78qtl23w: The **Avangard** (“vanguard”) is a nuclear-armed [[planeador-hipersonico|hypersonic glide vehicle]]. Unlike a classical warhead, which follows a predictable ballistic trajectory after separating from the missile, the Avangard re-enters the atmosphere, **glides** tens of kilometres up at a speed of about twenty times the speed of sound and can **manoeuvre** over thousands of kilometres, which makes it enormously harder to intercept. Russia declared it in service in **December 2019**, mounted on silo-based intercontinental missiles.

6bmtx1w4j4: The **UR-100N UTTKh**, a liquid-fuel missile of the 1970s, was chosen as an interim carrier; Russia kept unused examples bought from Ukraine in the 1990s. In the long term, the Avangard is also to be installed on the heavy [[cat-rs-28-sarmat-ojiva-rusia|Sarmat]].
ba30vh8opq: Today's anti-missile systems are designed to intercept warheads that follow calculable ballistic trajectories, or to detect them at high altitude with early-warning radars. A glider that flies lower and changes course complicates both tasks. Its real military value, compared with the already enormous capability of conventional ballistic warheads, is disputed; for many analysts it is above all a political guarantee that Russian deterrence cannot be neutralised. The United States and China are also developing hypersonic gliders but, as far as is publicly known, only those of Russia and China can carry nuclear payloads.

16eu8r6i6q7: The **B83** is a free-fall thermonuclear bomb of **variable yield**, from a few kilotons up to **1.2 megatons**. Since the retirement of the [[cat-b53-w53-ee-uu|B53]] it has been the highest-yield weapon in the arsenal of the United States: its maximum yield is equivalent to about eighty [[hiroshima|Hiroshima]] bombs. It entered service in 1983 to replace several bombs of the 1960s and is carried today by the B-52H and B-2A strategic bombers. The current version is the **B83-1**.

nnxx7rqm0o: At the end of the 1970s, Strategic Air Command needed a modern megaton bomb for its bombers, which could no longer fly high over Soviet territory without being shot down. The new bomb had to be capable of being dropped at very low altitude and high speed, slowed by a parachute, withstanding the impact with the ground and exploding after a delay, when the aircraft was already far away: the technique called *laydown* (see [[bomba-de-caida-libre|Free-fall bomb]]). The Livermore laboratory designed it from 1979 and combined in it the functions of several older bombs, such as the [[cat-b28-ee-uu|B28]], the [[cat-b43-ee-uu|B43]] and the B53 itself.
1r3m71xlcxq: The B83 was also one of the first American weapons to incorporate as standard the safety systems developed after the accidents at [[palomares|Palomares]] and [[thule|Thule]]: an **insensitive explosive**, which does not detonate even if struck or burned in a fire, a core designed not to disperse fissile material in a fire and mechanisms that prevent its detonation without the authorisation codes. The internal design is secret; what is shown in the viewer is a generic diagram.
1sv6kuzbhzl: With the end of the Cold War, the number of B83s was reduced. The original version, the B83-0, has already been retired, while the B83-1 was kept as the American weapon with the greatest capability to destroy large or heavily protected targets, such as command centres buried at great depth. In the 2010s it was planned to retire it once the B61-12 entered service; the 2018 Nuclear Posture Review decided to keep it until a replacement was found, and the 2022 one again announced its retirement. Its supporters in Congress maintain that an alternative against deep bunkers must be available first, and its future remains under discussion.
n6j3igc1w1: The table summarises the evolution of American bombs: from the gigantism of the early 1950s to bombs that are ever lighter, lower in yield and more accurate. That trend reflects an idea that was already apparent after the [[cat-tsar-bomba-urss-1961|Tsar Bomba]]: with good aim, extreme yield is superfluous.

1ms3exbiair: In the 1980s, the combination of accuracy, yield and number of warheads of the SS-18 made the United States fear that the USSR could destroy almost all the Minuteman silos in a first strike, which was called the “window of vulnerability”. That fear justified the development of the MX Peacekeeper missile (with the [[cat-w87-ee-uu|W87]] warhead) and lay behind the American insistence, in the disarmament negotiations, on limiting “heavy missiles”. The START I treaty halved the number of SS-18s, and START II, which never came into force, aimed to eliminate them.

oeec8mbs96: At its greatest extent, in the late 1980s, the USSR came to have **308 silos** for heavy missiles, the maximum allowed by the SALT agreements. Each silo was several kilometres from the next, so that a single explosion could not destroy two at once.
2e469dbqgxm: The break-up of the USSR left **104 SS-18 missiles on Kazakh territory**. Kazakhstan renounced nuclear weapons, the warheads were moved to Russia and the silos were destroyed in the mid-1990s with the help of the American Nunn-Lugar Cooperative Threat Reduction programme. In Russia, the reductions under START I and the ageing of the missiles gradually closed bases until only those at Dombarovsky and Uzhur were left, where a few dozen missiles remain according to the FAS.
1leg17on339: One of the most striking curiosities of this family is its peaceful conversion. The missiles retired under the treaties were transformed into the **Dnepr** rocket, marketed by the joint venture Kosmotras, with Russian and Ukrainian participation, which between 1999 and 2015 put dozens of commercial and scientific satellites from many countries into orbit. It was launched from Baikonur and from the Dombarovsky silos themselves, and took advantage of the missile's own cold launch. The programme ended with the rupture between Russia and Ukraine.
20d8lsx4iy9: The table shows why the SS-18 was so feared: its payload was several times that of the American missiles, which allowed it to carry ten warheads of much greater yield. The United States opted for smaller, more accurate missiles and for distributing its warheads among submarines, such as those with the [[cat-w76-1-ee-uu|W76]] and [[cat-w88-ee-uu|W88]] warheads.
383w6n8qi0: The R-36M2 sums up the logic of the [[carrera-armamentistica|arms race]] of the 1970s and 1980s: the multiplication of warheads through [[mirv|MIRV]] made missiles in fixed silos at once more powerful and more vulnerable, because a single enemy missile could destroy several. That is why disarmament treaties concentrated on heavy missiles, and why Russia, on losing START II, decided to keep them. Half a century after their design, they remain in service waiting for a successor that is reluctant to arrive. See also [[destruccion-mutua-asegurada|Mutually assured destruction]].
dploats08k: The new Russian heavy intercontinental missile, successor to the SS-18. It is meant to carry up to ten warheads of about 750 kilotons, or Avangard gliders. Successfully tested in 2022, its entry into service has been delayed after several failures.
1j239mx63lx: The **RS-28 Sarmat** (after the Sarmatians, a nomadic people of antiquity who inhabited the steppes of southern Russia) is a heavy liquid-fuel [[misil-balistico|intercontinental ballistic missile]] intended to replace the [[cat-r-36m2-ojiva-mirv-rusia|R-36M2]]. It is even larger than its predecessor and, according to Moscow, will be able to carry up to **ten high-yield warheads**, a greater number of light warheads or [[cat-avangard-rusia|Avangard]] hypersonic gliders, and follow trajectories over the South Pole to evade warning radars. The Western press has nicknamed it “Satan II”. This entry simulates one of its warheads, with an estimated yield of about **750 kilotons**.

1tkegbii26f: In the 1990s and 2000s, Russia bet on smaller solid-fuel missiles, such as the [[cat-topol-m-rusia|Topol-M]] and the [[cat-yars-rs-24-ojiva-rusia|Yars]], mobile and difficult to destroy. But the R-36M2, built in Ukraine, was irreplaceable in one respect: its enormous payload capacity. Russian military leaders consider that this capacity is the best guarantee against American missile defences, because it allows them to be saturated with warheads and decoys. Development of the Sarmat, entrusted to the Makeyev bureau, famous for its submarine missiles, began at the end of the 2000s and accelerated after 2014.
hpf0jzlyvs: Its main declared novelty is flexibility. A missile so powerful could follow trajectories impossible for others: instead of crossing the Arctic, the shortest and most closely watched route between Russia and the United States, it could go round by the South Pole. The possibility of a partially orbital trajectory has also been mentioned, an idea that the USSR already tried in the 1960s. None of these capabilities has been demonstrated publicly.
po405glwqy: After years of delays, the first full test took place on **20 April 2022**, in the midst of the war in Ukraine, and Putin presented it as a warning to those who “try to threaten” Russia. In September 2023 the head of the Russian space agency, Yuri Borisov, stated that the system had entered combat service, something that has not been confirmed. In **September 2024**, a new test failed at the Plesetsk cosmodrome: commercial satellite images showed a crater of about 60 metres where the launch silo had been. According to FAS estimates, in the mid-2020s deployment at the Uzhur division (Krasnoyarsk) was still pending or very limited.

8we9coex2q: As with all modern Russian weapons, the design of the warheads is secret, and the figures for yield, range and capacity come from official statements, often propagandistic, or from estimates by independent analysts. What is certain is its scale: a single Sarmat loaded with ten warheads of about 750 kilotons would total about 7.5 megatons, enough to destroy the centres of several large cities at once. Its arrival, together with the expiry in 2026 of the New START treaty (see [[tratados|Treaties]]), forms part of the renewal of arsenals described in [[arsenales-actuales|Current arsenals]].

23a02mxqhit: When the USSR disappeared, a good part of the missile industry was left outside Russia: the R-36M was built in Ukraine and some components of other missiles came from different republics. At the same time, the START II treaty, signed in 1993, aimed to eliminate missiles with multiple warheads. Russia needed a new missile of its own, with a single warhead. The Topol-M, derived from the Topol (SS-25) of the 1980s, was the answer, developed despite the economic crisis of the decade.
29i5b9d7yxk: Among its notable features are a shorter boost phase and a flatter trajectory than those of its predecessors, designed to make detection and interception harder, and protection against the effects of nearby nuclear explosions, such as the [[pulso-electromagnetico|electromagnetic pulse]]. Its mobile version can move through the forests and roads of central Russia, which makes it very difficult to locate and destroy in a first strike.
1cyehaywyzz: When START II was definitively abandoned in 2002, Russia developed from the Topol-M a version with several warheads, the [[cat-yars-rs-24-ojiva-rusia|Yars]], which since 2010 has replaced the Topol-M in production. 1i5krhg732i: The silo-based Topol-Ms were installed in the **Tatishchevo** division, in the Saratov region, in refurbished silos that had housed Soviet liquid-fuel missiles. Making use of existing facilities made a programme born in the middle of an economic crisis cheaper, when the Russian military budget was a fraction of the Soviet one. The mobile version was assigned to the **Teykovo** division, in the Ivanovo region.
1tav1vvh8yq: The mobile launcher is a gigantic eight-axle, sixteen-wheel truck, built by the Minsk wheeled-tractor plant in **Belarus**, one of the few parts of the system not produced in Russia. Each vehicle carries a missile inside a container and can raise and fire it from prepared positions in the forest or from the road itself. In a crisis, the units leave their bases and disperse along patrol routes, so that an attacker would not know where to aim.
1ztgeimormv: A little-known curiosity: the Topol-M and its predecessors were built at the **Votkinsk** plant, in the republic of Udmurtia, west of the Urals, and at its gates lived a small group of American inspectors. From 1988, first under the INF treaty and then under START I, the United States maintained a permanent monitoring facility there which checked, with scales and imaging equipment, every missile container that left the factory. The mission ended in December 2009, when START I expired; the New START treaty that replaced it relied on inspections at bases instead of permanent monitoring. See [[tratados|Treaties]].
1k21op2j3qz: Compared with the great liquid-fuel missiles such as the [[cat-r-36m2-ojiva-mirv-rusia|R-36M2]], the Topol-M represents the other Soviet and Russian school: smaller, solid-fuel missiles that can be launched within minutes and hide by moving. It is the same philosophy that China has followed with mobile missiles such as the [[cat-df-41-ojiva-china|DF-41]].
zyhnlonytl: Current situation and place in history
18mk1ceehwt: The Topol-M was the symbol of the rebirth of the Strategic Missile Forces after the chaos of the nineties, and its mobile launchers paraded for the first time through Red Square in 2008, when the Victory Day parade again included heavy weaponry. Today it is a transitional system: it remains in service at Tatishchevo and Teykovo, but the [[cat-yars-rs-24-ojiva-rusia|Yars]] has taken its place in the factories and, according to the FAS, is expected to relieve it progressively. Its technology also survives at sea, in the submarine-launched [[cat-bulava-ojiva-rusia|Bulava]] missile, designed by the same institute. Its story is that of a missile tailor-made for a treaty, START II, that never came into force.
dwzbvwz2is: The highest-yield warhead of the Trident II missiles carried by American submarines: about 475 kilotons in a re-entry vehicle of less than two metres. About 400 were built in 1988–1989, before the closure of Rocky Flats interrupted production.
1jaxuha2f48: The **W88** is a thermonuclear warhead of about **475 kilotons**, some thirty times the [[hiroshima|Hiroshima]] bomb, mounted in the **Mk-5** re-entry vehicle of the **Trident II D5** missile, the main weapon of the American Ohio-class strategic submarines. It is the most powerful submarine warhead in the arsenal of the United States and, thanks to the combination of yield and the accuracy of its missile, one of the weapons most capable of destroying hardened targets, such as missile silos. Its internal design is secret; only what is public is described here.

16mq6obkyqt: For decades, submarine-launched missiles were less accurate than land-based ones, because a submarine never knows its position as exactly as a silo does. For that reason they were considered retaliatory weapons against cities, while land-based missiles were reserved for hardened military targets. The **Trident II**, deployed from 1990, changed that situation: its guidance system, which corrects the trajectory by observing the stars during flight, gave it an accuracy comparable to that of the best land-based missiles. Combined with the high yield of the W88, it turned submarines into a weapon capable of attacking silos and bunkers (see [[triada-nuclear|Nuclear triad]]).
1d7vhnoown4: Each missile can carry up to eight independent warheads ([[mirv|MIRV]]), although the limits of the disarmament treaties led to loading fewer, often combining one or two W88s with several lower-yield [[cat-w76-1-ee-uu|W76-1s]]. The same missiles are used by the United Kingdom with its own warheads (see [[cat-holbrook-trident-reino-unido|Holbrook]]).
i06pf7mo9w: Manufacture of the W88 began in 1988, but in June 1989 agents of the FBI and the Environmental Protection Agency raided the **Rocky Flats** plant, in Colorado, where the plutonium cores of American weapons were made, for serious environmental violations. The plant never produced again, and the W88 was left at about 400 units, far fewer than planned. For almost twenty years the United States did not manufacture new cores; between 2007 and 2012 Los Alamos produced a small replacement batch for the W88, and efforts are now being made to recover regular production.
1uh8glzr0fx: In 1990 a panel of experts headed by the physicist Sidney Drell criticised the fact that the W88 used a conventional explosive instead of the insensitive explosive of other modern weapons, which is safer against impacts and fires, and that the warheads were arranged on the missile next to the third-stage motor. The Navy kept the design, arguing that insensitive explosive would have required a heavier warhead and reduced the range.
4su7anu8ra: In 1999 the so-called **Cox Report** of Congress asserted that China had obtained information on the design of the W88 through espionage. The investigation focused on the Los Alamos scientist **Wen Ho Lee**, who spent nine months in pre-trial detention in very harsh conditions; in the end he was convicted only of improper handling of information, and the judge apologised to him on behalf of the Government. What China obtained, if it obtained anything, has never been clarified publicly.
18359ds8g8r: As with all modern weapons in service, the internal design of the W88 is secret. The viewer shows the carrier missile and a generic representation of the re-entry vehicle, without any internal detail.
2bm6sijawyi: Penetrating version of the B61 bomb, designed to bury itself a few metres in the ground before exploding and destroy buried bunkers. In service since 1997 on B-2 bombers; its yield is estimated at up to about 400 kilotons.
e9xl2di188: The **B61-11** is a variant of the B61 family of bombs prepared to **penetrate the ground**. Its reinforced casing and hardened nose allow it to bury itself several metres in the earth before exploding. When it detonates below the surface, a greater part of the energy is transmitted to the ground as a seismic wave, much more effective for destroying buried bunkers and command centres than an explosion in the air. It entered service in 1997, replacing the old [[cat-b53-w53-ee-uu|B53]], and is carried by the B-2A stealth bomber.

283na9zctgw: After the Cold War, American military planners became concerned about the deep bunkers that countries such as Russia, China, North Korea and Iran were building to protect their leaders and their weapons. An explosion in the air or at the surface wastes a good part of its energy in the atmosphere; if the weapon explodes after penetrating the ground, the transmission of energy to the ground is multiplied, and the same yield produces seismic effects equivalent to those of a much larger surface weapon (see [[explosiones-aereas-y-de-superficie|Air bursts and surface bursts]]).
1aoo7i6zh0d: The B61-11 was developed in a short time by modifying existing B61-7 bombs, with a more resistant casing and a weighted nose. In tests without a nuclear charge carried out in Alaska in 1996, dropped from aircraft onto frozen ground, it penetrated between two and six metres. The Government presented it as a simple modification of an existing weapon, not as a new weapon, something that was criticised by those who saw in it a distinct military capability.
1epmeekoykl: A 2005 study by the United States National Academy of Sciences recalled a physical limit: no bomb dropped from an aircraft can penetrate the ground deeply enough for the explosion to be contained. A B61-11 would throw large quantities of radioactive earth into the atmosphere, with intense [[lluvia-radiactiva|fallout]], and would not destroy the deepest bunkers. That debate led Congress to cancel in 2005 a more powerful penetrator, the RNEP. The B61-11 remains in service, although its role overlaps with that of the new [[cat-b61-13-ee-uu|B61-13]].
1fdgbbee7ut: The B61 is the longest-lived and most numerous family of nuclear bombs in the American arsenal. Its development began at Los Alamos in 1963 and the first version entered service in 1968. Since then there have been more than a dozen variants, numbered from B61-0 to B61-13, with different yields and uses: tactical bombs for fighter-bombers, such as those NATO has kept in Europe, and higher-yield strategic bombs for the large bombers. The B61-11 was derived from one of the latter, the B61-7, of the mid-1980s.
1jkwuu5d7jx: The decision was taken during the presidency of Bill Clinton, at a time when the United States had stopped designing new nuclear weapons and had suspended its nuclear tests in 1992. In the mid-1990s the Pentagon was seeking to replace the [[cat-b53-w53-ee-uu|B53]], a nine-megaton bomb of the 1960s which, according to public sources, was reserved for the deepest Soviet command centres. In 1996 a senior Defense Department official cited the underground chemical plant that Libya was building at Tarhuna as an example of the type of target for which a penetrating weapon was being considered, a statement that caused controversy and that the Government hastened to qualify.
3t6fiphi9x: The B61-11 was assembled without any nuclear test: the [[pruebas-nucleares|Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty]] opened for signature in September 1996, a few months before its entry into service. For that reason it was insisted that the nuclear “physics package” was the same as that of the already tested B61-7, and that only the casing was new. Critics replied that a new military capability was, for practical purposes, a new weapon.

zzds2dj1dg: The only carrier of the B61-11 is the **B-2A Spirit** stealth bomber, based at Whiteman (Missouri), capable of penetrating defended airspace. The existence of these non-nuclear weapons reduces, according to their defenders, the need to resort to a nuclear penetrator.
1m37vi0zrs2: Estimated at up to about 400 kt
163wmj35pta: No bomb dropped from an aircraft goes deep enough to contain a nuclear explosion. That is why, even if the B61-11 explodes underground, the result is more like a very “dirty” [[explosiones-aereas-y-de-superficie|surface burst]] than an underground test.
182amdiupmf: According to estimates by the Federation of American Scientists (FAS), the B61-11 remains in the arsenal in small numbers, on the order of a few dozen. Unlike other versions, it was not included in the renewal that gave rise to the [[cat-b61-12-ee-uu|B61-12]], and its long-term future will depend on the decisions taken about the B61-13 and weapons against buried targets. In the history of the Cold War and its aftermath, the B61-11 occupies a singular place: it is usually regarded as the first new nuclear capability that the United States deployed after the end of its nuclear tests.

1hspuetw4sk: The most recent variant of the B61 family, announced in 2023: it combines the guided casing of the B61-12 with a much higher yield, estimated at about 360 kilotons. The first unit was completed in 2025.
todd2f9qqw: The **B61-13** is the most modern version of the B61 family of bombs. The US Department of Defense announced it on **27 October 2023** as a bomb of **higher yield** than the [[cat-b61-12-ee-uu|B61-12]], with a yield similar to that of the old B61-7, about **360 kilotons**. It retains the guided tail kit of the B61-12, which gives it great accuracy, and is intended for the B-2A strategic bombers and the new B-21 Raider. The American nuclear security agency (NNSA) announced in May 2025 that it had completed the first production unit, ahead of schedule.

2ae3tiyxoi5: The B61-12, which unified several earlier versions, has a maximum yield of about 50 kilotons. For some targets, such as large military installations or hardened bunkers, American planners considered a greater yield necessary, which until then had been provided by the B61-7 and the [[cat-b83-1-ee-uu|B83-1]], both of the 1970s and 1980s. The B61-13 combines the yield of the B61-7 with the accuracy of the B61-12's tail kit, which makes it possible to attack difficult targets with fewer weapons or with less yield than that of a B83.
1bn1z6qnfpa: The American Government justified the decision by the “changing security environment”, in reference to the growth of the Chinese arsenal and to Russian nuclear threats since the invasion of Ukraine. It was also presented as a way of facilitating the retirement of the B83-1. Its critics pointed out that, although it did not increase the total number of weapons, it contradicted the commitment not to develop new nuclear capabilities.
16mcieaj5tq: As with all modern weapons, the internal design of the B61-13 is secret. Its production has been carried out at the Pantex plant, in Amarillo (Texas), making use of the B61-12 manufacturing chain.
18ki3xi7gh3: The B61-13 was born of a debate that had been running for years. The Nuclear Posture Review of the Joe Biden administration, published in October 2022, announced the retirement of the [[cat-b83-1-ee-uu|B83-1]], the highest-yield bomb the United States had left, and the cancellation of a new nuclear submarine-launched cruise missile. Part of Congress and of the military leadership opposed this: they wanted to keep a high-yield option against heavily hardened targets. The B61-13 was presented, to a large extent, as an intermediate solution: keeping that capability with a more modern and accurate weapon, without increasing the total number of bombs.
2crwwec8og6: The announcement came at a moment of strong tension: Russia had suspended its participation in the New START treaty in February 2023 and had multiplied its allusions to its nuclear weapons during the war in Ukraine, while the Pentagon calculated that China could exceed a thousand warheads by 2030. Congress backed the programme, and development advanced very quickly because it reused almost everything done for the [[cat-b61-12-ee-uu|B61-12]].

zsvsgrdg1l: The B61-13 is a **strategic** weapon: it is not planned to deploy it in Europe, where the B61 bombs assigned to NATO are of the B61-12 version. Its carriers are the **B-2A Spirit** stealth bomber, based at Whiteman (Missouri), and the new **B-21 Raider**, which is to replace the B-2 and other bombers from the end of the 2020s. The first base planned for the B-21 is Ellsworth (South Dakota). Bombers are the most visible and flexible part of the [[triada-nuclear|nuclear triad]]: they can be deployed as a political signal and withdrawn before releasing their weapons.
178bonacorx: Accuracy counts as much as yield: a weapon that lands much closer to its target can achieve the same effect with a lower yield. That is why the defenders of the B61-13 argued that it would allow the B83-1, with more than triple the yield, to be retired.
wuwu6c2x8v: Organisations such as the Federation of American Scientists (FAS) and the Arms Control Association criticised the decision on the grounds that the arsenal already had enough weapons for those targets and because, in their view, it sent a signal contrary to the disarmament efforts of the [[tratados|Non-Proliferation Treaty]]. The Government replied that it was not a new weapon, but a version of an existing family, and that the total number of bombs would not grow.
1jiaj3dqkzf: Whatever the political judgement, the B61-13 marks a change of era: it is one of the few new versions of a nuclear weapon announced by the United States since the end of the Cold War, alongside the [[cat-b61-11-ee-uu|B61-11]] and the [[cat-w76-2-ee-uu|W76-2]], and it comes in a context of rearmament and of [[arsenales-actuales|arsenals]] that are growing again. With it, the B61 family, born in the 1960s, will foreseeably remain in service for several more decades.
249skyanaww: Warhead of about 335–350 kilotons for the Minuteman III missile, in the Mk-12A re-entry vehicle. It was built between 1979 and 1982 and is to be replaced by the new W87-1 on the Sentinel missile.

It is the oldest of the warheads still deployed on American missiles. Its internal design is secret.

1pn7faddqzn: In the mid-1970s, the USSR was deploying its new heavy missiles, such as the [[cat-r-36m-ojiva-unica-urss|R-36M]], in ever more hardened silos. To enable the Minuteman IIIs to threaten them, the United States improved their guidance system and developed a more powerful warhead, the W78, in a new re-entry vehicle, the Mk-12A. The combination roughly doubled the yield of the W62 and improved accuracy, which greatly increased the probability of destroying a silo.
l9cw5wypgu: With the reduction of arsenals imposed by the START and New START treaties, each Minuteman III came to carry a single warhead, although it retains the capacity to carry more (see [[tratados|Treaties]]). Since the mid-2000s, some of the missiles carry the more modern [[cat-w87-ee-uu|W87]], with better safety systems, and the rest keep the W78.
f74spy4zv8: The W78 lacks some of the safety systems that are required today, such as insensitive explosive. After several abandoned modernisation plans, the United States decided to replace it with a newly built warhead, the **W87-1**, based on the design of the W87, for the new **Sentinel** missile, which is to relieve the Minuteman III from the 2030s. Its programme has suffered major delays and cost overruns. In the meantime, the W78 will remain in service, with more than forty years behind it.
4q1sib36n5: In the 1970s, the Minuteman III was the first missile in the world with multiple independently targetable re-entry vehicles ([[mirv|MIRV]]), and the USSR responded by deploying its own MIRV missiles. Both sides began to fear the same thing: that a very accurate first strike could destroy the enemy's silos before their missiles took off. In the United States there was talk of the “window of vulnerability”. The W78 and the Mk-12A were part of the response: giving the Minuteman III the capability to threaten the most hardened Soviet silos while a new missile, the MX Peacekeeper, was being developed.

mqgjqye2jl: The Minuteman IIIs are divided among three Air Force missile wings, with about 150 silos each: F. E. Warren (Wyoming), Malmstrom (Montana) and Minot (North Dakota). Of the 450 silos, about 400 have a missile loaded. Each group of ten silos depends on an underground control centre where two officers stand watch in shifts. The silos are scattered across great agricultural plains, often within sight of farms and roads, separated from one another by several kilometres so that a single strike cannot destroy more than one.
22wgvom9lw9: To check the reliability of the system, the Air Force launches several times a year a randomly chosen Minuteman III from Vandenberg base (California), with a re-entry vehicle carrying no nuclear charge that falls some 6,700 km farther on, at Kwajalein Atoll in the Marshall Islands. These tests are announced publicly and notified to Russia.
1912enpst65: The history of the W78 is also the history of the [[tratados|arms-control agreements]]. START II, signed in 1993, banned intercontinental missiles with multiple warheads; it never came into force, but the United States ended up reducing each Minuteman III to a single warhead to comply with the limits of New START, signed in 2010. That is why, according to FAS estimates, there are more W78s in storage than deployed, and some of them are kept as a reserve for a possible “reload” of the missiles.
kcqbl8jkfn: In 2024 the Sentinel programme suffered a sharp rise in costs that forced the Pentagon to review it under the Nunn-McCurdy Act; the Department of Defense decided to continue it with changes, which delayed the arrival of the new missile and, with it, the retirement of the W78.
vulgd0vadu: The W78 is a survivor of the last great arms race of the Cold War. Designed for a world of thousands of warheads and first-strike calculations, it has remained on alert through the reduction treaties, the end of the USSR and the return of rivalry between great powers. If current plans are met, it will have spent more than half a century in silos on the American plains by the time the W87-1 replaces it.
1wf7afejauw: Thermonuclear warhead of about 300 kilotons designed for the MX Peacekeeper missile and later moved to the Minuteman III. It was among the first with all the modern safety systems, and its design is the basis of the future W87-1.
15nea2s0j1f: The **W87** is a thermonuclear warhead of about **300 kilotons** that was designed for the **MX Peacekeeper**, the most modern intercontinental missile of the American Cold War, capable of carrying ten warheads. When the Peacekeeper was retired in 2005, its warheads passed to the **Minuteman III**, mounted one per missile in the **Mk-21** re-entry vehicle. It is one of the American weapons that incorporate all the modern safety systems, and its design will serve as the basis for the new W87-1. The internal design is secret.

1m2fehvp541: The MX was born at the end of the 1970s as a response to the “window of vulnerability”: the fear that Soviet multiple-warhead missiles, such as the [[cat-r-36m2-ojiva-mirv-rusia|R-36M2]], could destroy the Minuteman silos in a first strike. For years there was debate over how to protect the new missile: it was proposed to move it among thousands of shelters in the desert, or to mount it on trains or aircraft. In the end President Reagan called it the *Peacekeeper* and only 50 were installed, in old Minuteman silos in Wyoming. Each carried ten W87s.
13glq782bl0: The START II treaty, although it never came into force, led the United States to retire the Peacekeeper, the only American land-based missile with more than three warheads. From 2005 the W87s were moved to the Minuteman IIIs under a programme called SERV (Safety Enhanced Reentry Vehicle). Today they share with the [[cat-w78-ee-uu|W78]] the load of the roughly 400 deployed Minuteman.
2c3qwpuq4v2: The W87 was designed after Congress demanded greater guarantees following decades of nuclear weapons accidents (see [[palomares|Palomares]] and [[damascus-titan|Damascus]]). It uses an **insensitive explosive**, which does not detonate from impacts or fires, a core designed not to disperse fissile material in a fire and systems that isolate the weapon from accidental electrical discharges. For that reason its design was chosen as the basis for the **W87-1**, the first newly built American warhead since the end of the Cold War, planned for the Sentinel missile, whose cores began to be produced at Los Alamos in the 2020s.
2bqaay48jww: The airborne component of French deterrence: the supersonic ASMP-A missile, launched from Rafale fighters, with the TNA warhead of up to about 300 kilotons. France conceives of it as a “final warning” weapon.
2fvvgtjh6bq: The **ASMP-A** (*Air-Sol Moyenne Portée-Amélioré*, “improved medium-range air-to-surface”) is a French supersonic cruise missile armed with the **TNA** (*Tête Nucléaire Aéroportée*, “airborne nuclear warhead”), with an estimated yield of up to **300 kilotons**. It is carried by the **Rafale** fighters of the Strategic Air Forces and the Naval Air Arm, which can operate from the aircraft carrier *Charles de Gaulle*. Together with the submarines and their M51 missiles (see [[cat-tn-75-tno-francia|TN 75 / TNO]]), it forms France's nuclear deterrent.

23at7hv5cra: French nuclear doctrine includes a peculiar idea: if an adversary were to threaten the country's vital interests, France could launch a single, limited nuclear strike, a **“final warning”** (*ultime avertissement*), to demonstrate its resolve and restore deterrence before resorting to its whole arsenal. The air component, more visible and flexible than the submarines, is designed for that role: aircraft can take off, show themselves and even be called back. The fighters carrying the ASMP-A are based mainly at Saint-Dizier, in the north-east of the country.
1q9c21z00ri: The missile flies at about three times the speed of sound thanks to a **ramjet**, an engine with no moving parts that compresses air by means of the vehicle's own speed, after being accelerated by a rocket. Its speed and its ability to fly at very low or very high altitude are designed to get through air defences (see [[misil-de-crucero|Cruise missile]]).
1uyqhz4z5zj: The TNA was the first French warhead to enter service without having been tested with a real explosion. France carried out its last test campaign in 1995–1996 (see [[cat-canopus-francia-1968|Canopus]] for context) and has since relied on a simulation programme using supercomputers, the Epure radiography machine and the Laser Mégajoule near Bordeaux, which allow the physics of weapons to be studied in the laboratory. The TNA is based on a so-called “robust” design, conceived so that it could be certified with those tools.
1k3zegxeefp: France maintains an arsenal of about 290 warheads, the fourth largest in the world. In 2025 President Emmanuel Macron opened the debate on the possible contribution of French deterrence to European security (see [[arsenales-actuales|Current arsenals]]).
umpwvmprj5: Sixty years of deterrence from the air
1uy9d1p3ztm: The air component is the oldest part of French deterrence. The **Strategic Air Forces** (*Forces aériennes stratégiques*) were created in January 1964, and that same year the **Mirage IV** bomber went on alert with the first French nuclear bomb, the AN-11. For two decades, doctrine required the aircraft to fly to the target and drop a free-fall bomb, an increasingly risky mission in the face of Soviet air defences.
27hwwlu4t0i: The answer was the first **ASMP**, a supersonic ramjet missile that made it possible to fire from a distance. It entered service from 1986 with the TN 81 warhead, with an estimated yield of about 300 kt, and armed the Mirage IV P, the Air Force's Mirage 2000N and the Naval Aviation's Super Étendard. The ASMP-A, with a longer range and the new TNA warhead, replaced it from 2009. When the Cold War ended, France reduced its arsenal: in 1996 it closed the missile silos on the **plateau d'Albion** and withdrew the Hadès tactical missiles, so that its deterrent was left with two components, the submarines and the aircraft.
1hz2cywkb2w: The cuts continued. In his Cherbourg speech of March 2008, President Nicolas Sarkozy announced that the air component would be reduced by a third and that the total arsenal would fall below 300 warheads. In February 2015, at the Istres base, François Hollande specified that France had **54 ASMP-A missiles** and about 300 nuclear weapons in total, an unusual degree of transparency among nuclear powers.
1j9tt4661jv: The Strategic Air Forces' nuclear Rafales are concentrated at the **Saint-Dizier** air base, in north-eastern France. Long-range missions depend on the **A330 Phénix** tanker aircraft, which replaced the veteran C-135FRs and are based at Istres, in Provence. Naval Aviation maintains a **Nuclear Air-Naval Force**: its Rafale Ms can carry the ASMP-A aboard the aircraft carrier *Charles de Gaulle* when the president so decides, which gives France a nuclear component able to move across the oceans. In March 2025, Emmanuel Macron announced that the **Luxeuil** base, in the east of the country, will host new nuclear-capable Rafale squadrons by around 2035.
1sgqgjzvw6s: Four times a year, the Strategic Air Forces carry out the **Poker** exercise, which simulates a nuclear attack from start to finish: dozens of aircraft take off at night, refuel in flight, get through simulated defences and fire their missiles, in a notional sense. In addition, test ASMP-As without nuclear warheads are fired periodically to check the reliability of the system.
3e5z90026e: France acceded to the Non-Proliferation Treaty in 1992 and in April 1998 ratified the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty, together with the United Kingdom, the first nuclear-weapon states to do so. It also dismantled its Pacific test site and its weapons-material production facilities at Pierrelatte and Marcoule. Because its forces are not subject to the bilateral treaties between Washington and Moscow, the only limit on its arsenal is the one decided by its own government (see [[tratados|Treaties]]).
1r4vvkq7sfm: In July 2025, France and the United Kingdom signed the **Northwood Declaration**, in which they announced for the first time that their nuclear forces, although independent, could be coordinated, and that an extreme threat to Europe would provoke a response from both countries. The air component, the most visible, is the one most often mentioned when a European dimension to French deterrence is discussed.

1lnegemkfm0: The ASMP-A embodies the French idea of a strictly national deterrent, decided solely by the President of the Republic, and at the same time the evolution of that idea towards Europe. It is carried by the Russian **Tu-95MS** and **Tu-160** bombers, which can fire it thousands of kilometres from its target without entering enemy airspace. It is the nuclear version of the **Kh-101**, its conventional twin, and is credited with a thermonuclear warhead of about **250 kilotons**. 29wfasj9f3f: Since the 1980s, strategic bombers no longer need to overfly their targets: it is enough for them to launch cruise missiles from far away. The Soviet Kh-55, the equivalent of the American [[cat-w80-1-ee-uu|AGM-86B]], played that role for three decades. The Kh-101/102 is its successor: larger, longer-ranged and with a shape designed to reflect radar waves less. It flies at subsonic speed and low altitude, following the terrain, and combines satellite and inertial navigation with sensors for the final leg.
22dlx506vt0: In the Russian arsenal, cruise missiles launched from bombers are the air “leg” of the [[triada-nuclear|nuclear triad]]. Bombers are slower than ballistic missiles, but they can take off as a warning signal and be called back, which makes them useful in a crisis.
a9qaohmtej: What is best known about this family comes from its conventional version. The Kh-101 was first used in combat in Syria in November 2015 and, since 2022, Russia has launched it in the hundreds against Ukraine, including attacks on the electricity grid and on urban areas. Recovered remains have allowed analysts to learn details of its construction and its electronic components. Externally, the conventional and nuclear versions are hard to tell apart, a classic problem of “dual-use” systems: an adversary who detects a launch cannot know what warhead it carries.
xa0wnlp193: The predecessor of the Kh-102 was the **Kh-55** (AS-15 *Kent* to NATO), a subsonic cruise missile about 6 metres long that entered service around 1983–1984 on the new Tu-95MS bombers, a modernised version of the veteran “Bear” of the 1950s, and later on the supersonic Tu-160. It is credited with a warhead of about 200 kt. It was the Soviet answer to the American AGM-86B, and its arrival completed the transformation of the bombers of both blocs into stand-off launch platforms.
144tlq3dt2: The collapse of the USSR left this force divided. A significant part of the Tu-160s and Tu-95MSs, with their missiles, ended up at bases in the new Ukraine. In 1999–2000, Kyiv handed over to Russia eight Tu-160s, three Tu-95MSs and several hundred Kh-55 missiles in exchange for settling part of its gas debt; the rest of the bombers were scrapped with the help of the American Nunn-Lugar threat reduction programme. In 2005, the Ukrainian prosecutor's office revealed that, years earlier, a group of traffickers had illegally sold several warheadless Kh-55s to Iran and China, one of the best-documented episodes of missile proliferation of the post-Cold War period.
vudciw3h6o: The Kh-101/102 was developed at the Raduga design bureau from the 1990s onwards, in the midst of budget shortages, which greatly lengthened the programme. The aim was a missile with longer range and greater accuracy than the Kh-55, and with a shape designed to reduce its radar signature.

1ud354rg8iq: Russia's strategic bombers belong to Long-Range Aviation and have their main bases at **Engels**, on the Volga near Saratov, where the Tu-160s and some of the Tu-95MSs are concentrated, and at **Ukrainka**, in the Amur region, in the Russian Far East. The Tu-160 carries up to twelve missiles in two internal bays with rotary launchers; the modernised Tu-95MSs carry about eight under their wings. In peacetime, according to the Federation of American Scientists (FAS), the warheads are not fitted to the missiles: they are kept in storage depots near the bases.
26b2drxu2db: Russia has resumed bomber production: in January 2022 the first newly built **Tu-160M** flew. At the same time, the war has shown the vulnerability of these aircraft on the ground. bswvghuex: In the annual exercises of the Russian strategic forces, such as those known as **Grom** (“Thunder”), the Tu-95MSs and Tu-160s launch cruise missiles without nuclear warheads over test ranges in the north of the country, together with launches of ballistic missiles from silos, mobile launchers and submarines.
17q966h8fyg: Air-launched cruise missiles have almost always escaped the major agreements. The 1987 INF Treaty only banned land-based missiles with ranges of 500 to 5,500 km, not those launched from the air. New START counted each deployed bomber as **a single warhead**, even though it could carry a dozen missiles, which meant that the real bomber arsenals were larger than those declared. Russia suspended its participation in the treaty in February 2023, and it expired on 5 February 2026 (see [[tratados|Treaties]]).

h9i2v6hxwl: The Kh-102 is the most modern piece of the air arm of the Russian [[triada-nuclear|triad]]. Its history sums up that of the bomber force itself: half inherited from the USSR, rescued after years of neglect and renewed in the midst of confrontation with the West. And through its conventional twin, the Kh-101, it has become one of the best-known weapons of the war in Ukraine, a reminder of how blurred the border between a conventional and a nuclear weapon can be.
11xhnj4z8fv: China's most modern intercontinental missile: solid-fuelled, mobile and able to carry several warheads. Unveiled in 2019, it is one of the key pieces of the rapid expansion of the Chinese arsenal.
1lgn12y16dz: The **DF-41** (*Dongfeng-41*; **CSS-20** to the Pentagon) is China's most advanced [[misil-balistico|intercontinental ballistic missile]]. It is a three-stage solid-fuelled missile transported on eight-axle launcher trucks, can travel by road and hide, and carries several independently targetable warheads ([[mirv|MIRV]]). With an estimated range of about 12,000–15,000 km, it can reach any point in the United States. It was publicly unveiled at the great parade of **1 October 2019**, on the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic. This entry simulates one of its warheads, with an estimated yield of up to about **250 kilotons**.

c6f0de4ap3: For decades, China maintained a small arsenal, of about two hundred warheads, and a few liquid-fuelled intercontinental missiles, such as the [[cat-df-5-ojiva-unica-china|DF-5]], slow to prepare and vulnerable. The DF-41, after almost twenty years of development, represents a leap: it is quick to launch, hard to locate and carries several warheads. Combined with the new submarines and bombers, it gives China a true [[triada-nuclear|nuclear triad]].
16fnqej322p: In 2021, independent researchers discovered in commercial satellite imagery three large fields with some 300 silos under construction in northern China, near Yumen, Hami and Ordos. They are believed to be able to house DF-41s or other solid-fuelled missiles. According to the Federation of American Scientists (FAS), the Chinese arsenal now stands at around 600 warheads, and the Pentagon calculates that it could exceed a thousand by 2030. China, which maintains its no-first-use policy on nuclear weapons, does not publish figures.
1uwdnbcaxrr: As with the rest of the Chinese arsenal, the design of the warheads is secret, and the figures for yield, range and number of warheads come from intelligence estimates and independent analysts (see [[arsenales-actuales|Current arsenals]]).
1p195sa5s2c: The origin of the DF-41 goes back to the late 1980s, when China set out to replace its liquid-fuelled missiles with solid-fuelled ones, which can be stored fuelled and launched within minutes. The first fruit of that effort was the **DF-31**, unveiled at the 1999 parade; the DF-41, larger and longer-ranged, progressed more slowly. According to many analysts, the programme gained new impetus in the early 2000s, when the United States withdrew from the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty (2002) and began to deploy missile defences. For Beijing, a mobile missile with several warheads was the cheapest way of making sure that some would get through any shield.
27awfu09qol: Since 2012, the American press has reported, citing intelligence sources, a long series of flight tests, normally within Chinese territory. The Chinese government rarely confirmed them with anything more than a brief note about “routine scientific tests”. The missile's existence was only openly acknowledged with its appearance at the parade of 1 October 2019, in which **16 launchers** with their canisters rolled past.
1f0dpwrh370: The DF-41 is operated by the **Rocket Force** of the People's Liberation Army, the name given at the end of 2015 to the former Second Artillery Corps. Its brigades are organised in regional bases spread across the interior of the country, far from the coasts. The launchers can take shelter in extensive networks of tunnels dug into the mountains, which the Chinese official press once called the “Underground Great Wall”, and emerge to firing positions prepared in advance. Reports have also been published of tests of a version that would move by rail, never officially confirmed.
2esud0584p9: The three silo fields discovered in 2021 were identified by different groups of open-source researchers: **Yumen** (Gansu) by the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies; **Hami** (Xinjiang) by the Federation of American Scientists; and **Ordos** (Inner Mongolia) by an American Air Force studies institute. Pentagon reports indicate that China has probably loaded at least some of those silos with missiles. On 25 September 2024, China launched an intercontinental missile with a dummy warhead that fell into the Pacific Ocean, the first test of that kind towards the open sea since that of the [[cat-df-5-ojiva-unica-china|DF-5]] in 1980. Beijing did not specify which missile it was.
e38hocj1rn: China officially maintains its policy of no first use of nuclear weapons. However, the Pentagon considers that its Rocket Force is preparing for an “early-warning counterstrike” posture, that is, to launch its missiles as soon as it detects an attack and before enemy warheads arrive. Silos and solid-fuelled missiles such as the DF-41 make that shift possible.
1xzclim2uv4: No treaty limits the DF-41. China was not part of New START and in 2019 and 2020 rejected American proposals to negotiate a three-way agreement, arguing that its arsenal was far smaller than those of the United States and Russia. In 2024 it also suspended arms control consultations with Washington, in protest at American arms sales to Taiwan (see [[tratados|Treaties]]).

1bml7rb30uf: Like almost everything in the North Korean programme, the history of the Hwasong-17 is full of unknowns. 19spe0smfpy: By the late 1970s, Soviet air defences made it very risky for a B-52 bomber to overfly its targets. The solution was to turn it into a launch platform: from outside enemy airspace, the aircraft would fire small, low-flying cruise missiles that were hard to detect, guided by a system that compared the terrain relief with stored maps. The AGM-86B entered service in 1982 and some 1,700 were built. monjv361by: On 29 and 30 August 2007, one of the most embarrassing incidents in American nuclear history took place. A B-52 flew from Minot base (North Dakota) to Barksdale (Louisiana) with six AGM-129 missiles that, by mistake, still had their W80-1 warheads fitted. Nobody noticed for about 36 hours, during which the weapons were left without the required custody, parked on the tarmac. The case, together with other failures in the custody of nuclear material, led to the forced departure of the Secretary of the Air Force and the Air Force Chief of Staff and a complete reorganisation of the command of the air-based nuclear forces.

t3g0ad2c9h: Traditionally, Soviet submarine missiles were designed by the Makeyev bureau, in Miass, which specialised in liquid-fuelled missiles. In the late 1990s, after the failure of an earlier project, the Russian government commissioned the new missile from a very different institution: the **Moscow Institute of Thermal Technology**, creator of the land-based [[cat-topol-m-rusia|Topol-M]] and, later, [[cat-yars-rs-24-ojiva-rusia|Yars]] missiles. 24sdmld5lgc: Development was highly troubled. Between 2004 and 2009, close to half of the tests failed; one of them, in December 2009, left a spectacular luminous spiral over northern Norway that was seen from wide areas of the country and went around the world as a “UFO”. The failures led to a review of manufacturing processes and to Solomonov's resignation as the programme's chief designer. Later tests were more successful, and the missile entered service in 2013 on the first Borei, the **Yuri Dolgoruky**.

21o2nm37v4d: Mobility is the Yars's main defence. 6wm888d7oz: The United States has opted to keep all its intercontinental missiles in fixed silos and relies on submarines for the invulnerability of its arsenal. 2ect04k2o03: The Yars is the workhorse of the Russian strategic force in the 21st century. k8jd6qhkpg: Since April 1969, at least one British submarine armed with nuclear missiles has always been patrolling somewhere in the ocean, hidden, in what the Royal Navy calls **continuous at-sea deterrence** (*Operation Relentless*). 10uwkwz0ww0: Since 1972, France has kept at least one missile submarine on permanent patrol, and often two. 1e2whqllfvr: The original B61, designed at Los Alamos in the 1960s, was one of the first thermonuclear bombs with **selectable yield** (*dial-a-yield*): the pilot or the armourer could choose between several yields before the mission. Over the years a dozen versions, tactical and strategic, and more than 3,000 units were built. At the beginning of the 21st century, those that remained needed a thorough refurbishment, and it was decided to take advantage of it to unify four versions into one and reduce the total number of bombs.
84ysxg3414: The guided tail kit allows the bomb to land within a few tens of metres of the intended point, much closer than a conventional free-fall bomb (see [[bomba-de-caida-libre|Free-fall bomb]]). ipfs9hfcaf: The story of the Iskander begins with a sacrificed missile. p7pb6rxbve: A [[explosivos-convencionales|conventional explosive]] carries within itself everything needed to react: fuel and oxygen in the same molecule or mixture. A thermobaric weapon works in two stages. First, a small charge bursts the container and disperses a cloud of finely divided fuel into the air. Then that cloud ignites and burns almost instantaneously using the **oxygen in the air**. Because it does not need to carry its own oxidiser, it can release more energy per kilogram than a classic explosive. The result is a pressure wave that is less sharp but much longer, a large fireball and an especially destructive effect in enclosed spaces (caves, tunnels, buildings), where the pressure is reflected and the oxygen is consumed. Hence the popular name “vacuum bomb”. Its use near civilians has been strongly criticised by humanitarian organisations.

1bapkk9l9z7: For decades the Mk 84 was a “dumb” bomb: it fell along a ballistic trajectory and its accuracy depended on the skill of the pilot and the aircraft’s sight. In Vietnam the first laser guidance kits appeared, the **Paveway** family, which add a seeker on the nose that follows the reflection of a laser aimed at the target, and movable fins that correct the fall. Their limitation was that they needed good weather and someone illuminating the target.
qmebtc1nrx: In the 1990s, Boeing developed the **JDAM** (*Joint Direct Attack Munition*), a relatively cheap kit that replaces the bomb’s tail with one containing a GPS receiver, an inertial navigation system and movable fins. The aircraft tells it the coordinates before release and the bomb guides itself, in rain, at night or through smoke, to land within a few metres of the chosen point. The Mk 84 with this kit is called the **GBU-31**. Its first use in combat was in Kosovo in 1999, dropped by the new B-2 bombers. Since then hundreds of thousands of JDAM kits of various sizes have been made. There is also a penetrator version with a stronger body for attacking shelters.
1krvyeiz1cv: An Mk 84 combines the [[onda-expansiva|blast wave]] of its charge with thousands of fragments from its steel casing, which are flung out at high speed to hundreds of metres. On striking the ground it can open a crater more than ten metres across. It is a weapon designed to destroy solid military targets; when used in dense urban areas, the radius of its effects makes it very difficult to avoid harming the civilian population. For that reason its use in cities, for example in the Gaza war from 2023, has been strongly criticised by humanitarian organisations and in 2024 led the United States to temporarily suspend a shipment of bombs of this size to Israel.
ge6wh1qghl: At about 600 kg of TNT equivalent, it would take some 25,000 Mk 84s to match the energy of the [[hiroshima|Hiroshima]] bomb, and hundreds of thousands for a modern strategic warhead. The Mk 84 also serves as a reference at the other extreme: it is the “unit” of modern conventional air warfare.

5ymp9aeo3b: Many thought nothing would be left, but the astronomer **Peter Jenniskens**, of the SETI Institute, and **Muawia Shaddad**, of the University of Khartoum, organised a search in the desert in December 2008 with dozens of Sudanese students and teachers. They were named **Almahata Sitta**, “station six” in Arabic, after a nearby railway halt. Studying them held another surprise: although most are ureilites, a rare type of meteorite, the fragments include many different classes. The asteroid was a mixture of pieces of different bodies, joined together after ancient collisions.
jh6tdwckr4: It was the first time scientists were able to study both an asteroid in space and its meteorites in the laboratory. ux0t2tuxv: The energy of 2008 TC3 was of the order of a tenth of the [[hiroshima|Hiroshima]] bomb, but released at 37 kilometres altitude, where the air is so thin that the shock wave barely reaches the ground. oiczujh3zg: On 12 February 1947, an iron meteoroid of tens of tonnes broke up over the Sikhote-Alin mountains, in the Soviet Far East, and caused a shower of metallic meteorites that opened more than a hundred craters. It is the largest iron meteorite fall ever observed.
ugj8wqmwon: At around 10:30 on the morning of **12 February 1947**, the inhabitants of Primorye Territory, in the Soviet Far East, saw a fireball brighter than the Sun cross the sky, leaving a smoke trail tens of kilometres long and followed by thunderous noises audible at a great distance. The object fell in the forested mountains of **Sikhote-Alin**, north of Vladivostok. The painter P. I. Medvedev, who saw it from his window, sketched it immediately; his painting later appeared on a commemorative Soviet stamp of 1957.

k1h1hgh17p: Metallic meteoroids are much stronger than rocky ones, but they too cannot withstand intact the pressure of entering the atmosphere at 14 km/s. The Sikhote-Alin one was already fractured and broke up at an altitude of about 6 kilometres into thousands of fragments, which fell in an ellipse of a little over a square kilometre. The largest buried themselves in the ground and opened impact craters several metres across; the smaller ones lodged in tree trunks. Because the body fragmented, there was no single large crater like that of [[meteor-crater|Barringer]], formed by a considerably larger metallic object.
wmasah0ebq: The USSR Academy of Sciences promptly sent an expedition led by the specialists **Vasily Fesenkov** and **Yevgeny Krinov**, which studied the area for years and collected about 23 tonnes of meteorites. The largest, of about 1,750 kilograms, is on display in the Fersman Mineralogical Museum in Moscow. Many others have reached collections and the meteorite market around the world.
1hxi71mn834: The entry energy was of the order of a few kilotons, comparable to that of a small tactical [[arma-de-fision|nuclear weapon]], but it was spread along the trajectory and in the breaking up of the body.
