It is the opposite case to [[cat-cheliabinsk-rusia-2013|Chelyabinsk]]: a small, dense object that reaches the ground almost whole, against a larger, rocky one that bursts high up.
24vau5nigt2: On 15 February 2013, an asteroid about 19 metres across exploded at about 30 km altitude over the Russian region of Chelyabinsk with an energy of about 500 kilotons. The shock wave injured some 1,500 people, almost all by broken glass. Nobody saw it coming.
1rp9hlytcjz: Chelyabinsk is the best-documented cosmic impact in history and the most energetic since [[tunguska|Tunguska]]. It happened in daytime, over a region of more than a million inhabitants, in a country where a great many drivers keep dashboard cameras to have evidence in case of an accident. Hundreds of videos recorded the flash, the trail and, a minute or two later, the arrival of the shock wave. This entry focuses on the data used by the simulator; the full story is in the article [[cheliabinsk|Chelyabinsk]].

vq7z2crrym: The asteroid came from the part of the sky near the Sun, where telescopes cannot observe at night. By coincidence, on that same day another, unrelated asteroid, 2012 DA14, about 30–40 metres across, passed only 28,000 kilometres from the Earth, an approach that had been known for a year. Many initially thought the two were related; their orbits showed they were not.
jv4eg2gkh9: Entering at 19 km/s, the air in front of the asteroid was compressed and heated until it shone brighter than the Sun: some witnesses felt heat on their faces and suffered mild burns to the skin and eyes. The aerodynamic pressure exceeded the strength of the rock, which broke up in several stages between about 45 and 25 kilometres altitude. In the process the body was “flattened” and slowed within a few seconds, converting almost all of its energy into heat and a [[onda-expansiva|shock wave]], as in a very high nuclear [[explosiones-aereas-y-de-superficie|air burst]]. Because the trajectory was so shallow, the energy was released along tens of kilometres of its path.
1g5dt2vrlw9: The wave took between one and three minutes to reach the ground. By then, many residents had gone to their windows to look at the trail. The overpressure was small, far below what is needed to bring down buildings, but enough to break glass, tear out frames and bring down the odd roof, such as that of a zinc factory. A teacher, **Yulia Karbysheva**, who had seen the flash, ordered her pupils to get down under their desks; the classroom glass injured her, but not the children. The wave circled the Earth several times and was recorded by the international infrasound network created to monitor compliance with the [[tratados|Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty]].
23nlwq10ha8: Chelyabinsk changed the perception of the risk from small asteroids: it showed that objects a few tens of metres across, much more frequent than large ones and almost impossible to detect in advance, can cause damage and thousands of injuries. It spurred short-warning alert programmes, such as ATLAS, designed to give days or hours of notice, and reinforced [[proteccion-civil|civil protection]] advice: on seeing a very bright flash in the sky, move away from windows, as after an explosion. It also provided unique calibration data for atmospheric entry models such as the one used by this simulator.
1qnq53iwx1k: At about 500 kt, the bolide released roughly thirty times the energy of the [[hiroshima|Hiroshima]] bomb, comparable to a modern strategic warhead. In the simulator the difference can be seen by simulating a nuclear explosion of the same energy at the height that maximises damage.
1ab76vywt4n: About 50,000 years ago, an iron meteoroid some 50 metres across struck the Arizona plateau and excavated a crater 1.2 km in diameter. It is the best-preserved impact crater in the world and the first whose cosmic origin was proved.
11d2b4wdi24: In the desert of northern Arizona, between Flagstaff and Winslow, lies a large, almost circular hole 1.2 kilometres across and about 170 metres deep, surrounded by a rim that rises about 45 metres above the plain. b13io2f26w: In 1891, the geologist Grove Karl Gilbert concluded that the crater was due to a volcanic steam explosion, because he had not found beneath it the large mass of iron he expected. In 1903 the mining engineer **Daniel Barringer** became convinced of the opposite and bought the land to extract the meteorite’s iron, which he imagined lay buried beneath the floor. He drilled for more than twenty years without finding it. In 1929 the astronomer Forest Ray Moulton calculated that a body at that speed would vaporise and melt almost completely on impact, so there could be no large buried mass. Barringer died that same year, ruined, but right in the essentials: the crater was an impact crater. His family’s name became attached to the place.
229kdnmya2: The definitive proof came in 1960, when **Eugene Shoemaker** and Edward Chao found **coesite** in its rocks, a form of quartz that is created only at enormous pressures, such as those of an impact. Shoemaker had also studied the craters left by nuclear tests in Nevada and saw that the structure of the overturned rock layers on the rim was the same. It was a key step towards geology accepting impacts as a real process on Earth and on the Moon; years later, astronauts of the Apollo programme trained at the crater.
1tnckec0oqk: Ten megatons is of the order of the yield of the first hydrogen bomb, [[ivy-mike|Ivy Mike]] (10.4 Mt), whose crater on Enewetak Atoll measured about 1.9 km across but only about 50 metres deep. The difference is because Ivy Mike exploded on the surface, whereas the meteoroid penetrated the rock before releasing its energy, which excavates far more efficiently. An impact like this today on a city would wipe it off the map within a radius of several kilometres. It is estimated that objects of this size hit the Earth, on average, once every few centuries or millennia, although most are rocky and burst in the air like the one at [[tunguska|Tunguska]].

1e50b6adrlq: On 30 June 1908, a cosmic object some 50–60 metres across exploded over the Siberian taiga and flattened about 80 million trees over more than 2,000 km². It is the largest explosion of cosmic origin in recorded history.
gu3z3dslah: At around 7:15 on the morning of **30 June 1908**, in the basin of the Podkamennaya Tunguska river, in the heart of central Siberia, the few inhabitants of the region, Evenk reindeer herders and Russian settlers, saw a bluish column of light, as bright as the Sun, cross the sky. A flash, a wave of heat and a series of bangs like cannon shots followed. At the **Vanavara** trading post, some 65 kilometres away, a man sitting on the porch felt his shirt burning and was thrown several metres by the blast wave. Seismographs in Irkutsk and other cities recorded the shock, and barographs in Britain recorded the pressure wave that circled the Earth. The article [[tunguska|Tunguska]] tells the full story; this entry summarises the simulator scenario.

up5f1ddz8z: The first scientific expedition, led by the mineralogist **Leonid Kulik**, did not arrive until 1927. Kulik expected to find a large crater and an enormous iron meteorite. Instead he found an unheard-of landscape: millions of trees laid flat in a radial pattern, pointing outwards from a centre where, curiously, the trunks were still standing, dead and stripped of branches, like telegraph poles. There was no crater. Decades later, detailed study of the direction in which the trees had fallen showed that the flattened zone is **butterfly**-shaped, the footprint left by an air burst when the object arrives on an inclined trajectory. The trees at the centre remained standing because the shock wave reached them from above, vertically, and only tore off their branches: exactly what was observed at [[hiroshima|Hiroshima]] beneath the point of the explosion.
2apekj7vidf: The absence of a crater and of large meteorites fuelled all kinds of speculation for a century: a piece of antimatter, a tiny black hole, the explosion of an extraterrestrial spacecraft or even an experiment by Nikola Tesla. None has any basis. The accepted explanation is that a rocky body some tens of metres across, entering at high speed, broke up and was “flattened” by air pressure until it released almost all its energy at once several kilometres up, as in a nuclear [[explosiones-aereas-y-de-superficie|air burst]]. Modern simulations reproduce the shape and size of the devastated zone well. The debate between asteroid and comet remains open, although today most lean towards a stony asteroid. Tiny spherules in tree resin and in the soil have been proposed as possible remnants, and some researchers suggested that nearby Lake Cheko might be a crater from a fragment, a much-disputed idea.
1z2cl1064ee: For several nights after the event, the sky over much of Europe and western Asia glowed so brightly that in London one could read a newspaper at midnight, probably because of dust and ice injected into the upper atmosphere. 1p6yer8ewui: The **DART** probe (*Double Asteroid Redirection Test*), the size of a vending machine with two long solar panels, launched in November 2021. For ten months it travelled towards the Didymos system without braking: its aim was to crash. In the final hours its single camera transmitted ever closer images of Dimorphos, which until then nobody had seen as anything more than a point of light. It turned out to be an oval body covered in rocks and large boulders. On **26 September 2022**, at 23:14 UTC, DART hit it at about 6 km/s. 164ynxizx99: The result exceeded expectations. NASA had set as minimum success a change of 73 seconds in the orbital period; the actual change was about **33 minutes**. 2engu63frx0: If each fission causes, on average, *k* new fissions, the neutron population is multiplied by *k* in each “generation”. The factor *k* decides everything: below 1 the reaction dies out, at 1 it sustains itself (a reactor) and above 1 it grows exponentially.
